Thailand’s US$4.1 Billion Pledge Book, Line by Line

The BOI’s own release is the primary document here, and its structure is worth reading slowly. The agency groups pledges by product category, and three of those categories carry figures that anyone tracking the supply chain should memorize. Battery electric vehicles (BEVs) account for US$1.18 billion across 18 projects. Batteries and energy storage systems (ESS) account for US$1.00 billion across 57 projects. Critical components, meaning drive motors, battery management systems (BMS) and power control units, account for US$373 million across 49 projects.

Those three lines add up to roughly US$2.55 billion, or about 62% of the headline total. The remaining US$1.5 billion or so sits across 74 projects in categories this article does not break out, because the verified figures we hold do not itemize them. The table below lays out what is confirmed and the shares are our own arithmetic against the more-than-US$4.1-billion total, so treat them as approximate.

Look at the project counts before the dollar figures. BEVs draw the most money from the fewest projects (18), which is what you expect from vehicle plants. Components draw the least money from nearly three times as many projects (49). Batteries and ESS sit in between. A pledge book with that shape signals a broad base of mid-sized and smaller component investors rather than a handful of mega-factories.

Why Components Matter More Than Assembly Now

Final assembly is the easiest part of an EV supply chain to relocate. A plant needs land, power, permits and a labor pool. The value-added content is thin if most of the vehicle arrives as imported subassemblies. Components work the other way. A drive motor line, a BMS board or a power control unit requires process know-how, qualified suppliers and long-term volume commitments. Once those exist, they tend to stay put.

That logic explains why governments and investment agencies now brag about parts. A country that hosts only assembly captures wages and a slice of tax revenue. A country that hosts motors, battery management and power electronics captures engineering jobs, supplier ecosystems and some resilience when tariffs or export rules change. The same instinct shows up in the trade fights that Tesla and Samsung are contesting over a US tariff probe tied to Vietnam ahead of a November 29 deadline, where goods are made carries real price consequences.

What the Per-Project Math Shows

Dividing each category’s pledge by its project count gives a rough sense of ticket size. This is our own calculation from the BOI figures, and it is a floor, because the total is stated as more than US$4.1 billion. Averages also hide big outliers, so read the numbers as a texture check rather than a ruling.

A BEV project averages close to nine times the size of a component project. That gap is normal. A vehicle plant needs a stamping, body and paint footprint that a motor or BMS line does not. What matters is the direction of travel. Components are no longer a rounding error in the pledge book. At about US$7.6 million per project, they are the kind of ticket that mid-sized tier-two suppliers can write, which widens the pool of who can participate.

Critical Components: Drive Motors, BMS and Power Control Units

The BOI specifically names drive motors, battery management systems and power control units inside its critical-components bucket, and the choice is telling. These three parts sit at the heart of an EV’s electrical architecture. The drive motor turns stored energy into motion. The BMS watches cell voltage, temperature and state of charge, and it is the main safeguard against thermal problems. The power control unit manages how electricity flows between the battery, the motor and the vehicle’s other systems.

None of these is a commodity bolt-on. Each combines mechanical, electrical and software work, and each carries safety and warranty exposure for the carmaker. Localizing them means a supplier must pass automaker quality audits, run production at predictable volumes and support software updates over a vehicle’s life. That is a higher bar than stamping brackets, which is partly why the US$373 million pledge is smaller than the batteries line today.

It is also why the 49-project count deserves attention. Forty-nine separate commitments in a category this technical suggests that suppliers see durable demand and are willing to commit capital before every volume target is locked. Whether those projects ship on schedule is the open question, and we cover the execution risks further down.

Batteries and Energy Storage: US$1.00 Billion Across 57 Projects

The batteries and ESS line is the second-largest confirmed category, and its pairing is deliberate. Battery factories built for EVs can also serve stationary storage, which gives investors a second revenue stream if vehicle demand swings. A plant that makes cells or packs for BEVs can, with tooling changes, supply grid and commercial storage customers. Fifty-seven projects is the highest count in any of the three confirmed categories.

The energy side of the story is moving in parallel across the region. When we covered VinEnergo’s 22 MWp solar and 45 MWh battery system for three Vietnam EV plants, the point was that factories now plan their power alongside their production lines. Thailand’s pairing of batteries with energy storage in one pledge category reflects the same thinking.

One more detail from the BOI figures: the planned annual domestic production capacity for BEVs exceeds 370,000 units. Set that next to the US$1.00 billion batteries pledge and the US$373 million components pledge, and you get a crude ratio. The component pledge works out to roughly US$1,000 of investment per unit of planned BEV capacity, and the batteries pledge to roughly US$2,700. These ratios are our arithmetic and mix different project timelines, so they only suggest scale. They do show that the supporting industry is being funded at a level that could plausibly serve the planned vehicle output.

Malaysia’s Chery Matchmaking: 35 Suppliers, 4 Agreements

Thailand shows what a pledge book looks like. Malaysia shows what it takes to build one from a thin base. In May 2025, the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) brought together 23 domestic parts suppliers and 12 technology suppliers with Chery. The session produced four commercial agreements covering components, technology transfer and joint investment, according to the reports we reviewed.

Four agreements out of a 35-supplier room is a modest tally, and nobody should oversell it. But the format is the point. Instead of waiting for a foreign automaker to find local vendors on its own, the investment agency put both groups at one table and pushed for contracts. That is a deliberate industrial-policy tool, and it targets the exact weakness that critics raise about Chinese EV investment in Southeast Asia: foreign brands arrive with their own supplier networks and leave local firms on the sideline.

The session happened roughly 18 months before this article. That is long enough that readers should ask what happened next, and the reports we reviewed do not detail follow-on contracts or volumes. We will not guess. The honest read is that matchmaking opened a door and the proof will come when those four agreements show up as shipping parts.

The Local Content Gap: 20%-30% vs Up to 70%

The sharpest statistic in the Malaysian reporting is a comparison of local content. Domestically assembled EVs reportedly carry 20% to 30% local content. Foreign-branded conventional-engine vehicles assembled in the same market carry up to 70%. That is a gap of 40 to 50 percentage points, and it is the plainest measure of how much work localization still has to do.

Why does the gap exist? Conventional-engine supply chains in the region took decades to build. Local firms learned to make seats, wiring, brake parts, exhaust systems and stampings to the exacting specs of established carmakers. An EV removes much of that content. There is no exhaust, no conventional transmission and far less engine-related machining. What replaces it is a battery pack, an electric drive unit and power electronics, which are exactly the items local suppliers have not yet had time to master.

For perspective, El Nasr’s MAGE EV output in Egypt was reported with 45% local content, which sits above Malaysia’s reported 20% to 30% range for EV assembly. Different countries use different measurement rules, so the comparison is loose. Still, it shows that localization targets in the mid-40s are being set elsewhere for early-stage EV programs in other emerging markets.

What Analysts and Suppliers Are Saying

The South China Morning Post’s Week in Asia section ran a piece under the headline “Southeast Asia’s EV boom sidelines local car parts suppliers.” In it, Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, Executive Director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, told the paper: “The supply chain is very different between Japanese autos and Chinese EVs.” His remark addresses Chinese EV investment in Southeast Asia and its limited integration with established local automotive-component suppliers.

In the same SCMP coverage, Adhinegara described the obstacles facing local parts makers who want a place in Chinese EV supply chains: “The biggest barriers are financing, technology and access to manufacturers.” Those three barriers map neatly onto the policy responses we are now seeing. Pledge incentives address financing. Technology-transfer clauses address know-how. Matchmaking sessions like the MIDA-Chery event address access.

On the investor side, BNP Paribas has published an APAC electric-vehicle discussion with several of its executives. Jean-Christophe Vallat, Managing Director and Head of Industrials and Consumer at BNP Paribas, said: “Supply chain considerations are of key importance to the development of the EV market, with significant growth opportunities and geopolitical challenges that will influence the entire industry’s value chain.” In the same BNP Paribas discussion, Giulio Pescatore, Director of Automotive Research at BNP Paribas Exane, said: “The automotive industry is going through one of the most disruptive and transformative periods in its history.”

Read together, the quotes frame a tension. Bankers see opportunity and geopolitical risk in the value chain. Local economists see a risk that the opportunity bypasses domestic firms. The pledge data from Thailand suggests that at least one government is trying to keep the opportunity at home by funding the middle of the chain.

Market Impact: Who Wins and Who Gets Squeezed

Likely Winners

Component makers with existing automotive quality certifications hold the best position. A firm that already supplies motors or electronic modules to conventional-engine programs can pivot faster than a startup. Battery-pack assemblers also benefit, since the 57 batteries and ESS projects create demand for cell handling, thermal management and testing equipment. Suppliers of those tools and materials gain a regional customer base.

Investment agencies that run structured matchmaking also come out ahead. MIDA’s Chery session gave Malaysia a template it can repeat with other automakers. Agencies that simply publish incentive schedules without brokering introductions risk watching foreign automakers import their own supplier base.

Likely Losers

Suppliers tied to engine and exhaust content face the hardest road. As EV share rises, demand for those parts shrinks, and the 70% local content that conventional-engine vehicles reportedly achieve in Malaysia will not transfer automatically to EVs. Firms in that group need to retool toward electric drive components or lose volume.

Consumers and fleets also feel indirect effects. Demand for EVs depends partly on price and incentives. Our earlier look at EV sales falling 23.8% without tax credits showed how sensitive buyers are when subsidies disappear. Localized supply chains can lower costs over time, but they do not remove the need for demand support in the near term.

Competitive Comparison: Thailand’s Pledges vs Malaysia’s Matchmaking

Thailand and Malaysia are pursuing the same goal with different tools. Thailand leads with a large, categorized pledge book. Malaysia leads with brokered introductions to a single automaker. The table compares what each approach has produced based on the confirmed figures.

Neither model is clearly better. Pledges generate attention and signal confidence, but they are intentions and not factory output. Matchmaking produces signed contracts but at small scale. The most credible path combines both: a visible investment pipeline plus structured introductions that turn pledges into purchase orders. Other markets across APAC, including Indonesia, Vietnam and India, are working through their own versions, and the reports we reviewed describe battery materials, powertrains, recycling and localisation as the common themes. We have not itemized their figures here because the numbers were not part of our verified set.

Historical Context: From Assembly Hub to Parts Race

Southeast Asia built its auto industry on an assembly-first model. Foreign carmakers, many of them Japanese, set up plants, brought their own tier-one suppliers and gradually pulled local firms into the chain. Over time that produced the high local-content ratios seen in conventional-engine production today. It took years, and it rewarded patient partnerships between automakers and domestic vendors.

The EV transition scrambles that arrangement. As Adhinegara noted, the supply chain for Japanese autos differs sharply from the one Chinese EV makers use. New entrants bring different supplier relationships, different component architectures and often their own battery partners. Local firms that spent a generation qualifying with Japanese programs find the rules reset.

That is the backdrop for the policy shift now underway. Governments learned from the first wave that landing the assembly plant is not enough. If they want the second wave to leave more value behind, they need to fund motors, battery management, power electronics and recycling early, while sourcing decisions are still being made. The Thai pledge book and the Malaysian matchmaking session are two early attempts at that.

What It Means for Hardware Makers and Buyers

For hardware companies, the component pledges open a real market. Drive motors, BMS boards and power control units are electronics and electromechanical products with long design cycles. Firms that sell sensors, power semiconductors, connectors, thermal materials and test systems to automotive customers will see requests for quotations tied to these projects. The 49 component projects in Thailand alone represent dozens of separate sourcing decisions.

For EV buyers, the effect is slower and less direct. Local component production can trim logistics costs and shorten repair-part lead times. It may also improve warranty service in the home market. But those benefits arrive after factories ramp, and vehicle prices in the next year or two will still track incentives, currency and competition more than localization. Demand for EVs in India shows the same dynamic, as we saw when Mahindra eyed 12,000 EVs a month as demand ran into capacity limits: factory capacity, not just buyer interest, shaped what customers could get.

Risks and What to Watch

The main risk is conversion. A pledge is a statement of intent, and the gap between a BOI-recorded commitment and a running production line can be wide. Delays, changes in demand, shifts in automaker strategy or financing trouble can all stall a project. Anyone using the US$4.1 billion figure should remember it describes commitments, not delivered capacity.

A second risk is concentration. If a handful of foreign automakers anchor most demand, suppliers depend on their decisions. A strategy change at one automaker could ripple through dozens of component projects. That is one reason matchmaking with several carmakers matters more than a single marquee deal.

Third, technology can move faster than factory plans. Battery chemistries, motor designs and power electronics evolve quickly. A line built around today’s design might need retooling before it pays back. Suppliers that invest in flexible tooling and software capability will handle that better than those locked to one spec.

Five Predictions for APAC EV Component Investment

These are our analysis, not reported facts, and they rest on the confirmed figures above.

Matchmaking spreads. Expect more investment agencies to copy the MIDA-Chery format with other automakers within the next 12 to 18 months, since it targets the access barrier that local economists keep naming.

Component share rises. Critical components sit at about 9% of Thailand’s pledge total today. As tier-one suppliers follow vehicle and battery plants, we expect that share to grow in future BOI updates.

Local content for EVs inches up. Malaysia’s reported 20% to 30% range for assembled EVs should move toward the upper end first, because that requires only a few additional localized items rather than a full powertrain.

Recycling enters the headline. With investment emphasis already shifting toward recycling per regional reports, expect recycling and battery-materials announcements to appear beside component pledges in the next round of investment roundups.

Execution becomes the story. Within two years the question will shift from how much was pledged to how much is shipping. Watch for BOI or MIDA data on realized investment and production, which would be a sharper signal than pledge totals.

The Bottom Line on APAC EV Supply Chain Investment

The takeaway: the money is following the parts. Thailand’s more than US$4.1 billion across 198 projects, including US$373 million for motors, BMS and power control units, shows an investment base that goes well beyond vehicle assembly. Malaysia’s 35-supplier session with Chery shows a smaller economy building supplier depth one contract at a time. Both point the same way, toward component localisation as the next phase of the region’s EV build-out.

The numbers still need to turn into factories. Readers tracking this story should watch for realized investment data, follow-on agreements from the Chery session and any change in local-content figures for EVs. Those are the indicators that will show whether APAC EV supply chain investment is building durable industrial capacity or just a strong set of announcements.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much has Thailand attracted in EV supply chain investment?

The Thailand Board of Investment reports more than US$4.1 billion in EV-supply-chain pledges across 198 projects. BEVs account for US$1.18 billion across 18 projects, batteries and energy storage for US$1.00 billion across 57 projects, and critical components for US$373 million across 49 projects.

What counts as a critical component in the BOI figures?

The BOI’s critical-components category covers drive motors, battery management systems and power control units. These are the electrical and electromechanical parts at the core of an EV’s drivetrain and battery safety.

What did Malaysia and Chery agree in May 2025?

The Malaysian Investment Development Authority brought together 23 domestic parts suppliers and 12 technology suppliers with Chery. The initiative produced four commercial agreements covering components, technology transfer and joint investment.

How much local content do Malaysian-assembled EVs have?

Reports put local content for domestically assembled EVs at 20% to 30%. Foreign-branded conventional-engine vehicles reportedly reach up to 70%, which leaves a gap of 40 to 50 percentage points.

Why is investment shifting from assembly to components?

Regional reporting describes investment emphasis moving toward battery materials, electric powertrains, recycling and component localisation. Components are harder to relocate than assembly, create engineering jobs and give countries more control over their supply chains.

Are the pledges the same as built factories?

No. A pledge is a recorded commitment, and the time between pledge and production can be long. Realized investment and output data will be a better test than the headline total.

What do local suppliers say holds them back?

Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies told the South China Morning Post that the biggest barriers are financing, technology and access to manufacturers.

Which sources back the shift to components?

TNGlobal and other outlets report it as the leading regional automotive story. The Thailand BOI figures, the Malaysia-Chery reporting and BMI’s July 2026 APAC autos investment roundup all point in the same direction.

text:
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently announced two negotiated rulemakings to update federal safety standards for vehicle headlights and tires. Negotiated rulemaking is a rarely used regulatory process that gives nongovernmental stakeholders a direct role in shaping regulations. NHTSA appears to be turning to this approach to accelerate long-awaited updates to its safety standards.

Negotiated Rulemaking as a Regulatory Tool

Negotiated rulemaking is a process in which a federal agency convenes a committee of affected stakeholders to try to reach consensus on a proposed rule before it is published for public comment.

Negotiated federal rulemakings emerged in the 1980s, and Congress formalized the process with the Negotiated Rulemaking Act of 1990 (the “Act”). Under the Act, an agency may establish a negotiated rulemaking committee to negotiate and develop a rule if the agency determines that doing so would be in the public interest. That determination in turn considers a number of factors, including whether “there are a limited number of identifiable interests that will be significantly affected by the rule,” and “there is a reasonable likelihood that a committee can be convened with a balanced representation of persons who … can adequately represent” those interests.

Once established, the rulemaking committee “shall consider the matter proposed by the agency for consideration and shall attempt to reach a consensus concerning a proposed rule.” If it does reach a consensus, the committee transmits to the agency a report with the proposed rule. If it cannot reach a consensus, the committee may issue a report “specifying any areas in which the committee reached a consensus,” as well as any other “information, recommendations, or materials that the committee considers appropriate.” Individual committee members may also “include as an addendum to the report additional information, recommendations, or materials.”

Importantly, the use of a negotiated rulemaking committee does not obviate the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act. A proposed rule that comes out of a negotiated rulemaking committee still must undergo the standard notice-and-comment process and is still subject to judicial review.

Though not a common process in the federal government, especially in the last quarter century, negotiated rulemaking has been occasionally employed by other federal agencies, including the Departments of Education, Energy, Health and Human Services, Agriculture, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)—sometimes in response to statutory mandates specifically requiring it.

Negotiated rulemaking has several potential benefits: it gives affected stakeholders up-front involvement in the conception and drafting of the rule; it can help build consensus at the outset of the rulemaking process; it may encourage creative solutions through group interaction; and it can potentially do more to address and resolve objections to a rulemaking early in the process. But the evidence on whether the promises of negotiated rulemaking are borne out in practice is mixed: one study found that the EPA negotiated rulemakings took at least as long as conventional rulemakings, despite the extensive up-front efforts, and that negotiated rules were not less likely to be challenged in court. Other scholarship has challenged these conclusions.

The NHTSA Proposals

In a speech in January 2026, NHTSA’s Administrator previewed that the agency was considering using negotiated rulemaking.

On October 8, NHTSA released a notice of intent to establish a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Vehicle Lighting. NHTSA’s lighting standards, set forth in Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 108, have not kept pace with recent advances in automotive lighting technology. Headlight glare is a common complaint, as modern vehicles increasingly employ LED and xenon headlights that are brighter than the halogen lights used in older models. Glare has been cited as a factor in at least some crashes, although the magnitude of its effects is less evident.

On October 27, NHTSA followed up with a notice of intent to establish a Negotiated Rulemaking Advisory Committee for Tire Safety. Several existing FMVSS set tire safety standards. NHTSA explained that the agency has been considering updates to those tire standards since 2018, and that this would be the “first major overhaul in more than 20 years.” In particular, the rulemaking would consider updating testing methods and setting rules for new designs such as airless tires.

Both negotiated rulemaking announcements proposed similar committee memberships:

Four representatives from equipment manufacturers or retailers;

Two representatives from national motor vehicle manufacturers;

Four representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment manufacturing associations;

Two representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment safety organizations;

Three representatives from educational or research institutions, or testing organizations within the United States; and

Three representatives from national professional engineering associations or standard-setting associations.

The two announcements also provided for similar procedures. Committee members would be nominated and appointed in accordance with the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA). The rulemaking committee would meet publicly approximately four times per year. The committee would be tasked with “developing a detailed term sheet consisting of consensus recommendations to inform the agency’s rulemaking proposal.” NHTSA then would publish a notice of proposed rulemaking “promptly after the committee submits its consensus recommendations, the Secretary approves them either as submitted or in modified form, and after appropriate consultation with the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.” Each committee’s charter would expire after two years, unless the Secretary of Transportation renews it.

Takeaways:

As the saying goes, if you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu. Parties interested in the outcome of these proposals should make every effort to have a voice in the negotiated rulemaking process, either directly or through trade associations or other representatives. Stakeholders not represented on the committee would still have an opportunity to comment on the proposed rules, although committee members would likely have considerably greater influence over their development.

These negotiated rulemakings amount to something of an experiment for an agency that has not deployed the method in decades. In some ways, the subject matter of the proposed actions may be well suited to negotiated rulemaking: the lighting and tire standards are highly technical rules that would benefit from outside expertise and the number of regulated parties—primarily manufacturers of vehicles and equipment—is limited.

The timeline for these rulemakings is unclear. Both proposals indicated that NHTSA expects the committee to “finalize its deliberations and provide its detailed term sheet within the active period of its charter”—namely, two years, though in principle the committees could complete their work more quickly. But following the completion of the term sheet, the agency would then need to draft and publish the actual notice of proposed rulemaking, followed by a public comment period and then completion of the final rule. And there is normally substantial lead time between the publication of an updated FMVSS and the actual compliance date for manufacturers.

text:
Construction is progressing well at the 3.0-GW North Carolina facility as it moves into the equipment installation phase

GREENVILLE, N.C., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Inox Solar Americas LLC, a U.S.-based solar technology and manufacturing company specializing in advanced PV cells and high-performance PV modules, today announced that its planned PV cell manufacturing facility in Greenville, North Carolina, with an annual production capacity of 3.0 GW, remains on schedule to begin production in the second quarter of 2027.

The 515,460-square-foot facility is a key part of Inox Solar Americas' strategy to build a more vertically integrated U.S. solar manufacturing platform. Once operational, domestic advanced PV cell production will complement the company's existing U.S. PV module manufacturing capabilities, providing customers with greater access to U.S.-manufactured solar technology and a more transparent, resilient, and reliable domestic supply chain.

Domestic Manufacturing & Regulatory Compliance

Inox Solar Americas' vertically integrated U.S. manufacturing strategy is designed to provide customers with greater access to domestically manufactured PV cells and PV modules while increasing domestic content across the company's product portfolio. The addition of U.S. PV cell manufacturing will further support customers addressing evolving U.S. domestic-content requirements, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) and Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) considerations, applicable trade requirements, and federal energy-policy provisions. The company's approach emphasizes qualified sourcing, documented manufacturing processes, and compliance readiness to help customers manage increasingly complex procurement and project requirements.

Supply-Chain Security, Transparency & Traceability

Integrating U.S. PV cell and PV module manufacturing will provide greater visibility and control across critical stages of the solar supply chain. Inox Solar Americas is strengthening supplier qualification, component-origin documentation, material traceability, production records, and supply-chain due diligence to support customers seeking greater transparency regarding where and how their products are manufactured. Increased domestic production is also designed to reduce dependence on imported PV cells, mitigate exposure to global supply disruptions and trade-related risks, and provide more reliable product availability for U.S. project pipelines.

Advanced Technology, Quality & Performance

The Greenville manufacturing platform will integrate advanced Galaxion™ monocrystalline PV cell technologies with Inox Solar Americas' U.S.-manufactured Gamma Series™ monofacial and Vega Series™ bifacial PV modules. Advanced automation, precision cell processing, integrated inspection and testing, process controls, documented quality procedures, and production traceability are designed to provide greater manufacturing control from PV cell production through finished-module assembly. This integrated approach will support consistent product quality, high efficiency and energy yield, durability, and dependable performance across demanding U.S. solar applications.

Bankability, Supply Reliability & Customer Confidence

Expanding from U.S. PV module manufacturing into domestic PV cell production further strengthens Inox Solar Americas' manufacturing capabilities and ability to support large-scale, multiyear customer requirements. The company is building greater manufacturing scale, supply continuity, domestic-content capability, traceability, compliance readiness, and product support. Together with product performance, quality systems, warranty support, and a commitment to the U.S. market, these capabilities are designed to strengthen customer, developer, investor, and lender confidence in Inox Solar Americas and the projects its products support.

"Our continued progress on U.S. PV cell manufacturing represents an important step in building a more integrated and resilient domestic solar supply chain," said Ashok Nair, President & CEO of Inox Solar Americas. "By bringing advanced cell technology, high-performance module manufacturing, and rigorous quality control together within our U.S. manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with reliable supply and the bankability required for their project pipelines."

INOX SOLAR AMERICAS

Inox Solar Americas, founded in 2026 in the United States, is a leading solar technology and manufacturing company specializing in advanced monocrystalline PV cells and high-performance Gamma Series™ monofacial and Vega Series™ bifacial PV modules. Inox Solar Americas' photovoltaic solutions are engineered to meet the needs of residential, commercial, industrial, community solar, and utility-scale applications, delivering exceptional efficiency, reliability, and long-term value.

Inox Solar Americas acquired Boviet Solar's U.S. PV manufacturing assets in Greenville, North Carolina, USA, including 3.0 GW of annual PV module manufacturing capacity and 3.0 GW of planned annual PV cell manufacturing capacity, expected to come online in 2027. Through localized manufacturing, resilient supply chains, operational excellence, and efficient logistics, Inox Solar Americas is helping strengthen the U.S. solar supply chain and meet growing domestic demand.

Inox Solar Americas is part of the broader renewable energy platform of Inox Clean Energy and the INOXGFL Group, headquartered in India. Backed by the group's financial strength, business stability, manufacturing capabilities, technological innovation, and industry expertise, Inox Solar Americas is committed to delivering high-quality, reliable, and sustainable solar solutions to customers across the U.S. solar energy market.

For more information, visit: inoxsolar.us, inoxclean.com and inoxgfl.com.

text:
Research effort will explore recycling materials from spent nuclear fuel into fuel for future molten salt reactors.

ABILENE, Texas, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Natura Resources today announced its participation in a Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station (TEES)-led research effort, Turning Nuclear Waste into Fuel with a Thorium Molten Salt Reactor, selected to receive $5.4 million in funding from the U.S. Department of Energy's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E). The funding, provided through ARPA-E's High-performance Optimized Recycled Nuclear Isotopes for Gen IV reactors (HORNIG) program, is part of an up to $50 million investment across eight selected projects to advance next-generation nuclear fuels.

The effort will develop a fuel form compatible with Natura's technology that could help reduce America's spent nuclear fuel stockpile while minimizing the creation of new long-lived radionuclides. The work supports HORNIG's goal of accelerating the commercial deployment of advanced reactors and strengthening America's domestic nuclear fuel supply chain.

"Texas A&M has played an important role in Natura's journey from our company's founding," said Jordan Robison, CEO of Natura Resources. "Our work together through the Natura Resources Research Alliance has established a strong foundation for collaboration, and with the Department of Energy's investment, this gives us another opportunity to turn advanced research into action. With Texas A&M also being identified as one of the proposed sites for our MSR-100, we see this as part of a much larger partnership focused on bringing advanced molten salt technology to market."

"Texas A&M University and Natura Resources have established a strong and successful partnership, and this new project builds upon that foundation. Natura Resources will serve as our technology commercialization partner, contributing not only to research and development but also to data collection, validation, and documentation in accordance with industry standards. This seamless integration of academic research, industry standards, and technology commercialization is a distinctive feature of our project and one of the key strengths of our team," said Lin Shao, Regents Professor of nuclear engineering and associate dean for research in the Texas A&M University College of Engineering.

"America's energy future depends on bold innovation and strong partnerships between the federal government, national laboratories, universities and industry," said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly in announcing the award. "This project demonstrates how we can address long-term nuclear waste challenges while advancing technologies that strengthen our nation's energy security. The Department of Energy is proud to support research that has the potential to unlock new value from existing nuclear materials and accelerate the deployment of advanced reactor systems."

"The Energy Department is delivering on President Trump's vision to unleash an American nuclear renaissance by investing in next-generation nuclear technologies that strengthen our energy independence and bolster our national and economic security," said ARPA-E Director Conner Prochaska. "These projects will help bring tomorrow's reactors online faster and power American prosperity for decades to come."

Over 36 months, researchers and engineers from TEES, Savannah River National Laboratory and Natura Resources will explore how materials found in spent nuclear fuel could be recycled and used as fuel in advanced molten salt reactors. Natura's portion of the work is valued at $1 million. The research could help address one of the nuclear industry's longstanding challenges while creating new opportunities to make better use of existing nuclear material.

Unlike conventional approaches that treat these materials primarily as a disposal challenge, the research will study how long-lived transuranic materials found in spent nuclear fuel could be incorporated into a thorium-based molten salt fuel and consumed in an advanced reactor. The work will help build the scientific and engineering foundation needed to qualify this type of liquid fuel for future reactor use, including understanding its chemistry, performance and compatibility with reactor materials.

The research will begin at Texas A&M using cerium as a non-radioactive surrogate for plutonium to develop and validate methods for understanding the fuel's chemistry, performance and compatibility with reactor materials. The work is then expected to move to Savannah River National Laboratory, where those methods will be validated using plutonium-bearing fuel salts.

Natura will serve as the effort's industrial partner and prospective commercial end user, helping bridge laboratory research and commercial reactor deployment. Natura will help integrate the research findings into reactor design and lead the techno-economic and commercialization work, including evaluating licensing, manufacturing, supply chain and deployment considerations.

About Natura Resources

Natura Resources LLC is a leading advanced small modular reactor developer committed to answering increasing domestic and global demands for reliable energy, medical isotopes, and clean water. Natura's reactors are liquid-fueled and molten salt-cooled, which enhances safety and reduces waste. With the first construction permit for a liquid-fueled reactor from the NRC, Natura has established itself as a leading force in the advanced nuclear industry, fueled by a commitment to support America's energy future. The company is privately owned and has secured more than $120 million in private funding and a commitment of $120 million from the State of Texas. For more information, www.naturaresources.com.

text:
The ceremony brought together local and state officials, community members, and representatives of the project partners. Speakers included Mayor Joshua L. Marsh;Curt Publow, Environmental Compliance Manager of Decatur Hills Landfill; Guénaël Prince, CEO of Waga Energy Inc.; and Allison Gladstone, Director of Business Development at U.S. Energy®, a U.S. Venture company.

Joshua L. Marsh, Mayor of Greensburg, said, "It is great to see additional international investment happening in Decatur County. Innovative alternative energy projects like this show how energy generation can be part of our community while supporting local jobs, encouraging further investment, and contributing to a stronger domestic energy supply."

The facility captures the gas naturally released by decomposing waste at the landfill, which was previously flared, and upgrades it into RNG for the local community. At full capacity, it can process up to 1,000 standard cubic feet per minute of landfill gas and produce approximately 203,000 MMBtu of RNG per year. text:
Brussels, Belgium, 12 October-15 October 2026

Europe’s industrial future depends on its ability to combine competitiveness with climate ambition. Against this backdrop, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) participated in Brussels Climate Week (12-15 October), a leading platform for dialogue on climate action and industrial transformation with thematic days on Technology and Innovation, Energy, Industry, Urban Development and Nature.

This momentum continued at European Sustainable Industry Summit 2026 (13-14 October), by European Business Network for Corporate Sustainability and Responsibility flagship gathering which focused on sustainable competitiveness and business leadership. Through both events, UNIDO contributed its global expertise on industrial decarbonization, clean energy, digital innovation and sustainable industrial development.

Throughout the week, UNIDO experts contributed to a series of keynote addresses, high-level panel discussions, high level interviews and strategic dialogues which focused on advancing the objectives of the European Union’s Clean Industrial Deal, strengthening Global Gateway partnerships. Representing the Organization were Christophe Yvetot, UNIDO Representative to the European Union, Georgia Iordanescu, Chief of the Sustainable Energy and Just Transition Unit, Akos Koeszegvary, Chief, Division of Public Private Partnership, Ms. Anna Jardanovsky, Partnership and Communication Expert, Division of Public Private Partnership, and Eleonora Gatti, Head, Climate Technology Innovation Unit, Division of Climate Innovation and Montreal Protocol, UNIDO.

On 12 October, during Tech and Innovation Day at Brussels Climate Week, Christophe Yvetot joined a roundtable on advancing green digital action, alongside partners from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and the European Commission.

He underscored the importance of international cooperation to ensure that the benefits of the digital transition are shared across regions, supporting the objectives of the EU’s Clean Industrial Deal and contributing to a more competitive and sustainable industrial future. He highlighted the critical role of the private sector in mobilizing investment and scaling impact, referring to UNIDO’s partnerships with Orange and Nokia in Egypt under the EU and Finland co-funded Switch to Circular Economy Value Chains (SWITCH2CE) programme, implemented by UNIDO.

UNIDO’s engagement at the European Sustainable Industr y Summit was framed by the opening high-level plenary, “Europe’s Industrial Reset: A New Mandate for Sustainability Leadership,”. The plenary was opened by Michele Fracchiolla, President and CEO of Hitachi, Jessika Roswall, European Commissioner for Environment, Water Resilience and a Competitive Circular Economy, and Kurt Vandenberghe, Director-General for Climate Action (DG CLIMA) at the European Commission.

Building on these discussions, Georgia Iordanescu, Chief of the Sustainable Energy and Just Transition Unit at UNIDO, joined the high-level panel “Aligning Policy and Scaling up Collaboration to Enhance Energy, Water and Circular Innovation,” where she highlighted the importance of international cooperation, policy coherence and strategic partnerships in advancing industrial decarbonization, sustainable competitiveness and inclusive economic growth.

During Energy Day at Brussels Climate Week, Christophe Yvetot delivered a keynote address on “Clean Energy and Industry: Europe’s Transition in a Global Context.” Reflecting on the global implications of Europe’s energy transition, he noted:

“As Europe accelerates its industrial transition, global value chains must adapt alongside it. Industrial decarbonization cannot end at Europe’s borders. Through cooperation, technology and investment, we must ensure that partner countries are equipped to participate in a competitive and low-carbon global economy.”

At the same time, UNIDO’s contribution extended across both events. At the European Sustainable Industry Summit, Akos Koeszegvary, Chief of the Division of Public-Private Partnerships, and Anna Jardanovsky, Partnership and Communication Expert, joined the Leadership Roundtable on “Local Value Chain Creation and Due Diligence for Responsible Materials Sourcing”, bringing UNIDO’s perspective on sustainable value chains, responsible sourcing and private sector engagement. Reflecting on UNIDO’s contribution, Stefan Crets, Executive Director of CSR Europe, noted: “UNIDO’s engagement in our Leadership Roundtable on responsible materials sourcing brought an essential global and industrial development perspective. Working alongside downstream companies, policymakers and producing countries, their contribution showed how due diligence can become a catalyst for responsible investment and real local value. We look forward to building on this partnership.”

UNIDO’s climate and resilience agenda was further advanced through the participation of Eleonora Gatti, Head of the Climate Technology Innovation Unit, in the IOM roundtable “From Risk to Resilience: Unlocking Investment for Climate Mobility”. Joining representatives from DG CLIMA, the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, she highlighted the importance of connecting climate technology investments with local innovation ecosystems, building local capacity, and strengthening industrial resilience in communities affected by climate mobility.

A highlight of the day was UNIDO’s participation in the Climate Leadership Reception, hosted by the Carbon Trust. During the event, UNIDO exchanged views with Teresa Ribera, Executive Vice-President for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition of the European Commission, on accelerating industrial decarbonization and clean energy deployment, reinforcing the shared commitment to a competitive, resilient and inclusive net-zero future.

Industry Day focused on one of the defining questions of our time: how can countries turn climate ambition into industrial opportunity? Addressing this challenge, Georgia Iordanescu, Chief of the Sustainable Energy and Just Transition Unit at UNIDO, delivered a keynote address highlighting, “What happens after the energy transition? The answer is not a destination. It is a direction. It is electrification plugged into industrial corridors, productive enterprises anchored at energy nodes, and resilient economies that generate value through disruption rather than being destroyed by it. The transition is not an endpoint. It is a way of becoming.”

While Industry Day explored how the energy transition can drive economic transformation, Urban Day at Brussels Climate Week examined how these ambitions can be translated into sustainable and climate-resilient cities. On 15 October, Eleonora Gatti, Head of the Climate Technology Innovation Unit at UNIDO, delivered a keynote address on “District Cooling as a Vital Component of Sustainable Urban Planning.”, calling for cooling to be embedded in urban planning as an essential infrastructure for climate adaptation. She highlighted the growing importance of innovative district cooling solutions in improving energy efficiency, reducing emissions and helping cities adapt to climate challenges while advancing sustainable urban development. Drawing on UNIDO’s experience in Colombia, she illustrated how district cooling measures can translate cooling demand into viable investment opportunities.

Beyond the conference sessions, UNIDO’s messages were further amplified through a series of high-level media engagements. On the sidelines of the events, Christophe Yvetot and Georgia Iordanescu participated in interviews with The Parliament, where they reflected on the interconnected challenges of energy security, industrial competitiveness and sustainable development. Drawing on discussions held throughout the week, they highlighted the importance of industrial decarbonization, Team Europe partnerships and investments that link clean energy deployment with productive capacity, value chain development and job creation.

The week’s engagements strengthened UNIDO’s partnerships with European institutions, industry leaders and development actors, while reinforcing the Organization’s role as a bridge between Europe’s sustainability ambitions and global industrial development priorities. Discussions throughout the week highlighted growing convergence around a shared objective: building competitive, resilient and low-carbon industries that create jobs, foster innovation and deliver tangible benefits for communities worldwide.

text:
In Arizona, where summer temperatures regularly hit triple digits, air conditioning can be a matter of life and death. This year, as the state recorded its hottest summer on record, Diali Avila’s monthly power bill went up to $400, the highest it has ever been.

Avila, the state director for Climate Power, an advocacy group, said the upcoming elections offered voters an opportunity to elect candidates who can ease their utility bills. “People are making the connection: they’re looking at their electricity bills that they get at the end of the month, and then they’re looking at their ballot, and they’re [realizing], this is my moment to take action,” she said.

Avila is among several clean energy and consumer advocates who say soaring bills such as hers – along with broader questions about affordability – could help move votes in November, as Democrats across the country seek to retake control of Congress.

“This midterm election cycle has the potential to become the first election cycle where electricity and utility bills become a top tier national political issue,” said Charles Hua, founder and executive director of PowerLines, a national non-partisan non-profit that aims to modernize utility regulations. “We’re entering a new politics of electricity.”

National average electricity prices have increased about 10%, in the last two years, according to federal figures, and a recent Pew survey found 74% of Americans said they were “very concerned” about gas and energy prices. A new poll from left-leaning Hart Research found that voters in battleground districts ranked utility bills among the three most important issues in the upcoming midterms.

The cost of energy has always been a political issue in America, but historically it has focused on the gas pump, said Hua. However, in recent years energy demands from datacenters, an ageing grid in need of repairs, climate emergencies such as wildfires and hurricanes that further weaken the grid, and the war in Ukraine has pushed up electric bills. (The war in Iran, meanwhile, has raised the price of gas).

Power bills are one part of a broader concern about affordability that has dominated this midterm cycle, said Geoffrey Henderson, who has researched candidate messaging on climate and energy this election.

“Utility bills were already on people’s minds in prior election cycles, but what’s changed is that datacenters are being proposed and advanced at such a fast rate, and there’s been so much community-level opposition to the datacenters that I think it’s elevating the utility bill question,” Henderson said.

In several races, Democrats are tying their opponents to those high utility bills and datacenters.

Ohio

In Ohio, which has the fourth highest number of datacenters of any state, Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate for Senate, has run ads calling Jon Husted, his incumbent, Republican opponent, the “face of datacenters”, connecting his support for the industry to rising electricity bills.

Electricity rates have gone up by 34% in Ohio since 2022, according to state figures, and a new poll from Ohio Northern University found 55% of Ohio residents oppose datacenter construction; 79% believe datacenters will drive up water and electricity costs.

Husted served as lieutenant governor in an administration that offered tax breaks to bring datacenters to the state, but in July, introduced a bill he said would help prevent utilities from shifting datacenter costs on to ratepayers; Senate Democrats blocked the bill, calling it “toothless”. In a leaked memo from 18 August, Republican strategists acknowledged: “More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

“This is an issue that has legs in rural Ohio, and I think it’s going to really help [Brown] close the margin in some of those Republican areas,” said Spencer Dirrig, vice-president of government affairs for the Ohio Environmental Council Action Fund Pac, which backs more regulations on datacenters. “That could be the difference in the election.”

In the state’s tight race for governor, both candidates – Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy – say they would support halting new datacenters until new regulations come into effect. Acton has criticized Ramaswamy for holding investments in the datacenter-related industry, calling it a conflict of interest; Ramaswamy has said he would divest if elected. (Acton herself held stock in companies tied to datacenters, but her campaign says she sold off individual stocks earlier this year to avoid conflicts of interest).

Acton has also said she would appoint commissioners to state utilities who would focus on lowering consumer costs, a move Dirrig says could have a real impact on Ohioans’ wallets. “If you want the clearest possible connection between your vote and your energy bill, it’s who you elect to be governor and who they appoint to be the public utilities chair,” he said. Ramawasmy has not publicly said who he would appoint, and his campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Michigan

In Michigan, the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has sought to tie his opponent, Mike Rogers to DTE Energy, the state’s unpopular, large private utility. El-Sayed has gone after Rogers for accepting donations from the company, which has been criticized for rate hikes and frequent outages as it signs contracts with datacenters. DTE did not respond to a request for comment.

A statewide ballot measure would ban regulated utilities such as DTE Energy from contributing to politicians; El-Sayed has said he supports the measure, while Rogers has not taken a public stance. Rogers did not respond to a request for comment.

“[El-Sayed] has done a good job of making himself an anti-DTE candidate,” said Brian Geiringer, executive director of Ann Arbor for Public Power, which is advocating for replacing DTE with a public utility. “He often names DTE explicitly.”

In Ann Arbor, a ballot measure proposes replacing DTE Energy altogether with a public utility; the city’s mayor and city council have opposed the measure. Despite these headwinds, Geiringer said the measure touches on a resonant theme this election season. “Paying your monthly bill and having your power go out in DTE territory all the time certainly is one of the most salient [examples] of corporations taking your money.”

Arizona

In Arizona’s sixth congressional district, which covers suburban Tucson, advocacy groups have run ads against the incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani, saying his vote for the One Big Beautiful Act would increase residents’ utility bills by more than $200 a year and cut clean energy production. (The $200 figure is based on an estimate from the left-leaning Center for American Progress.)

Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, who is seeking to unseat Ciscomani, supports investments in clean energy and says her “top concern” is that constituents have the ability to pay for energy to cool their homes. In October, the Cook Political Report shifted its outlook on the race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic”.

Starting in 2024, Ciscomani signed letters asking his party leadership to keep some Biden-era clean energy tax credits, but ultimately he voted for legislation that phased them out. (Ciscomani has defended his vote, pointing to compromises that he said would lessen the blow to wind and solar energies).

Since then, hundreds of workers were laid off at an EV factory in his district, and several clean energy projects have been cancelled in Arizona, which could have helped supply energy in periods of high demand, Avila said. “[Ciscomani’s vote] is really affecting not only electricity prices, but also people’s livelihoods and jobs,” she added.

text:
Mexico is emerging as one of the key strategic markets for Cox, a company specializing in energy infrastructure and water management, which plans to allocate an additional US$6 billion to projects in the country between 2025 and 2030. The investment aims to expand electricity generation capacity, strengthen the supply of essential resources, and support industrial growth.

According to an official statement from Cox, the company's Executive Chairman, Enrique Riquelme, reaffirmed this commitment during the 2026 International Economic Forum on Latin America and the Caribbean, organized by CAF. The company seeks to consolidate its presence in Mexico through new energy and water infrastructure facilities, as well as projects linked to the energy transition.

The strategy comes at a time when manufacturing expansion, industrial parks, and rising electricity demand are creating new infrastructure requirements. For Cox, Mexico represents a long-term investment opportunity due to its commercial integration with North America and its renewable energy potential.

Mexico, a Priority Market for Cox's Expansion

According to Agencia EFE, Riquelme explained that the investment plan primarily focuses on new renewable power generation, energy storage systems, and water infrastructure projects. The company also seeks to collaborate with the Mexican government and develop solutions for private companies with significant energy and water requirements.

The US$6 billion investment commitment is part of a broader regional growth strategy. Cox announced investments exceeding US$7 billion across Latin America, including additional projects in Ecuador and Chile.

In Mexico, the expansion is linked to the acquisition of power generation assets previously operated by Iberdrola, a transaction announced at US$4.2 billion.

According to Mexico's Ministry of Energy (SENER), the transaction included 15 power plants with an installed capacity exceeding 2,600 megawatts (MW) and a generation portfolio producing more than 20 terawatt-hours (TWh) annually.

However, the announced US$6 billion represents projected investments for the 2025–2030 period and should not be interpreted as funds already deployed or as a new investment announcement made exclusively in November 2026.

Renewable Energy and Storage to Expand Capacity

According to El Economista, Cox secured projects representing at least 1,000 MW of renewable energy capacity through mixed public-private arrangements with the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE). The company expects these developments to increase its installed generation capacity in Mexico by approximately 38%, reaching 3,600 MW.

José Antonio Hurtado, CEO of Cox México, explained in September 2026 that the projects were expected to operate under 20-year agreements, although further adjustments were still required before formalization.

Water Infrastructure: A Second Investment Priority

According to a Cox statement published in August 2026, the company secured a contract to build the Rosarito desalination plant in Baja California, with an announced contract investment of US$304 million.

The first phase is expected to have a production capacity of 2,200 liters per second, equivalent to approximately 190 million liters of drinking water per day. In a subsequent phase, capacity could reach 4,400 liters per second, making it, according to company projections, one of Latin America's largest desalination facilities for human consumption.

The project is part of Mexico's National Water Plan and aims to strengthen water supply in Tijuana and Playas de Rosarito.

According to the official Proyectos México platform, construction contractually began in September 2026 and is scheduled for completion in August 2029.

According to Forbes México, Cox views Plan Mexico and the country's infrastructure programs as opportunities to participate in strategic energy and water projects, including those linked to new industrial development hubs.

Financing and Execution: Challenges for Expansion

According to Cox de México's third-quarter 2026 financial report, published on October 29, Cox Asset México completed an US$800 million issuance of subordinated hybrid securities in September. The proceeds were used to prepay bank financing associated with its capital structure.

However, investment announcements must be distinguished from projects that have been contracted, financed, or brought into operation. The execution of the US$6 billion investment program will depend on market conditions, capital availability, and the technical and economic feasibility of individual projects.

title: Is long-duration energy storage procurement a hostage to lithium-ion's success?
description:

text:
Energy storage ranks among the premier technologies for supporting renewable energy deployment and enabling grid stability as capacities increase to meet skyrocketing demand. Lithium-ion battery energy storage systems (BESS) have emerged as cost-effective and widely deployed solutions for an array of storage applications, from frequency regulation to peak shaving to interruptions in service.

Researchers caution that this market dominance has a downside in that the relatively short duration of lithium-ion storage is not necessarily most appropriate for long-duration energy storage (LDES) needs. A recent webinar hosted by the Clean Energy States Alliance, a coalition of U.S. state energy agencies, worked to untangle some of the reasons why more appropriate technologies are not being commercialized in certain use cases.

In short, financiers have settled on the bankability of lithium-ion technology, so the fit for every storage need looks BESS-shaped.

According to Will McNamara, grid energy policy analyst at Sandia National Laboratories, LDES generally means those technologies able to provide at least 10 hours of storage duration, out to days, weeks or even months. The purpose of LDES is to be able to handle multi-day weather lulls and seasonal shifts. By contrast, medium duration energy storage is typically eight hours to 24 hours, he said, and primarily used for daily load shifting.

The caveat is that different entities have different definitions. The U.S. Department of Energy, which funds McNamara’s research, not surprisingly supplies its definition of LDES as 10+ hours of storage capacity. At the same time, you will find industry calling technologies with as little as four hours capacity as “long.”

“While we often refer to LDES kind of in the singular, it’s far from a singular technology,” McNamara said. “Within these definitions and these categories, we’re literally talking about hundreds of energy storage technologies that are claiming that they are able to provide this extended duration capability.”

With that said, the U.S. is certainly the world leader in deployed gird-scale energy storage. Citing industry sources, McNamara offered the following statistics:

Of the 1,643 operational energy storage projects worldwide, 49% are located in the U.S.;

As of July 2026, the U.S. has over 50 GW of utility-scale BESS operating capacity;

The U.S. installed 9.7 GWh of BESS in the 1st quarter of 2026 alone, up 32% over the same period last year;

California (60 GWh), Texas (29.2 GWh) and Arizona (20.2 GWh) are the top states in terms of utility-scale storage capacity installed; and

Cumulative BESS operating capacity is projected to reach 200GW/655 GWh by 2031.

“This [expansion] is driven mainly by the utility sector, which will make up about 85% of installations between 2026 and 2031,” McNamara said. “The forecast for energy storage as a general category remains very bullish.”

That said, the market is dominated by technologies, principally lithium-ion BESS, that are considered bankable if not necessarily the best fit for the application. McNamara said that while lithium-ion batteries are commercially mature and economical – and thus acceptable to project financiers – they are still limited to about four hours duration, which is a very generous extension of the LDES label.

At the same time, there is still room for future development. McNamara points out that the BESS-based Tumbleweed Energy Storage project in California has a capacity of eight hours, providing 125 MW for 1,000 MWh. Nevertheless, lithium-ion may not be the most suitable technology for LDES, and there is a lot of research and development work being done on alternative battery chemistries and architectures such as flow batteries.

McNamara points out that the total U.S. installed capacity of LDES under its more conservative definition sits at around 16 GWh of total capacity. Perhaps surprisingly given the milage given to BESS coverage, pumped hydro storage still represents over 90% of this capacity.

“Pumped hydro is really the ‘OG’ of LDES,” he said. “It continues to provide the bulk of multi-day gigawatt scale duration. So, we’re talking about that 10% of the LDES market that is now being developed for other technologies.”

One way to look at future storage technology trends is to evaluate electricity generation plans coming down the pike. This is because existing energy storage technologies tended to develop in tandem with the power sources they support. Jeremy Twitchell, a senior energy analyst at the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), says one of the issues his policy and regulatory team is studying is the near-term use cases for LDES.

“Pumped storage hydropower, still the king of long-duration energy storage, was created to help us integrate nuclear technologies,” Twitchell said. “Nuclear could not ramp up and down throughout the day, so we built pumped hydro storage to help take off that that load following.”

Similarly, understanding what the near-term demands are will help identify what kinds of generation are needed and then what storage technologies will best support these. This is important, Twitchell maintains, because markets and compensation mechanisms then can be adapted to better account for the values of LDES, thus giving them a better chance of success.

“Were not quite there yet,” he said.

A key focus of PNNL’s research is examining how pairings of different generation sources with various storage technologies produce the most efficient and cost-effective outcomes. For example, Twitchell says recent analysis shows combines-cycle natural gas generation combined with any LDES system with a round-trip efficiency (RTE) as low as 60% and still be more efficient than burning another unit of gas to follow the load.

Round-trip efficiency refers to the percentage of energy recovered from storage compared to what was put in. Sandia benchmarks show that lithium-ion batteries have the highest at 85% to 95% RTE. By comparison, flow batteries and metal-air batteries operate at 70% to 80% RTE.

“I’m better off using that long duration storage system to meet my high demand needs than I am using the peaker to meet my high demand needs,” Twitchell said.

The caveat here, he continues, is that four-hour lithium-ion BESS is the most cost-effective way of doing this now, yielding the highest returns. Eight-hour storage systems, while cost-effective, are not as cost-effective as four-hour systems. Ten-hour systems were very close to penciling out, but still: not yet.

“This analysis finds some indicators for LDES to meet this particular use case for improving the economics of base generators,” Twichell said. “We need to see some improvements in round-trip efficiency.”

Such improvements in LDES efficiency are not just needed for the overall effectiveness of the grid infrastructure but to enable financing for the sorts of storage technologies that can support base generation over prolonged periods, such as in the face of adverse weather conditions or other long-term emergencies.

Anna Siefken, director for North American policy and markets at the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, an industry trade organization, says technology development is not really the obstacle to commercial LDES deployment. Rather, bankability is a major issue again largely because of the market dominance of lithium-ion batteries serving many storage functions.

“Bankability really describes a project’s expected revenue, the risk profile and the technology performance that gives lenders and insurers the certainty that they need to make the investments,” Siefken said. “Many competing technologies; some chemical, some thermal, some mechanical; are fit for purpose. Some of them, like vanadium flow batteries, have been around for dozens of years. There are companies that have many, many deployments in other countries outside of the U.S.”

One challenge is communicating the information. The LDES Council publishes a number of reports for making apples-to-apples comparisons between different LDES technologies in various use cases. Ideally, such resources could help utility planners evaluate existing options they may not be aware of and financiers see examples of real-world deployments.

Another hurdle is getting governments and regulatory bodies to address policy frameworks that recognize LDES value. According to Sandia, U.S. electricity markets and capacity mechanisms compensate utilities for short-term power delivery, not the ability to continuously serve a load for multiple days. Siefken says her organization is seeing some promising movement on the policy front.

“There’s going to be a wave of state legislative sessions that are opening in early 2027, and we’ve seen dockets that are ready to go to talk about LDES procurements and carve-outs specifically for eight hours and longer,” she said.

title: Colorado methane pollution rules won't change — even if federal regulations are rolled back
authors: Mark Jaffe, Mark Jaffe Freelance journalist
description:

text:
The Trump administration has proposed a sweeping rollback of federal rules to cut methane emissions from oil and gas operations, but that regulatory broom won’t reach Colorado, which has its own controls on the pollutant.

In September, the Colorado Air Quality Control Commission finished two years of rulemaking aimed at reducing oil and gas methane emissions, including adopting most of the Biden administration’s Environmental Protection Agency rules that the Trump administration seeks to overturn.

The Colorado Energy and Carbon Management Commission has also banned venting or burning off methane — flaring — at well sites save for emergencies. The commission also set limits for fugitive emissions.

“Our rules are all now in state statute and state regulation, regardless of what happens at the federal level,” said Stefanie Shoup, the Air Pollution Control Division deputy director for regulatory affairs. “We feel strongly that we have all of the protections that are appropriate.”

Cyrus Western, the EPA administrator of Denver-based Region 8, which covers Colorado and five other mountain and plains states, agreed Colorado was a special case.

“In Colorado, you guys have got your own state regulatory framework for some of those issues,” Western said.

Methane is 80 times more potent as a greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide over the first 20 years. It begins to dissipate after that. The gas is also a component of ozone pollution.

Russia is the world’s largest methane emitter, followed closely by the United States, according to the International Energy Agency. In Colorado, the oil and gas industry accounts for 60% of the state’s methane emissions.

The Trump administration wants to relax regulations cutting emissions from “marginal” wells, which produce less than the equivalent of 15 barrels of oil a day. These wells produce 7% of domestic oil and gas, and about half the industry’s methane.

In Colorado, marginal wells make up 67% of all the wells in the state, almost 30,000 wells, according to Colorado State University analysis.

Marginal wells will continue to be regulated in Colorado under state laws that seek to curb emissions from wells and equipment and reduce overall emissions.

The Trump EPA is also proposing to allow flaring and the use of methane-powered pneumatic controllers — devices widely used to manage temperatures, pressure and liquid levels at oil and gas facilities and drill pads. The Biden rules limited both.

The proposed rule — which is now open for a 45-day public comment period — would require flaring to destroy 95% of the methane and that the controller gases be run through a pollution control device that would destroy 95% of the gas.

Beginning in 2021, the Colorado Air Quality Control Commission started requiring the use of nonpolluting controllers, first in new and retrofitted oil and gas sites and then phasing out of all polluting controllers, pumps and compressors by 2027 in areas suffering from ozone pollution and by 2029 for the rest of the state.

EPA’s Western said the administration is trying to balance economics and the environment.

”We can engage in high standards of environmental regulation while simultaneously allowing industry to fulfill their business models and create these really good middle-class jobs,” he said.

A problem with the Biden rules, Western said, is that “affected everybody, from the littlest guy to the biggest guy, and it really did increase their cost of compliance.”

“For a lot of these small mom-and-pop operators, if the 2024 rules went into full effect, it would seriously hurt their ability to operate or even to exist at all,” Western said. The Trump administration estimates that revised regulations would save $45 billion.

Critics do not see it that way. “At a time when Americans are struggling with energy prices, the Trump administration is going out of its way to allow industry to pollute with zero safeguards,” Ramesh Bhatt, chair of Colorado Sierra Club’s Conservation Committee, said in a statement.

In several ways, Colorado’s rules go beyond the EPA regulations with more extensive requirements for controls on storage tanks and continuous monitoring requirements for certain enclosed areas.

The state has also adopted the first-in-the-nation rule tying oil and gas production to methane emissions. The goal is to reduce the methane emitted for each unit of oil and gas produced, with the goal of ratcheting down the permissible level. Even marginal wells participate in this program.

“Colorado has pretty robust regulations around methane,” Nini Gu, senior regulatory and legislative manager at the Environmental Defense Fund, a national advocacy and policy group. “What Colorado has done is to go above and beyond federal level regulation.”
