name: EVs
title: One Year Without EV Tax Credits: 4 Key Takeaways - www.EV-ROUTE.com
description:
“In general, the EV market has been perhaps more resilient in some ways than we would maybe expect,” Tyson Jominy, JD Power’s senior vice president of data and analytics, told me.
JD Power puts September’s EV share of retail sales at 7.9%.
Between the second and third quarters, overall EV sales in the U.S. grew by 6.1% to hit some 262,000 units, their highest level since the tax credit ended, Cox Automotive says.
While Hyundai is investing heavily in various types of hybrids to buck the EV slowdown, Muñoz sees a future for electric cars in America too.
“What you see everywhere when you look at the trends in the market, EV is there to stay,” he told me.
text:
It’s been a year and change since the biggest shock America’s electric car market has ever seen. The $7,500 EV tax credit met its untimely demise on September 30, 2025, as the Trump administration and Congress also axed fuel economy regulations and other policies pushing EVs along.

So, a year after the great EV reset, what’s changed?

The EV Market Is Bouncing Back, Slowly

EV sales cratered at the end of last year—not just just because a big incentive to buy one abruptly vanished, but also because so many Americans had rushed to get one while the getting was good. In September of 2025, the electric share of retail car sales soared to over 14%, according to data from JD Power. In October, that plunged to 7.1%, but the pain wasn’t through. By November, just 5% of retail sales were battery-powered, a level not seen since 2022.

“That was something that nobody expected, and it made very important and sudden changes in the market, and for us too, right?” Hyundai CEO José Muñoz told me last month. “All of a sudden, you either add the incentive, or you lose sales, or you do something in between.”

It wasn’t clear how quickly or to what degree things would bounce back. But the market is showing new signs of life and has started to gradually rebound.

“In general, the EV market has been perhaps more resilient in some ways than we would maybe expect,” Tyson Jominy, JD Power’s senior vice president of data and analytics, told me. “Sales certainly fell as expected, but we kind of hit the floor quickly.”

Hyundai CEO José Muñoz says dealers started asking for more Ioniq 5s once the war in Iran raised the price of gas.

Photo by: Suvrat Kothari

Share bounced back over 6% in December, and climbed to over 8% in May, the firm says. JD Power puts September’s EV share of retail sales at 7.9%. “We only went back about two years,” Jominy said, “which doesn’t seem so bad.”

While high gas prices haven’t produced a big spike in sales like they have in other global markets, anecdotally they may be helping on the margins. Muñoz said Hyundai dealers who had been asking the company to dial back shipments of Ioniq 5s suddenly started asking for more of them after the war in Iran started.

There are other signs of a normalizing market. The number of days EVs are spending on dealer lots has dropped every month from April through September, according to data shared by Cars.com. In September, it took 89.4 days for the average EV to sell, down from 115.6 days in March and only slightly higher than the 80.5 days seen during last year’s EV-buying frenzy.

“That, I think, is showing that we're getting closer to the moment where the demand and the supply are in good balance,” Jenni Newman, the vehicle marketplace’s editor-in-chief, told me.

Tesla And Rivian Are Carrying The Team

That’s the macro picture. But the recovery is far from evenly distributed. A few automakers, notably Tesla and Rivian, are carrying much of the industry’s comeback.

Between the second and third quarters, overall EV sales in the U.S. grew by 6.1% to hit some 262,000 units, their highest level since the tax credit ended, Cox Automotive says. Take Tesla out of the equation, though, and the market would have shrunk slightly instead, according to the firm’s sales estimates. (Tesla doesn’t break out its regional sales.) On a year-over-year basis, Tesla’s sales fell 19.7% in Q3, Cox says, while the market as a whole contracted by close to 40%. It means Tesla’s share of the EV market is back up above 50%.

“Tesla has pretty much withstood the decline we've seen among the non-disruptors,” said Tom Libby, director of loyalty solutions and industry analysis at Mobility Global.

Tesla has weathered the EV slowdown better than most, and it's back up over 50% of America's electric car market.

Photo by: Patrick George

In part, that’s because Tesla has built a great product that people keep coming back to. Around half of Model Y owners get another one as their next vehicle, Libby said, while model-level loyalty across the board lands at 26%. At Rivian, deliveries have surged this year on the back of the new R2, one of the best all-around Model Y rivals in years and its first product with mainstream potential.

There’s another big reason for the divide: EV-only manufacturers couldn’t simply pivot to gas models when the policies shifted like other manufacturers did. Since last year, legacy automakers have canceled or delayed some two-dozen electric models, like the Ford F-150 Lightning, Volkswagen ID.4, and Honda Prologue. The product vacuum was bound to hurt sales, but cutting back on EVs also makes perfect sense as a reaction to looser regulations and changing incentives.

“A lot of people, myself included, tend to forget that the manufacturers are not really in business to make cars,” Libby said. “They're in business to make money.”

While many legacy players struggle to regain momentum, Toyota is a notable outlier, having steadily grown EV sales as it’s introduced new models this year.

Used EVs Are Having A Moment

The used EV market is another bright spot. It isn’t just surviving, it’s thriving, suggesting there’s strong demand for battery power at the right price.

Sales took a dive after the EV tax credit went away, but they rebounded quickly and have rocketed upward ever since. Last month, Americans snapped up over 47,000 used electric cars, Cox Automotive says, a 21% year-over-year jump that gave EVs their largest-ever share of the used car market.

The fact that your options aren’t limited to low-range Chevy Bolts and Nissan Leafs anymore is certainly helping. There’s better supply of lightly used EVs than ever, as an increasing number of modern, long-range cars, particularly ones that were leased over the last few years, hit the secondhand market.

And the demand is there too, boosted in part by $4-a-gallon gas, industry-watchers say. Used EVs are selling in 41 days on average, according to Cars.com, about 12 days faster than internal-combustion models. And while prices for lightly used gas cars have stayed roughly flat over the last year, used EV prices are up close to 10%, iSeeCars says.

The EV Revolution Isn't Canceled. Just Delayed.

Despite the rocky road, industry watchers and auto executives broadly think EVs will continue displacing gas vehicles in the U.S.—albeit at a slower rate than before.

“We remain optimistic, quite frankly, on the space,” Jominy said.

The Rivian R2 is part of a new class of EVs that could drive sales higher in the coming years.

Photo by: Mack Hogan/InsideEVs

EVs are taking off globally, he said, and data shows that once someone goes electric they tend to be hooked. Plus, electric cars have fewer parts and are cheaper to manufacture at scale than combustion vehicles, putting slower-moving automakers at a disadvantage as EV sales climb around the world. At some point, the economics of scale in the industry will be far more favorable to electric propulsion, he said. “Once you can produce something 30% cheaper,” he said, “you really can’t just maintain the old way for very long.”

On top of that, U.S. charging infrastructure is improving quickly; last quarter, the U.S. surpassed 80,000 DC fast charging ports, up from 70,000 at the end of last year. Promising new models like the R2, Ford’s $30,000 Fathom pickup, the Slate Truck, and a slew of high-tech cars from luxury manufacturers could take sales to the next level. While Hyundai is investing heavily in various types of hybrids to buck the EV slowdown, Muñoz sees a future for electric cars in America too.

What do you think?

“What you see everywhere when you look at the trends in the market, EV is there to stay,” he told me.

name: Detroit Environment
title: Why Water Is on the Ballot in Highland Park, Michigan - Next City
description:
As Election Day nears and Highland Park chooses its next mayor, water troubles continue to impassion the city’s residents.
Highland Park is requesting a $1.5-million reduction in its combined sewer overflow bill for fiscal year 2026.
Water runs through Highland Park mayoral race The mayoral candidates said they want to work with state legislators to create a statewide water affordability program.
Highland Park enacts water shutoff moratorium, plans outreach on payment plans On Oct. 5, Highland Park City Council passed a 90-day moratorium on water shutoffs.
Highland Park Water Department Director Damon Garrett did not respond to multiple requests for comment on water payment plans and shutoffs.
text:
This story was produced by Planet Detroit as part of Next City’s Local Reporting Hub, with funding from the Kresge Foundation.

In 1930, the city of Highland Park, Michigan, was home to nearly 53,000 residents. But its population and fortunes declined after Ford and Chrysler left the Detroit enclave, taking with them tax revenue and corresponding investments in the city’s infrastructure — including drinking water.

Due to mounting debt, an emergency financial manager was appointed to the city between 2001 and 2009. Highland Park’s water treatment plant closed in 2012. Today, the 3-square-mile city has an estimated 8,248 residents remaining.

As Election Day nears and Highland Park chooses its next mayor, water troubles continue to impassion the city’s residents.

Shamayim “Mama Shu” Harris, a longtime resident and developer of the eco-village Avalon Village, helped distribute water bottles when residents lived under two boil water notices that spanned a total of 13 days in March 2025. As a member of the Highland Park Community Crisis Coalition, Harris partnered with local organizations and faith leaders to distribute the water.

Harris is challenging incumbent Mayor Glenda McDonald on Tuesday’s ballot.

McDonald has led the city through an ongoing dispute with its water utility, the regional Great Lakes Water Authority. “I want everybody’s water to be affordable, mine included, because I pay a lot too, just like everyone else,” McDonald tells Planet Detroit.

Highland Park is disputing the wastewater charges levied by GLWA despite a 2024 settlement of litigation between the city and water authority that includes $70 million in state funding for the city’s water infrastructure.

Highland Park is requesting a $1.5-million reduction in its combined sewer overflow bill for fiscal year 2026. The charges are based on a 1999 allocation that uses population data and impervious area, according to city documents. The city’s position is that its CSO costs should be based on metered wet weather sewer volumes.

With the city’s population having fallen by half over the last quarter-century, remaining residents and advocates say they are making up for a shrunken tax base and inadequate cost-sharing formula.

“We have less than 10,000 people in our city, and it seems like we’re paying for ghosts,” said Linda Wheeler, a resident and member of the grassroots Highland Park Water Advocates organization.

Water runs through Highland Park mayoral race

The mayoral candidates said they want to work with state legislators to create a statewide water affordability program.

Harris wants to improve communication and coordination with residents who are struggling to pay their water bills, she tells Planet Detroit.

“What I’ve seen is a breakdown in the things that have happened with the infrastructure and how it has caused a crisis in the community,” says Harris.

“There’s been several water boil alerts. We have had to step in … in cases of an emergency, and so we’ve seen that over and over.”

The state-funded, multiyear project to replace water main pipes and service lines contributed to the water pressure drops behind the boil alerts, Planet Detroit reported at the time.

McDonald says her administration is “very forthcoming with people” on construction projects by the city’s water department.

“Citizens will be made aware of when they will need to turn off water or when they would need to dig up pipes and things like that,” and when workers will need to enter homes to make a connection, she says.

Highland Park’s water treatment plant was shut down indefinitely in 2012 due to lack of repairs. Before the shutdown, the city sourced its water from a Lake St. Clair intake.

The city switched to Detroit water on an emergency basis. GLWA, the regional utility, came into being in 2016 as part of a deal made as Detroit prepared to exit municipal bankruptcy.

Harris and McDonald are in agreement on the desire to reestablish the city’s drinking water facility.

In the longer term, Harris says she wants to explore reestablishing Highland Park’s water plant, beginning with reviewing contracts and understanding the city’s options.

“Talking to the citizens, they want their own water plant back, and any way that we can make that happen, that’s what I want to do,” she says.

McDonald says she is “very serious” about reopening the water plant, adding that the city’s agreement with the state requires it to first replace its century-old water mains.

Highland Park enacts water shutoff moratorium, plans outreach on payment plans

On Oct. 5, Highland Park City Council passed a 90-day moratorium on water shutoffs.

The moratorium calls for the city’s water department contractor, Metro Consulting Associates, to hold public meetings and explain water payment options during the three-month pause.

Residents who enroll in the city’s payment plan can pay 5% of income for current water bills and outstanding balances. It requires residents to opt in to the plan through a Water Department customer service representative. Information about the payment plan is available on the city’s website. A rrinted flyers at Highland Park City Hall shares information about programs available from two nonprofits to help residents pay their water bills: the Heat and Warmth Fund’s MI WATER program and Wayne Metropolitan Community Action Agency’s Water Affordability Program, which offers up to $3,000 in assistance for residents with overdue water bills or who are at risk of service shutoffs.

McDonald says water shutoffs have occurred in Highland Park within the last year-and-a-half since the city entered into the settlement agreement with GLWA. She did not provide the number of shutoffs.

Stipulations exist to prevent shutoffs that take place in the middle of winter, or affect vulnerable groups like low-income families or seniors, she says.

Highland Park Water Department Director Damon Garrett did not respond to multiple requests for comment on water payment plans and shutoffs.

Highland Park resident Carolyn Baker, executive director of the General Baker Institute, a community nonprofit, says the city’s payment plan is an attempt to limit the scourge of shutoffs that her mother and other water activists fought through the early 2000s.

“Whether you are low-income or senior, it doesn’t matter,” Baker says. “If you just couldn’t afford it, you can just go and say, ‘I can’t afford it,’ and you should be able to be put on this plan.”

Baker’s mother, Marian Kramer, a longtime welfare rights organizer, was a plaintiff in a 2015 water lawsuit as a member of the Highland Park Human Rights Coalition.

Although the Wayne Metro and THAW assistance programs are helpful, Baker says they serve as a “Band-Aid,” not a long-term solution to the affordability issues confronting Highland Park residents.

With a growing number of communities across the United States struggling to afford water, advocates have petitioned for moratoriums and income-based affordability programs to protect residents from the financial, physical, and emotional toll of water shutoffs.

In Metro Detroit, groups such as the Highland Park Human Rights Coalition, People’s Water Board Coalition, and We The People of Detroit spearheaded efforts to enact affordability policies at the municipal and statewide level in response to mass water shutoffs that impacted residents through most of the first quarter of the 21st century.

Cities such as Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Detroit have adopted and enacted the kinds of affordability programs that Highland Park advocates say the settlement’s payment plan offers.

In August, Baker said she began to hear about possible shutoffs after speaking with staff from local assistance programs. Baker and other residents raised the shutoff issue at multiple city council meetings, requesting a moratorium and better management of the payment plan, of which she said residents are unaware.

A 2022 University of Michigan statewide study found that shutoffs require families to ration water, and engage in the physically demanding task of transporting water from neighbors’ houses or businesses. In some communities, children were removed from homes after the loss of water access.

Water bill litigation

Highland Park residents were threatened with foreclosure when overdue water bills were placed as liens on properties during the emergency financial manager period, according to a 2007 Metro Times report.

In 2015, a handful of residents and water activists including Kramer sued the city, alleging illegal billing practices, no due process, illegal shutoffs, and rolling arrearages on property taxes.

“Our goal was to make sure that people were not getting their water shut off,” Alice Jennings, one of the plaintiffs’ lawyers in the 2015 lawsuit, said at a Thursday, Oct. 29 town hall meeting.

After Highland Park’s water treatment plant closed and the city began to receive water and sewer services from Detroit, some residents received inaccurate bills ranging from “several hundred to several thousand dollars,” according to the class action lawsuit.

“I remember some people’s water bills were $10,000,” said resident and water advocate Wheeler.

About 40% of Highland Park residents live below the federal poverty line. The median household income is $29,300.

The 2019 settlement of the lawsuit produced the city’s water affordability plan, which Jennings says should protect Highland Park residents “from being emotionally affected by worrying about your water being shut off.”

Beyond ensuring the affordability plan is in compliance, Jennings says she and other advocates want improved communication between residents, city government, and local nonprofits assisting residents with utility bills.

“We want a hotline, so if someone’s about to face water shutoff, they can immediately call that hotline, and they can get on the list, and it freezes them from getting shut off,” she says.

Mayoral candidates say they’ll work on utility affordability

Harris says the burden of utility affordability continues to fall on residents, and it’s one that has yet to be solved under McDonald’s administration.

One of Harris’ policy goals is to establish a Highland Park Initiative, a door-to-door intake process that would connect existing organizations and services to the city’s residents, and narrow communication gaps.

“I want to be able to touch each resident here face-to-face to know exactly what that household needs,” Harris says.

McDonald says that if she’s reelected, she wants “to continue making progress and working with the citizens to make sure that they have resources that they need in order to keep their water on.”

Ethan Bakuli is Planet Detroit's Climate Solutions and Service Journalism Reporting Fellow. He joins the team after covering education and community issues for Chalkbeat Detroit and working as a freelance journalist reporting on race and labor issues. Before launching his career as a reporter, he taught high school students how to produce audio and visual stories about their communities, an experience that cemented his belief in the power of community-led journalism.

text:
The Ministry of Panchayati Raj on Saturday said it has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Convergence Energy Services (CESL) to establish electric vehicle (EV) charging and battery swapping stations on Panchayat land across the country.

According to the official press release, the agreement is aimed at creating additional sources of revenue for Gram, Block and District Panchayats while expanding access to EV infrastructure in rural areas. The facilities are expected to cater to two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles and medium and heavy commercial vehicles.

Advt

The MoU was signed in the presence of Union Minister for Panchayati Raj Rajiv Ranjan Singh alias Lalan Singh and Secretary of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj Vineet Joshi. It was exchanged by Mukta Shekhar, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, and Akhilesh Kumar Dixit, Director, CESL.

Under the agreement, the Ministry will coordinate with state Panchayati Raj departments to identify and monitor suitable sites. CESL will be responsible for site assessment, demand aggregation, supply, installation, testing, commissioning, operation and maintenance of the charging and battery swapping facilities.

The infrastructure is proposed to be set up at suitable locations, including Panchayat premises and sites along state and national highways.

Secretary of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj Vineet Joshi said the Cabinet's approval of PM VGSY would provide a framework for decentralised and evidence-based planning. He said the People’s Plan Campaign, run by the Ministry since 2018 under the theme ‘Sabki Yojana, Sabka Vikas’, had evolved into a framework for preparing Gram, Block and District Panchayat Development Plans, localising the Sustainable Development Goals and converging schemes and resources.

Advt

Joshi said GPDPs should reflect people's needs and aspirations rather than being limited to available government schemes or funding. He also stressed the need to include an OSR component in the plans, as performance-based grants are linked to revenue generation by Panchayats.

He cited the Sixteenth Finance Commission's recommendation of grants amounting to ₹4,35,236 crore for duly constituted Panchayati Raj Institutions and rural local bodies across 28 states for the 2026-31 award period. He said the allocation placed greater responsibility on Panchayats to ensure the effective use of funds.

Joshi also called for the integration of Central and state government portals, including eGramSwaraj and the Samarth Panchayat Portal, to support data-based planning and monitoring.

Water, sanitation and local planning in focus

Ashok K K Meena, Secretary, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, said Panchayats had a role in ensuring the continued delivery of drinking water and sanitation services.

He said GPDPs should address water sources, quality, maintenance, availability of trained personnel and waste management. He also called for the effective use of tied grants under the Sixteenth Finance Commission and said assessments such as Jal Seva and Swachh Seva Aankalan could help identify gaps and inform local plans.

Meena said user charges were important for sustaining water and sanitation services and improving the financial position of Panchayats. He also stressed accountability through Gram Sabhas and the use of data for planning and investment decisions.

Palka Sahni, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Panchayati Raj, highlighted the progress made through thematic Panchayat Development Plans and called for improvements in their quality and alignment with local priorities.

Rohini R Bhajibhakare, Joint Secretary, Ministry of Rural Development, emphasised the need for comprehensive and convergent GPDPs for rural development.

title: Mobilizing the Clean Energy Workforce for Partners - SkillUp Coalition
description:
The clean energy revolution won't build itself.
Investing in AI-Resilient, Life-Changing Careersanchor If funders are looking to solve for the economic disruption of AI, clean energy construction is the data-driven answer.
Scaling Career Opportunities Regionally The clean energy transition is a hyper-localized effort requiring a localized talent pool to avoid the high costs of a traveling workforce.
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)anchor Why should philanthropy prioritize clean energy workforce development right now?
Philanthropy must fund intermediaries that actively collaborate with the clean energy industry to create standardized, industry-vetted micro-credentials.
text:
The clean energy revolution won't build itself. Driven by historic electricity demands from new data centers and the urgent need for grid reliability, the market is dictating an aggressive, immediate infrastructure build-out. However, we face a massive skilled trades shortage that threatens deployment. To meet this demand, we must aggressively open the door to inclusive pathways for workers skilled through alternative routes (STARs). At SkillUp, we are uniting philanthropy, workforce innovators, and industry to dismantle cultural stigmas, abandon failing training models, and scale high-paying, AI-resilient career pathways for workers without degrees.

Funding Intermediaries and Industry Alignment anchor

The era of funding siloed, "go at it alone" training programs must end. As Laura Wilson Phelan from the Clean Power Institute warns, too often students invest in programs only to "graduate and they're not necessarily more employable... because their program was never aligned to actually the jobs that are available in the marketplace". Philanthropy must pivot to fund intermediaries that connect public education with actual employer needs. As Alyssa Thomas from Invest in Our Future notes, we need seed funding to motivate the market, and "I encourage philanthropy to not think about industry as your opposition but as your partner in building the type of workforce that you want to have".

Investing in AI-Resilient, Life-Changing Careersanchor

If funders are looking to solve for the economic disruption of AI, clean energy construction is the data-driven answer. As Alyssa Thomas states, "You're not about to go train a model to go install solar on someone's roof like that just simply can't happen". More importantly, these are worker-first jobs offering immediate economic mobility. A worker can step onto a job site "with zero training as a wind technician in a rural area where cost of living is low at a minimum of $59,000". By investing in these pathways, partners are driving localized economic booms—sometimes yielding a "100% increase in household... median income" in rural project areas, delivering truly life-changing wages while helping workers avoid crippling student debt.

Cultural Activation and Breaking Stigmasanchor

The demand for these jobs among workers is surprisingly high, but the pipeline is clogged by a "ton of cultural stigma around jobs if you're not already in the trades". Jon van Gelder shared data that shows that workers are primarily driven by the prospect of "high pay... and avoiding student debt" rather than the climate narrative alone. Through innovative cultural activations—such as integrating with major music artists to reach diverse, working-class audiences—Tradesforce is actively shifting the narrative. These pilot events have achieved massive engagement, boasting 10% conversion rates from concert sign-ups directly into our union and industry talent pipelines.

How SkillUp Can Helpanchor

SkillUp serves as the critical connective tissue between latent worker demand, philanthropic capital, and urgent industry need. We provide the modern digital infrastructure required to overcome the "digital barrier" that historically keeps diverse talent out of the trades. Our platform data proves the demand is there: Skilled Trades training engagement is up to 41% among our users. We invite foundations, C3 organizations, and industry leaders to partner with us to fund inclusive pathways, align curricula to real jobs, and scale the "last mile" of job placement. Connect with our partnership team today to explore how your organization can co-invest in the workforce of the future.

Scaling Career Opportunities Regionally

The clean energy transition is a hyper-localized effort requiring a localized talent pool to avoid the high costs of a traveling workforce. We are scaling regional pathways to connect local workers directly with vetted, localized job training programs and employing companies. Partners can view our public-facing ecosystem by visiting skillup.org/tradesforce.

Online Career Support

Through the SkillUp and Trades Force platform, our national support services handle the critical top-of-funnel work—intake, cultural awareness, and career navigation—required to seamlessly funnel interested workers into specific union and industry opportunities without them getting lost in the noise.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)anchor

Why should philanthropy prioritize clean energy workforce development right now?

The market is dictating an aggressive build-out due to historic electricity load growth, which is projected to increase 35% to 50% by 2040. Investing in the clean energy workforce is not just a climate play; it is a direct investment in economic equity and AI-resilient careers that provide immediate, life-changing wages for workers without a four-year degree.

How can funders avoid investing in ineffective training programs?

Philanthropy must fund intermediaries that actively collaborate with the clean energy industry to create standardized, industry-vetted micro-credentials. We must stop funding isolated "go at it alone" programs that take students' time and money but do not align with actual marketplace demands or lead to higher employability.

text:
As Republican party campaigners crow about the tax cuts in t…

In this election, it’s not just the economy. Our democratic …



I could be wrong but I’m pretty sure the Sept. 22 Public Forum rant set the record for the most irrational Trump Derangement Syndrome venom ever expressed in under 300 words. Quite a feat, as the Public Forum airs a lot of emotional venom.

Any smear piece that starts with the claim “it’s reported that …” should be immediately suspect. When it is followed by heaps of wishful claims of corruption, directed at the writer's declared favorite target, should be laughable on the face of it. But apparently those afflicted with TDS need this kind of malicious gossip for their world to make sense. It is a kind of lynch mob mentality that leaves rational thought behind.

Please, when you vote try to think about what you are doing. Thinking requires a bit of work but it pays off in the long run.



Jim Seifert

Winterville

One hundred and thirty years ago, Swedish scientist S. Arrhenius showed that increasing the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would increase the temperature of the surface of the earth.

It has been shown recently that over 90% of the heat trapped by carbon dioxide goes into the ocean. Included effects are rising sea levels, and declines in the ice sheets in the polar regions.

In 2015, the Paris Accords on climate change set a goal to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. The USA has withdrawn from these Paris Accords, putting the burden of global warming mitigation on other countries.

Global warming will soon exceed the target of 1.5 degrees Celsius. This is alarming to the United Nations Environment Programme, and they have laid out measures to lower the rate of global temperature increase. This includes transforming away from fossil fuels and tripling renewable energy sources. As a real-world example, in my chemistry classes I taught the chemical properties of carbon dioxide that make it a good greenhouse gas.

When I was awarded a distinguished professorship at ECU in 2006, I donated my stipend to fund symposia on global warming and climate change. Invited speakers talked about more rapid increases in surface temperatures in the polar regions, computer modeling of climate change and the effect of increased atmospheric carbon dioxide on vegetation. Our attempt was to educate ourselves and the community about global warming and climate change.

Global warming is exacerbated by the proliferation of data centers. There are thousands of data centers with over half of them in the United States.

As Richard Feynman famously said “… reality must take precedence over public relations, for Nature cannot be fooled.”

Robert C. Morrison

Greenville

Morrison is a Navy veteran and distinguished professor of chemistry emeritus at ECU.

We might think it doesn’t matter; or we might not care. We might not take it seriously; this responsibility we share.

Whether we’re the older generation, middle aged or just out of youth; we all share the same power in the voting booth.

Lots of people can’t afford to put groceries on their shelves; while some of our leaders in Washington just want to help themselves. It’s obvious to everyone they have trouble with the truth. But we can turn it all around in the voting booth.

So many people are sick and suffering in the richest country on earth. While the president and his cronies are increasing their net worth. The only way to defeat a man who’s so dishonest and uncouth is to use the power we all have in the voting booth.

So we can’t just ignore it; can’t just sit on our hands. We all see what’s going on; we’ve got to take a stand. We’ve got to reinstall decency, honesty and truth. The only way we can accomplish this is in the voting booth.

title: Editorial: Marin Clean Energy made a promise in 2010. It's still achievable today.
description:
When Marin Clean Energy was launched in 2010, it promised ratepayers it would be a truly publicly run utility that would provide better rates and greener electrical power.
Some of MCE’s board members have also raised questions about its rates.
That’s a $85.9 million credit to its 1.8 million ratepayers because MCE’s mid-2026 energy costs are lower than what was projected.
Still, some of MCE’s board members urged a more cautious approach given uncertainties of the energy market these days.
It’s too bad it took the political tumult it did to get it headed back on the track it promised in 2010.
text:
When Marin Clean Energy was launched in 2010, it promised ratepayers it would be a truly publicly run utility that would provide better rates and greener electrical power.

It grew beyond Marin, to include four neighboring Bay Area counties as municipalities saw the agency, relabeled MCE, as a significant part of their strategies to meet their 2030 state mandate to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 40% below 1990 levels.

The agency, a public alternative to Pacific Gas & Electric Co., has run into some rough political waters of late, including drawing a Marin County Civil Grand Jury investigation that sharply criticized its governance and management.

Some of MCE’s board members have also raised questions about its rates.

In response, MCE is taking a look at reorganizing its governance. It has already established more special committees, such as a finance committee, and is considering changing its 34-member commission to a less cumbersome and more effective number.

The grand jury report shined a light on extensive absenteeism among MCE board members, their lack of expertise in the complex world of procuring energy and the agency’s staff making significant financial and management decisions outside of the board’s oversight.

Recently, MCE took action on its rates, approving a 22% billing credit for its ratepayers – a $14.20 monthly credit for typical residential accounts.

That’s a $85.9 million credit to its 1.8 million ratepayers because MCE’s mid-2026 energy costs are lower than what was projected.

That reduction will likely be welcomed by ratepayers who have been barraged (like everyone else) by the skyrocketing cost of living the last year.

The success of MCE relies on it keeping its promises, especially keeping its rates less or at least competitive with PG&E and its electrical power greener. MCE’s leadership is worried that some of its larger customers could find reenrolling in PG&E more advantageous.

State law that established “community choice aggregator” agencies such as MCE provided that ratepayers would be automatically enrolled in the CCA unless they chose to “opt out” and stay with PG&E. That automatic enrollment provided CCAs with a built-in strong ratepayer base.

In MCE’s case, most ratepayers have not “opted out,” but there’s always that possibility.

The MCE credit is a strategic move to retain its ratepayers, one its staff says it can afford because of the depth of its budget reserves.

Still, some of MCE’s board members urged a more cautious approach given uncertainties of the energy market these days.

Is it a short-term response to a longer-term challenge?

MCE is going through a lot of changes, among them hiring a new executive director.

Its management and governance missteps could have been identified and avoided if the board was more effective in its job of providing strong and knowledgeable public oversight.

While welcomed and in step with its promise to keep its rates competitive with PG&E (its much larger competitor), MCE’s leadership has to make sure it can continue to deliver on that public commitment.

The stinging grand jury report sets the stage for reform.

“The Board recognizes MCE’s governance practices did not keep pace with the agency’s growth, complexity, and financial responsibilities,” wrote Contra Costa County Supervisor Shanelle Scales-Preston, MCE’s board chair, in the agency’s posted response to the grand jury’s report.

“Lasting reform will require clearer accountability, stronger controls, more complete and comprehensible information, greater transparency, and sustained attention to the affordability and measurable environmental value of MCE’s decision,” she wrote.

MCE needs to be able to assure its customers that its primary focus is on keeping its promises. That includes being financially strong and resilient enough to keep its rates competitive, growing its ability to provide greener power and building that supply and keeping a focus on ratepayers’ bills rather than its shareholders’ returns.

In the coming months, MCE is headed toward some organizational changes. Some are probably long overdue. It’s too bad it took the political tumult it did to get it headed back on the track it promised in 2010.

title: Morocco's billion-dollar battery investment puts lithium supply in focus - Mining.com.au
description:
Chinese companies are investing US$6 billion ($8.5 billion) in Morocco’s battery supply chain, as previously reported.
An established automotive industry Morocco’s push into battery manufacturing builds on an established automotive export industry.
For lithium producers, the Morocco investment could provide an additional source of demand as battery manufacturing capacity expands beyond established production centres in China.
Developers: Global Lithium For developers and explorers, the expansion of battery manufacturing offers a potential opportunity for projects seeking a place in the evolving global supply chain.
Increased battery manufacturing capacity could support the investment case for new lithium discoveries.
text:
As the global race to secure electric vehicle (EV) supply chains intensifies, Morocco is positioning itself as a manufacturing base between Europe’s automotive market and Asia’s battery industry.

Morocco’s emergence as a battery manufacturing hub could create new opportunities for lithium miners, developers, and explorers as the country positions itself to supply Europe’s EV market.

Chinese companies are investing US$6 billion ($8.5 billion) in Morocco’s battery supply chain, as previously reported.

The investment targets battery cell and cathode material production as manufacturers seek to diversify their operations amid changing trade dynamics between China and the European Union (EU).

With the EU imposing additional duties on Chinese-made EVs, manufacturers are looking at production locations that offer access to international markets while reducing exposure to trade restrictions.

An established automotive industry

Morocco’s push into battery manufacturing builds on an established automotive export industry. The country is Africa’s largest vehicle manufacturing and export hub, generating MAD 93.7 billion ($13.5 billion) in exports by mid-2026.

The country is now gaining a greater share of the EV supply chain through the latest investment by Chinese companies.

The investment also signals the growing opportunities for the broader mining sector, as the expansion of battery manufacturing capacity increases the importance of securing reliable supplies of lithium for the energy transition.

For lithium producers, the Morocco investment could provide an additional source of demand as battery manufacturing capacity expands beyond established production centres in China.

However, the lithium sourcing arrangements for the planned facilities have not been disclosed, leaving uncertainty over which producers could benefit and how much additional demand the projects could generate.

Developers: Global Lithium

For developers and explorers, the expansion of battery manufacturing offers a potential opportunity for projects seeking a place in the evolving global supply chain.

As Morocco expands its downstream manufacturing capacity, projects that can show competitive production costs, reliable supply, and a clear pathway to production could position themselves to attract potential customers and strategic partners.

Global Lithium Resources (ASX:GL1) is focused on derisking its Manna Lithium Project in Western Australia, ahead of a final investment decision expected by the end of 2026.

Manna boasts a 51.6 million tonne (Mt) mineral resource base, which is considered the third-largest in the Kalgoorlie lithium province.

An optimised Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) for the project has been completed, confirming Manna has a long mine life and is an economically robust lithium asset.

Developers such as Global Lithium are demonstrating their projects’ economic viability, particularly as new production capacity enters the market.

Explorers: Venari Minerals

Meanwhile, for explorers, the latest investment in Morocco presents a potential longer-term demand signal rather than an immediate commercial opportunity.

Increased battery manufacturing capacity could support the investment case for new lithium discoveries. However, explorers will still need to establish commercially viable resources before they can benefit from any additional demand.

For example, Venari Minerals (ASX:VMS) is advancing its Red Mountain Lithium Project in Nevada, US, which hosts a resource of 500Mt @ 0.61% lithium carbonate equivalent.

The company recently announced it is seeking US Department of War (DoW) funding for Red Mountain. This follows its admission to the US Defense Industrial Base Consortium.

Membership provides access to DoW grant opportunities and a network of defence contractors to support domestic strategic mineral supply chains. It also enables faster collaboration between government, industry, academia, and non-traditional suppliers.

Venari has advanced metallurgical test work at the project, with Scoping Study-level leachability results showing that the lithium is highly leachable. Beneficiation test work also revealed that mineralisation has ‘excellent’ characteristics for removing gangue minerals while retaining valuable lithium-bearing clays and reducing acid consumption.

The extent to which Morocco’s expansion translates into opportunities for explorers depends on various factors. These include whether manufacturers seek to secure future supply through partnerships, project investments, or offtake agreements.

Morocco’s ambitions could create another source of demand for lithium across the supply chain.

However, the impact on individual companies will depend on the scale of additional consumption, the origin of raw materials, and how quickly Morocco’s planned battery manufacturing capacity moves into production.

Write to Aaliyah Rogan at Mining.com.au

title: Not Boston, Not Portland: iSeeCars Says This Is The Least EV-Friendly US City In 2026
description:
According to iSeeCars data, the charging network in the United States is still growing but has slowed considerably.
Still, iSeeCars projects that more than 40,000 new chargers will be added by the end of 2026, bringing the total to about 299,800 across the country.
Based on the number of residents per charger, San Francisco is the most EV-friendly metro area in the country, with an average of 334 residents per charger.
Conversely, Louisville, Kentucky, ranks as the least EV-friendly of the 50 largest U.S. metro areas, averaging 2,904 residents per charger.
L.A. and San Francisco make that easy, as do San Diego, Denver, and Boston.
text:
Making the change from a gas-powered vehicle to an electric one can be a big transition. Surging gas prices are drawing in some new buyers, but the decision to go electric goes beyond sticker price and fuel savings. Driving range is typically a top concern, but many consumers also worry about when and where they'll be able to charge. Charger density and availability are part of what some are calling EV-friendliness, which refers to how easy it is to own and drive an EV in a certain geographical area.

According to iSeeCars data, the charging network in the United States is still growing but has slowed considerably. Still, iSeeCars projects that more than 40,000 new chargers will be added by the end of 2026, bringing the total to about 299,800 across the country. But easy access to electric car charging points varies widely depending on where you live. Based on the number of residents per charger, San Francisco is the most EV-friendly metro area in the country, with an average of 334 residents per charger. Conversely, Louisville, Kentucky, ranks as the least EV-friendly of the 50 largest U.S. metro areas, averaging 2,904 residents per charger.

iSeeCars counts Level 2 and Level 3/DC fast-charging ports using data published by the U.S. Department of Energy's Alternative Fuels Data Center. When you look simply at the total number of chargers available, Los Angeles wins with 36,318 chargers, while Louisville again has the fewest, with only 621 available. Before you seal the deal on that new Mach-E, take a look at the latest data on charging infrastructure.

Read more: 12 Of The Most Popular Military Vehicles Civilians Can Actually Own

EV charger access varies widely by state and metro area

Some EV owners solve the charging problem by simply installing a home charger, but that's not a solution for everyone, especially city residents and those who live in apartments or condos. It's also expensive, typically costing between $800 and $2,500. If a home charger doesn't work for you, you'll have to rely on the public charging network. L.A. and San Francisco make that easy, as do San Diego, Denver, and Boston. If you live in Louisville, you may struggle to find a charger. Indianapolis, Milwaukee, Greensboro-Winston-Salem in North Carolina, and San Antonio round out the five least EV-friendly metro areas.

Taking a broader view of the data, California has more chargers than any other state, with almost 82,000 publicly available. That's more than three times the second-place winner, New York, which has about 24,500 chargers. Florida, Texas, and Massachusetts round out the top five and all have more than 13,000 chargers available.

Public chargers are scarce in Alaska. This large state only has 227 available! North Dakota, South Dakota, and Wyoming all have fewer than 500 public chargers for EV drivers, while Montana has just 502. Examining the number of chargers per resident, Vermont just edges out California as the winner, with 450 residents per charger. Louisiana loses that race, with a whopping 4,717 residents per charger. The regional differences are staggering, and buyers should definitely consider charging infrastructure challenges before making any big purchase.

title: LG Energy Solution Develops Hybrid Pouch-Prismatic Battery - The Elec Inc.
description:
LG Energy Solution is developing a new type of hybrid battery with General Motors (GM) that combines the advantages of pouch and prismatic cells.
LG Energy Solution has traditionally focused on pouch-type batteries for both electric vehicles and energy storage systems (ESS).
The technology involves placing multiple pouch battery cells inside a metal casing to create a structure resembling a prismatic battery.
LG Energy Solution is developing PtoP batteries to make use of its existing pouch battery production equipment.
"LG Energy Solution and GM are reviewing various potential applications for the battery," an industry official said.
text:
LG Energy Solution is developing a new type of hybrid battery with General Motors (GM) that combines the advantages of pouch and prismatic cells. The company recently began producing prototypes at its Ochang plant and is evaluating their potential use in electric vehicles.

Batteries are classified as cylindrical, pouch or prismatic according to the shape of the casing enclosing their cells. LG Energy Solution has traditionally focused on pouch-type batteries for both electric vehicles and energy storage systems (ESS). However, growing adoption of prismatic batteries by global automakers has increased the need to develop new form factors.

According to industry sources on Oct. 30, LG Energy Solution began a project to convert pouch-type batteries into a prismatic format in the second half of last year. It started investing in facilities this year. The technology involves placing multiple pouch battery cells inside a metal casing to create a structure resembling a prismatic battery. The company internally refers to the technology as PtoP (Pouch to Prismatic).

The company has also secured equipment needed to manufacture prototypes. It is using standalone equipment to produce prototypes at its Ochang Energy Plant 1. The equipment was supplied by System R&D, a major partner of LG Electronics' Production Engineering Research Institute (PRI).

LG Energy Solution is developing PtoP batteries to make use of its existing pouch battery production equipment. The company has established extensive pouch battery manufacturing infrastructure worldwide. Converting those facilities into dedicated prismatic battery production lines would require substantial additional investment. PtoP technology allows the company to use pouch cells manufactured on existing equipment, reducing investment in new facilities and manufacturing costs. Over the longer term, it could lower total cost of ownership (TCO) while meeting demand from customers that prefer prismatic batteries.

These economic advantages are also believed to have influenced the joint development effort with GM. The two companies established Ultium Cells, their North American joint venture, and built large-scale battery manufacturing facilities. If GM adopts PtoP batteries in its electric vehicles, it could improve utilization of existing pouch battery production lines. However, their use in actual vehicles has not been finalized.

"LG Energy Solution and GM are reviewing various potential applications for the battery," an industry official said. "They are still exploring multiple possibilities rather than preparing to install it in a specific vehicle."

A key feature of PtoP batteries is that they retain the internal structure of conventional pouch cells while adopting a prismatic exterior. In a typical prismatic battery, an internal assembly combining electrodes and separators is placed inside a metal can before electrolyte is injected. PtoP batteries, by contrast, combine several pouch cells that have already undergone electrolyte filling and sealing into a single product.

Specifically, the design can accommodate two to four pouch cells stacked side by side inside a metal casing. The casing consists of upper and lower sections. The upper structure encloses the top, front and rear of the battery, while the lower structure protects the bottom and both sides. The two sections are joined to secure the internal cells and protect them from external impacts.

Electrically connecting the individual pouch cells is critical. Battery cells have electrode leads, which are thin metal terminals that carry electrical current. The electrode leads from multiple cells are welded to a metal component called a busbar to combine their electrical currents. The busbar is positioned at the front of the metal casing and also serves as an external electrical connection terminal. Unlike conventional pouch batteries, PtoP batteries require the electrode leads of multiple cells to be gathered and connected within a confined space, making welding precision particularly important. The electrode leads and busbar are joined using laser welding.

In electric vehicles, PtoP batteries could be used in a cell-to-pack (CTP) configuration, which eliminates modules and integrates cells directly into the battery pack. A cell-to-chassis (CTC) configuration, which integrates batteries directly into the vehicle body without a separate battery pack, is also possible. Conventional pouch batteries are well suited to stacking thin, elongated cells, but face limitations when cells must be positioned vertically or arranged to fit available vehicle space. Prismatic batteries, by contrast, use standardized rectangular structures that make it easier to design cell orientation and spacing, offering advantages for CTP and CTC applications.

LG Energy Solution is not the only company developing such technology. SK On, which has also focused on pouch-type batteries, is developing a similar approach. At InterBattery 2026 in March, SK On unveiled its "Integrated Pouch Prismatic Cell."

A report attributed to the American Clean Power Association puts the US clean power project pipeline at a record 204.6 gigawatts, up approximately 20 GW in one year. If confirmed, the figure would highlight the scale of projects being developed to supply electricity from lower-carbon sources. Important Details: 204.6 GW in the Pipeline: The headline reports a record volume of clean power projects in development. 20 GW of Annual Growth: The reported increase suggests that the pipeline expanded substantially over the previous year. Multiple Technologies: Clean power pipelines can include solar, wind, battery storage and other eligible technologies, depending on the report's methodology. Meeting Rising Demand: New electricity projects could help supply homes, factories, electric vehicles and energy-intensive data centers. Energy Storage: Batteries can complement variable renewable generation by storing electricity and releasing it when needed. Projects Are Not All Operating: A pipeline includes projects at different stages, and not every proposed project will necessarily be completed. Capacity Is Not Household Electricity: Gigawatts measure power capacity, while annual household consumption depends on energy use over time and the capacity factor of each generating technology. The headline compares the pipeline with enough energy to power every American home twice over. That comparison needs careful interpretation: 204.6 GW is a measure of power capacity, not a quantity of electricity generated annually. The actual output would depend on the project mix, completion rates and operating conditions. Even with that caveat, tracking the project pipeline provides useful insight into where the US electricity system could be heading — and how much new infrastructure may be needed to meet future demand. Will the US be able to bring enough clean power projects online to meet its growing electricity demand by 2030? Source: American Clean Power Association, Q2 report, September 2026. text:
Ford's new Fathom electric pickup could make it considerably cheaper for drivers to charge their cars or even power their homes during an outage.

By putting an inverter inside the truck, the automaker says it can cut the cost of required home backup equipment by 60% before installation.

Here's what to know

On Oct. 27, the automaker announced that the $28,350 Fathom will have bidirectional charging capabilities, meaning it could power a home during an outage, according to Canary Media.

To draw power from the Fathom, the truck will switch from battery-supplied direct current to alternating current.

According to Ford's website, "When your home is properly equipped, Fathom can help power it when energy rates are high, potentially lowering your monthly electric costs. It can also help keep your home's essentials (such as lights, fridge, and Wi-Fi) running during a power outage."

Ford says the Fathom-compatible AC bidirectional charger will cost about half as much as its $1,300 Ford Charge Station Pro, according to Canary Media, putting the anticipated price at about $650. However, the home power management technology still lacks a finalized price.

An external DC-to-AC conversion equipment used by many systems costs anywhere from slightly below $7,000 to above $10,000, per the report, creating a major financial hurdle for customers seeking backup power. This means Fathom is a cheaper alternative for those interested in bidirectional charging.

Interest in this technology has been rising sharply over the past decade, as battery storage can protect your home during outages and provide more energy independence. Beyond the vehicle-based approach Ford is developing, home battery storage can also help households save money on energy by giving them greater control over their electricity use.

title: Clean energy's next big breakthrough might look just like an oil field | Dagens.com
description:
Now, in an ironic twist of engineering fate, that exact same heavy machinery is driving one of the biggest breakthroughs in clean energy.
In theory, that makes geothermal energy the ultimate clean resource—it is carbon-free, virtually inexhaustible, and runs 24 hours a day regardless of whether the wind is blowing or the sun is shining.
The real driver behind the technology’s sudden surge is the desperate hunt for round-the-clock clean power.
By turning the mechanical tools of the fossil fuel boom against their original purpose, engineers are finally untethering geothermal energy from rare volcanic terrain.
The rigs that spent decades digging for oil are now building an endless, reliable clean power plant right under our feet.
text:
For decades, hydraulic fracturing was the primary villain of the modern environmental movement. The technology unlocked oceans of domestic crude and fossil gas across North America, but it also became synonymous with industrial blight, wastewater contamination, and flaring smokestacks.

Now, in an ironic twist of engineering fate, that exact same heavy machinery is driving one of the biggest breakthroughs in clean energy.

A new generation of geothermal startups is buying up surplus oil rigs, hiring veteran petroleum crews, and pointing directional drill heads straight into hot subterranean rock. By borrowing the techniques that built the shale boom, engineers are solving the single biggest flaw in traditional geothermal power: the fact that nature almost never puts heat, water, and porous rock in the same zip code.

The natural lottery of old geothermal

Underneath our feet, the Earth’s core is as hot as the surface of the sun. In theory, that makes geothermal energy the ultimate clean resource—it is carbon-free, virtually inexhaustible, and runs 24 hours a day regardless of whether the wind is blowing or the sun is shining.

In practice, geothermal has historically been an economic footnote. Until recently, building a conventional geothermal plant required winning a rare geological lottery. You needed three specific ingredients at the same shallow location: blistering heat, a deep reservoir of underground water, and permeable, porous rock that naturally lets that water circulate.

If any one of those three variables was missing, the well was useless. That is why conventional geothermal plants have remained geographically trapped in rare volcanic hotspots like Iceland, New Zealand, or the geysers of northern California. If you did not live near an active tectonic plate margin, you were out of luck.

Stealing the shale playbook

The breakthrough behind Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) starts with a simple realization: heat is everywhere if you drill deep enough. The missing ingredients are almost always the fluid and the permeable pathways.

Rather than wandering the desert hunting for rare natural hot springs, drilling engineers decided to manufacture their own.

To do it, they leaned entirely on the horizontal drilling techniques perfected in the oilfields of Texas and North Dakota. A standard oil-field rig bores straight down two to three miles through the Earth’s crust until it reaches dense, impermeable granite baking at temperatures north of 200°C. Then, using specialized steerable drill motors and fiber-optic sensors, the crew gradually bends the wellbore 90 degrees, drilling horizontally through the hot rock bed for thousands of feet.

Next, they drill a second horizontal well parallel to the first, just a few hundred feet above it.

Once the twin wells are in place, crews adapt the oil sector’s hydraulic stimulation methods. Instead of pumping toxic chemical slurries to release trapped hydrocarbons, they inject high-pressure water to gently open up microscopic fractures in the tight crystalline granite between the two wells. They are not blasting the rock apart; they are turning an impermeable slab of baking granite into an interconnected, highly permeable subsurface radiator.

Circulating the radiator

Once the artificial reservoir is established, the operation runs as a closed loop.

Crews pump cool water down the injection well. As the liquid is forced through the maze of micro-fractures, it absorbs immense heat directly from the surrounding rock. By the time it collects in the second wellbore, the water is superheated past 200°C.

That pressurized fluid rushes up to the surface and enters a binary cycle power plant. Because the system is sealed, the superheated subterranean brine never touches open air; it simply passes through a heat exchanger to flash-boil a secondary working fluid with a low boiling point, spinning a turbine to generate electricity before being pumped straight back underground to repeat the cycle.

The entire process consumes virtually no water after initial filling, emits zero greenhouse gases, and takes up a tiny fraction of the surface acreage required by a commercial wind or solar farm.

The rush for clean baseload

This transition from fringe science to commercial power is moving fast. Startups like Fervo Energy—founded by former petroleum drilling engineers—are proving that applying oilfield supply chains directly cuts drilling times and capital costs.

The real driver behind the technology’s sudden surge is the desperate hunt for round-the-clock clean power. As power-hungry artificial intelligence data centers, semiconductor fabs, and electrified manufacturing plants place unprecedented strain on regional grids, intermittent renewables like solar panels and wind turbines are hitting physical limits. Batteries can buffer short fluctuations, but they cannot keep a multi-gigawatt industrial facility running through weeks of cloudy, calm weather.

By turning the mechanical tools of the fossil fuel boom against their original purpose, engineers are finally untethering geothermal energy from rare volcanic terrain. The rigs that spent decades digging for oil are now building an endless, reliable clean power plant right under our feet.

text:
Calls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.

Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies.

Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transform humanity’s relationship with nature. Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets. The UK is set to meet just three of the 23.

After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade.

During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss.

Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement.

“A lot of what’s going on out here at the Cop is just a bunch of baloney and beautiful speeches and BS,” he told AFP earlier this week. “We cannot have – we cannot expect – a consensus between every nation on Earth on every topic. That’s ridiculous. Cops have been designed to fail, and they are not disappointing.”

He also argued that the UN should host a single environmental Cop each year to tackle the climate, biodiversity, plastics and other issues in one go.

“This just makes my blood boil, because while we fiddle, Rome burns,” he said.

The negotiations in the Armenian capital have seen Argentina, Saudi Arabia and Russia water down language on environmental ambition in the final agreement, while wealthier governments were divided on who would contribute more financial resources.

European nations would like to see additions to the list of donor states, as China and several of the Gulf states are still classified as developing countries in the UN process despite decades of rapid economic development. The final agreement in Yerevan left this issue open.

Key decisions on a fund to mobilise resources from firms that make money from digital forms of biodiversity, such as pharmaceutical companies, were postponed to the next summit in Ecuador in two years’ time. It had been hoped that the fund would generate £1bn a year for nature conservation, with a significant share going to Indigenous communities, but it has so far raised just over $10,000.

The calls for changes to the biodiversity Cop process echo an intervention by leading policy experts during climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024 who said the summit was “no longer fit for purpose” and needed to shift to focus on implementation.

Ruth Davis, the UK’s nature envoy, said she recognised that the meetings could be “extremely frustratiing”, but a huge amount of implementation was happening around the world.

“We’ve got to make the system actually deliver outcomes for people, otherwise they’ll lose confidence in it,” she said. “In the end, this is a process that is owned by governments who are parties to it. But I know we are going to find friends and allies in making the process work for the citizens of countries for whom this is really important, not least because they are the ones facing the impacts.”

Efforts to reform the UN’s sprawling environmental agenda are already under way. Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, said that the current systems were driving change, but they were moving too slowly.

“Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen. “We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands.

“Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that.”

text:
Read: 6 min

Leaders from both sides of the Atlantic met at this week’s EU-Canada Summit in Montreal to discuss deepening trade, technology and defence ties.

A key focus of the summit, now in its 21st year, was critical minerals.

“Canada has rich resources and deep mining expertise. Europe brings industrial demand, technology and investment,” EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Thursday at a summit event hosted by the C.D. Howe Institute.

Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne similarly touted the opportunities, mentioning critical minerals numerous times in an Oct. 29 address.

“On critical minerals, we can help them with economic growth,” he told reporters.

But Stéphane Dion, a former Liberal Party leader, says he has been hearing the same message for years — and not seen much change.

Dion was the special envoy to the European Union from 2017 to 2025.

“Each summit we say ‘critical minerals, critical minerals,’ then the money does not come, the investment does not come, it’s only talk,” Dion told Canadian Affairs in an Oct. 29 phone interview.

“I hope we’ll get out of that and we come with concrete results.”

‘The new oil’

Critical minerals refer to a broad range of mined metals and materials, including lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, copper and rare earth elements.

They are used in a wide range of technologies, including mobile phones, wind turbines, solar panels, EV batteries and defence applications.

Critical minerals are so crucial to the green transition that Evan Pivnick, program manager at the industry association Clean Energy BC, dubs them “the new oil.”

“We have a civilization built materially on fossil fuels and now it should be done on minerals — that’s the big picture,” Dion said.

“To have a source of energy that is not fossil fuels, you need the minerals. And Europe is looking for that.”

Currently, the European Union relies heavily on China for critical minerals, creating a significant vulnerability.

China has “introduced an ever-widening set of export controls …. [that] concerns both critical raw materials and certain technologies. These controls are negatively impacting EU supply chains,” a European Commission factsheet says.

“The EU is committed to de-risking, not decoupling from China. This entails reducing critical dependencies and vulnerabilities,” the factsheet adds.

In 2023, the EU passed the Critical Raw Materials Act, which sets targets for how much critical minerals Europe should mine and process itself by 2030. The act says the bloc should not rely on any single external country for more than 65 per cent of a strategic material.

Philippe Le Billon, a professor of geography at the University of British Columbia, notes the EU’s progress toward these targets has been limited.

“It’s going very slow,” he said.

Globally, China accounts for over 90 per cent of battery-grade graphite production, 85 per cent of magnet rare earth separation, 75 per cent of cobalt refining, 70 per cent of lithium refining and nearly 50 per cent of global copper refining capacity.

Within the EU, China provides 97 per cent of the EU’s magnesium, a critical resource for the auto sector. And the bloc’s entire supply of rare earths — often used for green technology — are refined in China.

Dion notes there are limits to the EU’s ability to diversify away from China.

“I don’t think they may be completely independent of Chinese critical minerals, it’s not possible,” said Dion.

“But they would like to be less dependent. They would like to have other options. And Canada is key for that because we have the resources and we are a strong ally in NATO.”

Pivnick, of Clean Energy BC, says the EU is increasingly willing to pay a “security premium” for non-Chinese supplies.

“They’ve seen what happens when they’re overly reliant on a given country,” he said, noting Russia was the EU’s main supplier of natural gas before its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

“They’ve been in this place with Russia when it came to gas. They see the value of diversification.”

Opportunities

The EU’s desire to diversify suppliers could present Canada with an opportunity.

“Canada has meaningful reserves of critical minerals,” said Pivnick.

Canada is the world’s largest producer and exporter of potash, which is mainly used in fertilizer. It is the world’s second-largest uranium producer, and a significant producer of cobalt and nickel. It also holds a substantial share of the world’s lithium and rare earth reserves.

In total, Canada exported over $49-billion worth of critical minerals in 2025, with about 11 per cent going to the European Union.

This week, the European Investment Bank — an EU bank that invests directly in projects in line with EU goals — signed a framework agreement with Canada to allow investment into Canadian critical mineral projects.

“This Framework Agreement marks a critical step in strengthening Canada-EU economic ties and unlocking investment in Canadian resource projects,” Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said in a press release.

It is not clear how much the bank will invest into Canadian projects.

The deepening of ties is creating enthusiasm in the minerals industry, says Gillian Holcroft, CEO and co-founder of Green Graphite Technologies, a company that produces mined and recycled graphite for batteries.

“It’s an exciting time for a company like ours,” she said, noting that the company is starting work with a European battery cell firm that she cannot name.

“We love working with Europeans.”

Pivnick says the EU bank’s moves point to the bloc’s willingness to pay a security premium for non-Chinese supplies.

“Some of the funding from the European Union — whether it’s through the [European Investment Bank] or individual nation states — can be thought of as paying some of that security premium … that helps them achieve their diversification goals.”

Pivnick says Canada should be “leaning into” its relatively high regulatory standards, which are similar to the EU’s own regulations.

“We’re going to be a higher cost jurisdiction regardless. We develop things with higher standards, both environmental, social governance, you name it,” he said.

Holcroft agrees.

“It’s very difficult to compete head to head with China using the values for the environment and people that we have in North America and Europe,” she said.

“Copying what they do in China and trying to replicate it here in North America, I always say it’s like a race to the bottom.”

‘Very frustrated’

Canada’s big challenge, however, is getting its critical minerals to market.

In 2022, Canada launched a Critical Mineral Strategy aimed at jumpstarting the industry. The government pledged $3.8 billion for exploration, processing, recycling and manufacturing of 31 critical minerals, as well as $1.5 billion to develop mine infrastructure.

In March, Natural Resources Canada also committed a separate $3.6 billion to get new extraction projects off the ground.

And yet, progress has been slow.

“When I talk to people wanting to start critical mineral projects here, [they say] it’s super slow and they’re very frustrated,” said Le Billon, of the University of British Columbia.

In recent years, Canada’s refining capabilities have been flat. Canada currently has 31 operational critical mineral processing facilities, down from 33 in 2016.

There are signs of hope: 32 new projects are now in “advanced” stages of development.

Holcroft’s firm processes its graphite — which has to be over 99.95 per cent pure to be used in batteries — using a technique she says is both cost and resource effective. The Chinese method is much more water-intensive and uses large quantities of highly-toxic hydrofluoric acid, she says.

“To use Chinese technology in North America, you can do it, but it’s going to cost you a lot in terms of water treatment and water usage,” Holcroft said.

“To keep people safe is also extremely expensive because that’s one of the nastiest acids out there, so you need incredible personal protection [equipment].”

Le Billon says boosting Canada’s refining capacity will be essential for both sides to realize their critical mineral goals. But he worries Canadian governments often concentrate their support too heavily in select industries.

“We’ve seen these things collapse,” said Le Billon, referencing Quebec’s $510-million investment into the Northvolt battery plant, which went bust after its parent company declared bankruptcy in March 2025.

But Holcroft says funding from the Canadian government, particularly from the Business Development Bank, has been essential to getting Green Graphite Technologies off the ground.

She adds that government funding will be essential to rebuilding not just the mining industry as, but also Canada’s manufacturing and industrial sectors as a whole.

“These jobs and industries have disappeared and it’s not so easy to get them back. What the government’s doing is saying is ‘Canada has the resources in the ground, these critical mineral resources. Let’s be a complete solution,’” she said.

“It would be fantastic to build up this industry, but it takes a lot of government support.”

Pivnick points out that raw material extraction and processing are only one part of the puzzle. Ports and rail infrastructure are going to need to see major investments, he says.

“That’s going to be a really big signal about how serious Canada is in looking at exports to the EU — is whether we build the port infrastructure needed to both stockpile and store critical minerals, but also move it in meaningful quantities across the ocean,” he said.

Pivnick says he will regard this year’s summit as a success if it leads to concrete agreements and a pathway for European investment.

“For this to become real, we really have to move from MOUs to offtake agreements,” he said.

This point echoed a call by Tobias Cremer, a German member of European Parliament and the EU’s rapporteur on Canada, last week.

“For the last couple of months, we’ve been great, Canada and Europe, at writing each other love letters and saying how much we really want to work together,” Cremer said in the EU Parliament.

“But I think now is really the time to start to get serious and turn that love story into concrete commitments.”
