text:
Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, a global leader in electric vehicle (EV) and battery supply chain research, published its report on September 2026 EV sales, noting a 17% month-on-month increase despite a 2% year-on-year decrease.

The month saw 2.15 million EVs sold globally, led by the UK and Europe, while North America and China saw slowdowns.

Benchmark reports that Europe and the UK saw their strongest month on record, with nearly 600,000 EVs sold. Sales were up 39% year-on-year, led by battery EVs, followed by plug-in hybrids.

The growth across the region was broad, spanning the UK, France, Spain, Portugal, and Finland, with each country recording its highest-ever monthly EV sales.

September 2026 also saw the European Union (EU) and China agree to limit the imports of Chinese-built hybrids into the region to 350,000 units a year for four years from 2027.

According to Benchmark, around 14% of plug-in hybrid EVs sold in the UK, EU, and European Free Trade Association in 2025 were made in China, with that number rising to 29% in 2026.

Higher fuel prices, driven by the war in Iran, have in fact encouraged more EV purchases throughout the region.

North America’s decline was steep, down 44% year-on-year in September. Benchmark’s report notes that this decline reflects a comparison to September 2025, which saw record growth as US buyers rushed to purchase EVs before the expiry of the federal government’s tax credit.

The authors note that they expect the decline to narrow moving forward, as new figures will be measured against the months following the removal of the tax credit.

Notably, China’s EV sales declined 18% year-on-year in September, even as sales rose 7% month-on-month. That said, EV penetration across China remains strong. While domestic demand was down, manufacturers were able to maintain production and exports to other markets.

EV exports out of China reached a monthly record of 558,000 units in September, though policy changes, such as those out of the EU, could impact those figures moving forward.

China drives the global EV market

Wood Mackenzie notes that overall, the industry is trending up, with EVs now representing one in three new cars sold globally, despite the regional complexities.

The analytics and data company notes that Chinese-made EVs are setting a new benchmark for affordability, even if that’s not helping to turn around domestic sales. While Chinese EV penetration is at nearly 70%, sales are down nearly 1 million units since the 2025 peak of 9 million.

Wood Mackenzie notes that it’s not just EVs, but China’s entire vehicle market that’s seeing lower sales this year, with internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles accounting for the biggest drop in sales, mostly driven by a weak macroeconomic outlook.

While Chinese consumers may be buying fewer vehicles, Chinese EVs are being exported to global markets in larger numbers, with buyers noting that the prices are more competitive than Western-made EVs.

With Europe setting import quotas on Chinese EVs, Chinese automotive manufacturers are building capacity and battery supply chains within Europe itself, providing a new market for European-made Chinese EVs to replace those imports.

The critical metals behind every EV

Compared to ICE vehicles, EVs require a wider range of metals and significantly greater volumes overall.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that an ICE vehicle requires around 22.3kg of copper (Cu), 11.2kg of manganese (Mn), 0.1kg of zinc, and 0.3kg of other metals.

Compare that to an EV, which contains 53.2kg Cu, 8.9kg of lithium, 39.9kg of nickel, 24.5kg Mn, 13.3kg of cobalt, 66.3kg of graphite, from 0.5 to 1kg of rare earths, 0.1kg of zinc, and 0.3kg of others.

Benchmark Head of Battery Raw Materials Adam Webb highlights that the same raw materials needed for EVs are also fuelling another fast-growing sector: battery energy storage systems (BESS).

The most important material Webb highlights is lithium, which is used across all lithium-ion batteries, with about 90% of lithium demand coming from the battery sector.

Webb notes that the lithium market has been in deficit this year, largely driven by the BESS sector rather than EVs.

“We’ve seen new BESS deployments increase by around 40% year-on-year. We’re expecting that this year, the supply of those batteries will increase at an even greater rate,” Webb says.

The growth in production of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in particular has pushed demand up for lithium this year quite significantly, accounting for 30% of its growth.

On the supply side of lithium, there have been pockets of growth, with new projects coming online. This has pushed supply up around 20%, but it still does not keep pace with demand.

On the pricing front, the supply deficit has driven lithium carbonate prices up from about US$10,000 ($14,173) per tonne in mid-2025 to above US$20,000. Webb notes that while there’s been a recent pullback in prices, that’s more sentiment-driven, as the fundamentals still point to a supply deficit.

Nickel and cobalt are both used in the cathode of nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries, which are not used in the BESS sector but are prevalent in EVs.

Around 75% of mined cobalt supply comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The DRC has imposed export bans and quotas on copper and cobalt concentrates to encourage domestic processing and local value addition, as previously reported. This has reduced the amount of cobalt entering the market, pushing it into a deficit and driving a rally in prices.

Nickel has faced a similar situation, with Indonesia dominating the market and accounting for 60% of global supply. Indonesia has also imposed quotas through the Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya (RKAB) system, limiting the amount of ore that can be mined to supply its smelters.

With quotas much lower this year than in previous years, Indonesia’s output has been significantly affected, resulting in an overall drop in nickel production. At the same time, demand is rising from the battery and stainless steel markets.

Rare earth elements (REEs) too are essential, not just in EVs, but across renewable energies such as wind turbines, and in defence applications, including fighter jets, submarines, missiles, and radar.

Around 1kg of REEs is needed for an EV, while a 3 megawatt wind turbine uses 2 tonnes of rare earth magnets and a US F-35 fighter jet requires 920 pounds of REEs.

Building a rare earths and lithium future

Avalon Advanced Materials (TSX:AVL) is positioning itself as a key North American player in the energy transition through the sustainable development of lithium and REEs.

The company’s Nechalacho Project in Canada’s Northwest Territories is being advanced as a potential key supplier of magnet rare earth elements and other strategic materials to Western markets. China currently controls over 90% of total rare earth processing capacity.

Nechalacho provides exposure across terbium, dysprosium, praseodymium, and neodymium, key metals used in EVs, wind turbines, robotics, electronics, and in key defence technologies.

Avalon is taking a sustainable approach to rare earths processing, working in collaboration with Engina Corporation. Together, the companies have successfully recovered 15 REEs from Nechalacho concentrate, with over 90% total recovery in preliminary testing. This has been achieved using a CO2-based extraction process.

Avalon’s Lake Superior Lithium Project in Thunder Bay, Ontario, is a proposed lithium chemical processing facility that is looking to convert spodumene concentrate into battery-grade lithium for the BESS and EV sectors.

The company notes that demand for lithium is growing rapidly, with expectations that 96% of lithium demand will come from the battery space by 2040.

Avalon is advancing Lake Superior as an efficient and sustainable path to battery-grade lithium, using Metso’s (METSO.HE) proprietary alkaline leach process.

Avalon Advanced Materials is focused on securing and developing critical minerals projects to support domestic supply chains for the clean energy, advanced manufacturing, and technology sectors.

Backing battery-grade manganese

Black Canyon (ASX:BCA) is advancing ‘high-grade’ contained manganese deposits in Western Australia, including the Wandanya manganese and iron discovery.

The company notes the strategic nature of manganese, with the current supply chain mainly focused in South Africa, Gabon, and Australia. Manganese is essential in the production of steel, but has a growing role in lithium-ion battery cathodes, enhancing the energy density, capacity, and safety of the batteries while helping to reduce costs as compared to alternative chemistries that are high in cobalt.

Black Canyon has recently reported a maiden mineral resource estimate (MRE) for Wandanya, noting 23.6 million tonnes (Mt) at 25.8% Mn. The company is also expecting to complete its Scoping Study for the project by December 2026.

The resource at Wandanya comprises 66% measured, 26% indicated, and 8% inferred, at a 12% Mn cut-off. At higher cut-offs, the deposit contains 16.8Mt @ 30% Mn (20% cut-off) and potential direct ship ore material at 3.7Mt @ 38.9% Mn (35% cut-off).

Wandanya also contains a separate iron resource at 12.5Mt @ 54.9% iron.

Black Canyon is a Western Australian manganese explorer and developer, advancing the Wandanya Project in the Pilbara.

Chasing US lithium supply

Surge Battery Metals (TSX-V:NILI) highlights the importance of lithium in both BESS and EVs and is advancing the Nevada North Lithium Project (NNLP) in Elko County, US, to help supply that industry.

The company is focused on the potential to supply high-purity, battery-grade lithium made in the US from Nevada’s ‘battery belt’.

Surge Battery Metals is working with Cassidy and Associates, based in Washington, DC, on its federal and agency outreach. This includes building relationships with key government agencies and aligning with federal policies focused on US critical minerals and energy.

A Prefeasibility Study (PFS) delivered in 2026 outlined a mine life of 42 years, with approximately 411Mt mined over the life of mine and 218.3Mt of ore processed at an average grade of 3,928 parts per million lithium. For the first 10 years of production, the average grade processed would be 4,340ppm lithium.

NNLP is a joint venture between Surge and Evolution Mining (ASX:EVN), and has produced 99.95% battery-grade lithium carbonate from work that was completed in support of the PFS.

Surge CEO Greg Reimer says this milestone demonstrates the company’s potential to supply the US battery industry.

“We have now demonstrated the full chain — from sedimentary clay in the ground, through a conventional leach and purification circuit, to a refined product that meets battery-grade specifications,” Reimer says.

Surge Battery Metals is now focused on pilot-scale work testing recovery, consistency, reagent consumption, and energy performance under continuous operating conditions.

The company is working towards a final investment decision in 2028, with permitting, baseline studies, environmental reporting, Feasibility Study drilling, and PFS work underway. A pilot plant program is scheduled to commence in January 2027.

Graphite’s growing strategic role

E-Power Resources (CSE:EPR) is a pure-play graphite exploration company focused on the Tetepisca Flake Graphite Project in Québec, Canada.

The company notes the essential role of graphite in lithium-ion batteries for EVs, where it makes up the largest component by weight, with no known substitutes.

With more than 80% of current graphite supply coming from China, E-Power sees room to grow North American supply to deliver into local supply chains.

Tetepisca spans 230 claims over 12,620 hectares, and is around 300km north of Baie-Comeau on the north shore of Québec, within the Tetepisca Graphite District, a well-known graphite-bearing region.

E-Power’s near-term exploration work will focus on derisking the project, with a maiden MRE expected in Q1 or Q2 2027, followed by a preliminary economic assessment and Scoping Study.

As EV adoption continues to climb and BESS applications drive demand for critical minerals, securing reliable supplies of lithium, graphite, manganese, nickel, cobalt, and rare earths is becoming just as important as manufacturing the vehicles themselves.

While regional sales trends may fluctuate, the broader energy transition remains firmly intact, underpinning long-term demand for the raw materials that power electric mobility, renewable energy, and grid-scale storage.

The opportunity extends beyond automakers and battery manufacturers and into the miners and developers working to build the next generation of critical minerals supply chains. Companies advancing these projects are positioning themselves to support a market that is expected to expand for decades as governments, industry, and consumers continue to push for electrification and energy security.

Write to Amy Rotman at Mining.com.au

title: An 11,200-foot geothermal well drilled straight down into the Utah desert in under 11 days ...
description:
If you’ve read anything about geothermal power in Utah lately, it was probably about Cape Station.
But the hottest hole Fervo Energy has ever drilled isn’t at Cape Station.
Here’s how Blanford stacks up against the other rock Fervo has drilled into, using its own figures.
Fervo says Cape Station has more than 4 gigawatts of total potential, and the company is building 500 megawatts of it.
Fervo describes Blanford as a cluster north of Cape Station and hasn’t pinned it to a town.
text:
If you’ve read anything about geothermal power in Utah lately, it was probably about Cape Station. That’s the plant in Beaver County that started selling electricity at the end of September, and we covered it when its first 33-megawatt block hit commercial operation a day ahead of its contract.

But the hottest hole Fervo Energy has ever drilled isn’t at Cape Station. It’s one county north, in Millard County, at a site the company calls Blanford. And the rock down there is a lot hotter than the rock feeding the plant that just switched on.

The well is called Cottonwood. It went straight down to about 11,200 feet in under 11 days, and temperature logs at the bottom came back above 555 degrees Fahrenheit. The company says that’s the hottest well in its history. It first announced the result at Stanford’s annual geothermal workshop earlier this year, then repeated it in its first quarterly report as a public company.

That’s a company record, by the way. Nobody at the company claims it’s the hottest geothermal well anywhere, and I’m not going to claim it for them.

So why does 555 degrees matter?

A quick refresher if you’re new to this. Fervo’s kind of geothermal doesn’t go hunting for natural pockets of underground hot water the way older plants do. Its crews drill into hot, dry rock, crack it open with the same fracking equipment shale companies use, and pump water through those cracks so it comes back up hot enough to run a turbine.

Basically, the hotter the rock, the more energy every gallon of water carries back to the surface.

Fervo’s CEO, Tim Latimer, put a number on that when he talked to analysts on the company’s August 12 earnings call. Moving from 400-degree rock to the 430 degrees that Cape Station’s second phase is designed around should squeeze about 27% more power out of the same well flow and the same steel on the surface, he said. Blanford’s rock sits more than 125 degrees above that 430-degree design point.

Now, I wouldn’t stretch that 27% in a straight line all the way up to 555 degrees. Nobody has published a power estimate per well for Blanford, and I can’t do that math for them from a press release. Still, it’s pretty safe to say a well in 555-degree rock carries a lot more heat than one in 400-degree rock, and more heat per well is how a geothermal company gets more electricity out of every hole it pays for.

Here’s how Blanford stacks up against the other rock Fervo has drilled into, using its own figures.

There’s one more number in there that I think gets overlooked. Blanford’s geothermal gradient ranks above the 95th percentile of deep sites in the western US, according to the company’s temperature logs. Gradient is just how fast the rock heats up as you go down. So the ground there warms with depth faster than at least 95% of comparable spots in the West.

The rock is easier to drill, too

The other surprise is what the rock is made of. Fervo’s earlier projects went into metamorphic and igneous rock, the hard crystalline stuff (granite is the classic example) that enhanced geothermal usually goes after. Blanford’s reservoir is sedimentary, made up of sandstone, claystone and carbonate layers, and the company says those are easier and cheaper to drill than granite.

If you’ve ever put a drill through a wooden stud and then hit a concrete wall, you already get the idea. The company’s executives told analysts in August that granite is a much harder rock to drill through than shale, and that a good chunk of their engineering work goes into gear that can survive it.

Under 11 days for 11,200 feet is quick by Fervo’s own history. Latimer said on the same call that the company’s very first well at Project Red took over 70 days to reach roughly 11,000 feet. That’s not a perfect comparison, admittedly. As far as I can tell, the Nevada well turned and ran sideways for part of its length, which is slower work than going straight down. The crews have also gotten a lot faster since then, and Fervo’s Sawtooth 7 well at Cape Station reached 19,448 feet in 21 days this summer.

Still, a hotter field in softer rock is a pretty nice combination to stumble onto.

Except Fervo says it didn’t stumble onto it. According to the company’s announcement, its AI-driven subsurface analytics picked out the hot sedimentary basin as a new kind of target and helped plan the drilling. Jack Norbeck, Fervo’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said the result shows the team can “detect and develop EGS sweet spots” with AI-assisted geophysics. That’s a fairly corporate way of saying the computer picked a good spot. I’ll give them this one, though, because the first well the computer picked came back hotter than anything else they’ve drilled.

We still don’t know much about Blanford

So when does Blanford start making electricity?

Nobody outside the company can say yet. Fervo hasn’t put a power figure or a timeline on the site, and I can’t find a customer attached to it. As far as I can tell, there isn’t a horizontal well there yet either. Cottonwood is what the company calls an observation well. It’s a straight hole drilled to measure the rock, and that’s a long way from the sideways production wells that actually feed a power plant.

Fervo did run what’s called a diagnostic fracture injection test in the well. You pump fluid in until the rock cracks a little, shut the pumps off and watch how fast the pressure bleeds away. That tells engineers how the rock breaks and how tight it is, and Fervo says the test confirmed it can stimulate the formation.

Then there’s the size. An independent assessment based on the drilling data puts Blanford’s potential at multiple gigawatts, according to Fervo, but the announcement doesn’t name the firm that did it. I’d treat “multi-gigawatt” with some caution anyway. It’s an estimate of heat in the ground, and power plants are a different thing. Fervo says Cape Station has more than 4 gigawatts of total potential, and the company is building 500 megawatts of it.

Fervo describes Blanford as a cluster north of Cape Station and hasn’t pinned it to a town. Millard County is big, quiet country, with 12,975 people at the 2020 census.

title: Smart #2 Couture sells out in Europe in just two weeks: What's behind the rush?
description:
The Smart #2 made its debut at the Paris Motor Show on October 12.
Pre-orders opened across Europe just one day later, with the Couture Edition limited to 999 units – and every single one has now been snapped up.
The electric two-seater is powered by a rear-mounted electric motor producing 82 hp (60 kW) and 130 Nm (96 lb-ft) of torque.
Just 999 examples of the Couture Edition are available across Europe, featuring matte white paint, a gold-colored roof and matching wheels.
According to reports, demand for the other Smart #2 variants is also high, although no concrete sales figures have been released so far.
text:
The Smart #2 made its debut at the Paris Motor Show on October 12. Pre-orders opened across Europe just one day later, with the Couture Edition limited to 999 units – and every single one has now been snapped up. The company confirmed the sellout in an official announcement on October 30. Considering that the Paris unveiling has so far been the only opportunity to see the compact electric city car in person, and that customers will have to wait until the second quarter of 2027 for the first deliveries, that's quite an impressive sales success. But what's driving the demand?

One major reason is likely the return of the classic Smart concept. In recent years, the manufacturer has introduced significantly larger vehicles with the #1, #3 and #5 models. With the new #2, Smart is returning to its roots for the first time since production of the fortwo ended in 2024: a genuine two-seat city car measuring less than three meters in length.

The new Smart #2 measures just 2.75 meters (9 feet) long and, with a turning circle of only 6.95 meters (22.8 feet), should feel right at home on narrow city streets. The electric two-seater is powered by a rear-mounted electric motor producing 82 hp (60 kW) and 130 Nm (96 lb-ft) of torque. Its 35.8-kWh battery is expected to deliver a range of up to 290 kilometers (180 miles) under the WLTP cycle. DC fast charging is supported at up to 65 kW, allowing the battery to charge from 10 to 80% in around 20 minutes under optimal conditions.

The limited edition's exclusivity likely also played a role in its sales success. Just 999 examples of the Couture Edition are available across Europe, featuring matte white paint, a gold-colored roof and matching wheels. Those who aren't particularly interested in the exclusive styling can still pre-order one of the three regular variants: Pure, Pure+ and Premium. Prices start at €19,990 (approximately $22,400), while the better-equipped versions cost at least €20,990 (around $23,500) and €24,490 (around $27,400), respectively. According to reports, demand for the other Smart #2 variants is also high, although no concrete sales figures have been released so far.

title: Editorial: Surging oil costs spur renewables development - Rocky Mount Telegram
description: Despite continuing Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, oil shipments from the Middle East have now surpassed prewar levels. The might of the U.S. military is to thank for
text:
If a muscle atrophies, our bodies weaken. We can’t walk very…

Accusing political leaders of gerrymandering used to be quite the insult. It was…



A flare burns off methane and other hydrocarbons as oil pumpjacks operate in the Permian Basin in Midland, Texas, on Oct. 12, 2021.

Despite continuing Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, oil shipments from the Middle East have now surpassed prewar levels. The might of the U.S. military is to thank for the recovery of oil flows through the strait itself. But the proliferation of alternative routes around the region, new production outside the Middle East and declining fuel consumption are thanks to the might of the free market.

Oil flows throughout the Middle East averaged more than 24 million barrels a day last week, up from 23.3 million before the war, according to the ship tracker Kpler. Heavier reliance on Saudi and Emirati pipelines has allowed more crude to bypass the strait: 40 percent of non-Iranian Gulf crude is going through pipelines, up from 17 percent before the war.

At the same time, the U.S. military has helped restore flows through the strait even as an American embargo has mostly choked off Iranian crude. Oil flows through the strait have rebounded to 82 percent of prewar levels, facilitated by a clever ship-to-ship transfer system in which the military escorts shuttle tankers through Hormuz to cargo ships in the Gulf of Oman.

While the work-around has proved effective, oil flows cannot rely on costly military escorts in perpetuity. Attacks by Iranians and their proxies, combined with an expectation that hostilities will escalate following the midterm elections, keep prices elevated. These were foreseeable consequences of President Donald Trump’s war of choice. Picking this fight in February all but guaranteed trouble in the strait.

Oil production across the Western Hemisphere is projected to surge in the next decade, as high prices justify investments in marginal projects. Chevron, for example, plans to put nearly $14 billion into Argentina over the next decade, tripling production there. Four out of five institutional investors say that disruptions in Middle Eastern markets make them more likely to invest in Canada, according to a recent survey by ATB Cormark Capital Markets.

Thanks to a freer, more diversified energy market, the Iran war has not re-created the crippling shortages Americans endured in the 1970s. While high gas prices are certainly a major political headache for the party in power, the U.S. has been relatively insulated.

Over the past decade, the U.S. has expanded energy production through fracking and horizontal drilling, leading to record-high domestic crude output and growing exports. Before the war, Americans were already importing far more petroleum from Canada than the Middle East. Last year, only 8 percent of U.S. crude imports came from Gulf countries.

President Richard M. Nixon instituted disastrous price controls on oil after a 1973 OPEC embargo. Whenever prices are artificially capped below the market equilibrium, demand outstrips supply, leading to the shortages and gas lines that endured through the decade. Trump floated a ban on diesel exports last month, but advisers convinced him that the idea would backfire by causing supply disruptions.

Finally, high prices cause people to use less oil. Electric vehicles become more attractive. So does public transit. The IEA forecast in August that global oil demand would decline 1.6 million barrels per day this year.

The lesson for long-term energy security is that government should welcome abundance, competition and trade. Let prices rise when oil gets scarce. Let producers profit by finding more of it. Let consumers decide when substitutes make sense. Free markets cannot prevent wars, but they can make their fallout much harder for adversaries to dictate.

title: How tax credit transfers are opening clean energy finance to more players
description:
As the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) made its way through Congress last year, there was understandable concern that its curbs on wind and solar subsidies might slow clean energy finance to a crawl.
More than a year since the legislation was signed, tax credit volumes have thus far proved the doomsaying premature.
Transfers are absorbing the shock Under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, a developer can sell a clean energy tax credit to a corporate buyer rather than (or alongside) structuring a traditional tax equity partnership.
Nearly half of the credit volume purchased in 2025 covered other tax years, including close to $9 billion in long-dated production tax credit (PTC) strips.
The clean energy sector spent the last two years absorbing a policy shock that was supposed to shrink the market.
text:
This was authored for Banyan Infrastructure by Rob Glen , an energy markets and infrastructure strategist with more than two decades of experience advising technology companies, investors, and infrastructure developers on market strategy, commercialization, and strategic partnerships. Previously, he helped build and scale BloombergNEF's energy transition intelligence business and held senior leadership roles at 451 Research, bringing deep industry expertise to the convergence of AI, grid modernization, and the global energy transition.

As the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) made its way through Congress last year, there was understandable concern that its curbs on wind and solar subsidies might slow clean energy finance to a crawl. The final version accelerated the phase-out of the Section 45Y and 48E credits for wind and solar projects, imposed Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) rules, and left developers waiting on Treasury guidance for how to even calculate compliance. While certainly not the worst-case scenario feared at the outset of the legislative process, many still expected a chilling effect on project financing in the renewable sector.

More than a year since the legislation was signed, tax credit volumes have thus far proved the doomsaying premature. Total tax credit monetization is on pace to approach $70 billion by the end of 2026, up roughly 11% year-over-year, and the flow of capital to clean energy across power, manufacturing, and clean fuels is tracking toward more than $143 billion, a 19% increase over 2025. The market for credits didn't shrink under OBBBA. Thanks in part to growing demand for power and scaled-up 45X and 45Z volumes from manufacturers' investment and renewable fuel production, it expanded; part of that unexpected traction stems from credit transferability.

Transfers are absorbing the shock

Under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, a developer can sell a clean energy tax credit to a corporate buyer rather than (or alongside) structuring a traditional tax equity partnership. Transfer volume grew from $32 billion in 2024 to $42 billion in 2025, a 48% year-over-year increase. Crux — the marketplace and data provider that tracks the bulk of transfer activity — now projects $47.5–49 billion for the full year, up as much as 18% from 2025. That's a market absorbing a genuine policy shock within two quarters and coming out the other side larger than before.

A market growing in two different directions at once

The more interesting story isn't just that transfers grew; it's how. Two distinct dynamics are driving that growth, and they're pulling in different directions.

On the dollar side, growth is concentrated in large, complex transactions. Nearly half of the credit volume purchased in 2025 covered other tax years, including close to $9 billion in long-dated production tax credit (PTC) strips. The deals involve very large, multi-year commitments typically negotiated by banks and other sophisticated corporate buyers and large sellers and move enormous dollar volume.

On the participation side, by contrast, the market is broadening. Roughly 243 Fortune 1000 companies — nearly a quarter of the index — were active tax credit buyers through the third quarter of 2025, a nearly 60% year-over-year increase in the number of member corporations buying credits. This figure doesn’t include smaller taxpayers that have joined the supply side as their accountants and other financial advisers have become more comfortable using clean energy credits to offset taxable income. Crux's own market guidance is explicit about why: transferability exists precisely because traditional tax equity's scale and structuring requirements historically shut out smaller or newer developers on the sell-side and corporations and high-net-worth individuals with less predictable incomes on the buy-side. The transfer market gives them a simpler way in. As more of those developers and buyers enter, the number of individual deals in the market grows even where dollar volume doesn't grow at the same clip. A small handful of nine-figure PTC strips can dwarf hundreds of smaller transactions in dollar terms while the transaction count tells the opposite story.

The upshot: the market's dollar growth and its unit growth are being driven by different populations of participants, and the smaller end of that population — the C&I solar deal, the single-project ITC transfer, the first-time seller — is where the count is actually expanding.

Small deals don't get a smaller diligence burden

This is where the mechanics of a tax credit transfer matter, because they don't scale down with deal size.

A transfer isn't a simple bill of sale. Proceeds from a credit sale are tax-exempt cash to both the seller and the buyer. There’s no above-the-line impact on either side's taxable income, which is exactly why the cash has to be tracked as its own distinct line rather than folded into revenue. And that cash is never a dollar-for-dollar swap. Credits typically trade at a discount to par, commonly in the 85–95 cent range, sometimes less for higher risk technologies and weaker or smaller projects. Each transaction requires computing proceeds as credits sold times price per credit, with the credit quantity itself often still moving. ITCs are calculated as a percentage of build cost or fair market value through commercial operation, PTCs as a percentage of actualized generation and sales.

None of that complexity is a function of deal size. A $2 million single-project ITC transfer requires almost as much work as a $200 million PTC strip: verifying the credit amount, pricing the transfer, tracking the buyer relationship, screening for Prohibited Foreign Entity exposure, negotiating the tax credit transfer agreement, and reconciling projected proceeds against what actually clears. The $200 million deal can justify a bespoke team of advisors underwriting the diligence and transaction cost across a large transaction. The $2 million deal, run by a smaller developer who may be transacting for the first time, cannot. That developer is exactly the transfer market participant that Crux's data shows is growing the fastest.

Why the software layer matters more, not less

This is the gap the current generation of finance and compliance software is built to close. Tools that automate PFE screening against cap tables and supply contracts, price transfers using market-wide bid data rather than one-off negotiation, and track variance between projected and actualized credit quantities effectively substitute software for the fixed cost of diligence that used to require a specialized team on every deal, at every size.

Purpose-built FEOC and prevailing-wage compliance tools automate the legal review — cap tables, supply contracts, watchlist screening — that used to be manual and expensive regardless of transaction size. And project finance platforms like Banyan Infrastructure are extending that logic across the full deal lifecycle, applying the same AI-driven ingestion and scoring to legal, financial, and covenant data that a fixed diligence team once tracked by hand.

The pattern across all of these categories is the same: software absorbs a cost that doesn't scale down, which is exactly what makes it valuable to a market whose unit growth is coming from participants who can least afford to pay that cost themselves.

Where this goes next

If the transfer market keeps broadening the way 2025 and 2026 suggest — namely, more buyers, more first-time sellers, more small deals alongside a handful of enormous ones — the tools built for one narrow purpose (e.g., pricing, Prohibited Foreign Entity screening, proceeds tracking) are likely to keep converging into single platforms that can serve a deal at any size without changing the underlying workflow. The clean energy sector spent the last two years absorbing a policy shock that was supposed to shrink the market. Instead, it grew, fragmented into more and smaller pieces, and built exactly the kind of standardized, repeatable, data-intensive problem that software is positioned to solve.

title: The Share of Solar Generation with Co-located Battery Storage Is Increasing
description:
Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity.
Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year.
When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices.
Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity.
The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators.

Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028.

When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment.

We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies.

Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.

text:
It’s a good time to be a coal plant in the US. The Trump administration has given support to almost half of the nation’s coal plants, helping them to continue operating despite economic and regulatory headwinds, according to a new analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund.

The analysis, which looked at the 184 operating coal plants that are connected to the grid, found that 90 received support from the Trump administration through “cash handouts, free passes to pollute, and requirements to stay online past their retirement dates”.

The administration provided $950m in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and handed Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants, according to the EDF analysis.

“It’s extending the life of these coal plants,” said Surbhi Sarang, director and senior attorney at the Environmental Defense Fund. “The administration has leveraged a multitude of tools to prop up coal plants, and ultimately all of that is harming Americans even more by increasing electricity costs, by increasing pollution – it’s like Americans are getting hit twice.”

In 2015, the EPA’s Mercury and Air Toxics Standards first took effect, driving down dangerous pollution from power plants by more than 90%. In 2024, the EPA updated the standards to further reduce harmful pollution from coal-fired power plants. In the early days of the second Trump term, companies were invited to email the administration to request an exemption from the 2024 standards. According to emails obtained by the EDF through Freedom of Information Act requests, companies expressed concern that the standards would cost them too much money.

The Colstrip plant in Montana has operated for more than 40 years, affecting nearby communities like the Northern Cheyenne reservation by releasing toxic chemicals like mercury, arsenic, lead and nickel. “That’s one of the dirtiest coal plants that’s still operating in the nation,” Sarang said.

In 2024, the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for coal-fired power plants was strengthened in several ways. For example, the standard for fine particulate matter, or fPM, reduced allowable emissions of nickel, arsenic, lead and other toxic metals from coal plants by two-thirds. According to the EDF, NorthWestern Energy and Talen Energy, which own and operate the Colstrip plant, requested an exemption from the fPM requirement.

Brian Bird, president and CEO of NorthWestern, wrote an email to the Department of Energy in March 2025 asking for a 15-minute chat about the standards with administrator Lee Zeldin. In the email, obtained by EDF, he argued that it would cost $500m to comply with the new rule: “It is ludicrous that our customers would have to cover the costs of a $500m investment for such a slight improvement to particulate matter capture,” he wrote.

The Trump administration gave NorthWestern an exemption from complying with the 2024 updated standards, which the administration went on to repeal in February.

Sarang said the Colstrip plant had not installed modern pollution controls that could reduce emissions. If it had been required to comply with the 2024 updated standards, it would have had to upgrade its equipment, she said: “It would have had pretty significant impacts on air pollution.”

NorthWestern, which became Colstrip’s majority owner earlier this year, describes the coal plant as a “dependable bridge to a cleaner energy future” that supplies reliable energy “until viable, equivalent, carbon-free energy resources are commercially available”.

Asked to comment on EDF’s report, NorthWestern said its technology at the Colstrip plant is “state of the art” for removing sulphur dioxide, and is 99.6% efficient in removing filterable particulate emissions. The company said if the updated 2024 federal standards had taken effect, it would have required it to become 99.8% efficient by 2028, costing hundreds of millions of dollars. The company said its mercury emission control at the Colstrip plant meets current state and federal requirements.

Another coal plant that received a pass from the Trump administration is the WA parish coal plant outside of Houston, Texas. Community members living nearby have called for it to be shut down due to its planet-heating CO2 emissions and what they say are ‘hazardous’ levels of particulate matter.

The plant’s owner, NRG, asked the Department of Energy for an exemption for all of its coal-fired facilities including the WA parish plant, arguing that its facilities wouldn’t be able to comply with the new standards and would need to “derate in order to comply”, taking megawatts off the grid in “critical areas”, according to an email obtained by EDF. NRG wrote that complying with the regulations “with razor thin margins” would risk the affordability and reliability of the grid.

A 2018 Rice University study found that the plant is responsible for as many as 177 premature deaths each year from PM 2.5, which are particles small enough to enter the bloodstream through the lungs, causing increased rates of respiratory diseases, heart attacks and strokes. “Our research has shown that WA parish is the deadliest power plant in Texas,” explained Rice professor Daniel Cohan.

NRG did not respond to a request to comment.

Cohan said plants across the country were supposed to meet the 2024 updated standards. “Trump is letting them off the hook from the more stringent version of the standard,” he said.

“It lets them stay open longer,” Cohan explained. “Many coal plants in this country are barely on the edge of breaking even, and so any regulations that force them to spend more money to clean up their pollution is likely to cause some of them to choose to retire and be replaced by cheaper and cleaner sources.”

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Two sizable federal funding awards in southeast Oregon and southwest Idaho support projects designed to increase irrigation efficiency and improve Mid-Snake River water quality.

USDA’s Natural Resources Conservation Service recently approved more than $325 million combined for 42 projects through the NRCS Regional Conservation Partnership Program. Funded work includes irrigation upgrades in the Nyssa-Ontario, Ore., and Payette-Weiser, Idaho, areas.

Oregon

Owyhee Irrigation District’s Mid-Snake Irrigation Efficiency Project received nearly $7.7 million. Plans call for modernizing irrigation infrastructure and upgrading on-farm systems to improve water efficiency, reduce nutrient and sediment runoff and enhance drought resistance for agriculture, according to an NRCS project summary. Piping about 4.4 miles of laterals and carrying out about 32 high-efficiency irrigation upgrades are expected to save water and significantly decrease phosphorous, nitrogen and sediment loading in surface waters.

“It’s a great project from all perspectives,” district manager Clancy Flynn said. Benefits of the piping project — to involve two now-open laterals — include water savings, reduced vegetation growth and cleaner return flows.

The resulting lower sediment loads will improve water quality and require less labor for sediment removal, he said.

Another benefit of the project is lower cost for farmers, Flynn said. An example is reduced irrigation pumping costs, a function of pressure increasing as water moves down the piped system.

Irrigation system conversions from gravity/flood to overhead sprinkler pivot will be a major part of the project, he said. The Freshwater Trust will lead the on-farm component.

OID delivers from Owyhee Reservioir — on the Owyhee River, a Mid-Snake tributary — and also pumps water from the Snake.

Idaho

The trust also is partnering in the Snake River Modernization Program Payette-Weiser Priority Area Project, to which NRCS awarded nearly $8.4 million.

Plans call for converting flood-irrigated fields to precision sprinkler or micro irrigation on 5,000 to 6,000 acres to address field sediment and nutrient loss, according to a project summary.

Participation from 70 to 80 agricultural producers is expected. Reductions in phosphorous, nitrogen and sediment are anticipated along with improved operating efficiency and soil health. Co-funding and outcome monitoring are supported by Idaho Power and regional partners.

Freshwater Trust perspective

Given the major reduction in total phosphorous targeted basin-wide, “now is the time to significantly expand this program,” David Primozich, vice president of water for the trust, said in a news release. The USDA awards and Idaho Power matching funds “provide the resources to support a lot more farmers and improve water quality in the Snake River.”

A decade-long regional study by the U.S. Geological Survey found excess runoff from upstream contributes significantly to low-oxygen conditions that promote the production of toxic methylmercury in the Snake River and Idaho Power’s Hells Canyon complex of reservoirs. Methylmercury moves through the food web and accumulates in fish.

“The Nez Perce Tribe has long sought better water quality in the Snake River and will support this regional funding and implementation effort to address a major cause of methylmercury production in the watershed,” tribe chairman Samuel N. Penney said in the release.

The new funding builds on three years of pilot work, including a $5.6 million grant from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency in 2023. The program brings together funding from multiple partners to help farmers install irrigation upgrades that maximize phosphorus reductions, according to Freshwater Trust.

text:
Rural Texas voters have overwhelmingly backed Republicans for decades, but this year Democrats are hoping that voter opposition to data centers could give them a chance to unseat the Republican governor.

The Democratic candidate in that race, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has made opposition to data center construction a central part of her race against Gov. Greg Abbott. That race has become competitive for a state that hasn't elected a Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1990. ABC News ranks the race as Lean Republican.

Hinojosa told ABC she didn't expect this issue to be so central to her campaign "but the thing about the data centers is it's a physical manifestation of a government, a governor during doing the bidding of the moneyed interests and leaving the people to fend for themselves ... it's also told the story of a larger problem in Texas."

Hinojosa supports a moratorium on new construction, stricter regulations on water and power usage and an end to tax breaks.

She has criticized Abbott for signing tax breaks for data centers and promoting the industry's growth. Abbott once said he wanted Texas to be the "epicenter" of the industry.

Hinojosa says that she has gained support with rural Republican voters who have lost faith in the governor on the issue.

Several rural counties in Texas have sued to stop data center construction, citing concerns about pollution, water usage, and loss of family farmland.

An ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll conducted earlier this month found that in 69% of Texans oppose new data center construction in their communities.

For his part, Abbott announced a moratorium on new data center construction in rural communities in September and said he supports more stringent requirements on power and water use by the centers. He told ABC News, "When rural Texans know the detailed strategy that I have, they are coming to my side."

Republican Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller, who lost his re-election bid to a challenger backed by Abbott, called those promises from the governor "smoke and mirrors."

He said that voter voters' attitudes about data centers "will cost [Abbott] support because he's wrong on the issue. He's not listening to the people. He's listening to his donors."

Abbott press secretary Eduardo Leal told ABC News, "Governor Abbott has the strongest data center guardrails in the country. Sid Miller is a sore loser and has no idea what he's talking about."

Miller says he will not vote for Abbott or Nate Sheets, the Republican who beat him in the primary for agriculture commissioner. He cites policy on data centers as one of the reasons.

When asked if he planned to vote for the Democrats in those races, Miller said, "That's between me and God, and it's going to stay that way."

Another lifelong Republican told ABC News he planned to cast his first vote for a Democrat this year because of his stance on data centers.

Daniel McCoslin, a Marine Corps veteran living in Centerville in southeastern Texas, says a planned data center near his family's farm mobilized him to vote against Abbott, saying, "He needs to go."

He described his decision to switch his vote as a tough one saying, "I ate the cat turd instead of the dog turd."

One Republican warned that the backlash over data centers might be an overreaction that could hurt rural communities.

Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian, who serves on the body that regulates Texas' energy industry and is not up for re-election this year, argues that data centers provide jobs and revenue to parts of the state that are struggling, saying, "rural Texas is in trouble ... The money is moving out, and the population is going down."

Christian blames the voter backlash on outside sources like China and Democratic Sen. Bernie Sanders, saying that Texans have "been lied to. They've been told half-truths, or they've been told only the problems."

But even he admits this is the issue that could decide the midterms for his party: "The entire swing vote is rural Texas."

text:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Southwest Louisiana is entering a period of significant opportunity, where economic growth, coastal restoration and community resilience can reinforce one another. Local leaders say maximizing this potential will require thoughtful planning, strong partnerships and a shared commitment to protecting the region’s unique character.

Michael Hare, executive director of the Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority, warned that coastal erosion poses an existential threat to the region’s way of life.

“If we don’t address the high rate of erosion in this area and the loss of interior marsh in Sabine, we’re going to face meaningful threats to our communities,” Hare said. “That means some people won’t be able to live and work along coastal Louisiana. I have always viewed Southwest Louisiana as a working coast, and you can’t see that any more clearly than in the projects recently announced by the governor.”

Hare acknowledged that residents are rightly concerned about what these new initiatives mean for local coastal programs.

“This means we need to accelerate our work along the Gulf shoreline, the interior, the port and the ship channel, while securing the long-term sustainability of our restoration efforts,” Hare said. “This requires a sustained level of investment. We can solve a lot of these problems, but it takes a long-term commitment to reinvestment. We are facing a front-line threat and a front-line fight that will span generations.”

Despite the challenges, Hare emphasized the vital role the region plays on a larger scale. “We live here because this is what powers the nation, fuels the economy, and helps the world,” he said.

Balancing these environmental challenges with aggressive growth is the next hurdle. Scott Walker, president and CEO of the Southwest Louisiana Economic Development Alliance, noted the organization has launched a strategic plan for the five-parish region, aiming to increase the population by 100,000 residents by 2036.

“That’s a big goal — we’re at 300,000 people right now,” Walker said. “The economic tool that fuels that growth is job creation. We have to ensure companies are expanding and growing right here.”

Walker said the plan requires diversification and innovation.

“We’ve been a great place for companies to come and diversify technology. What we have to do is develop that innovation capacity in ourselves. A great example of that is Alcara, a company refining heavy rare earth elements. That production that they have is unique to the United States; it’s one of the first facilities in the country that refines these elements that are critical for our electronic and computer infrastructure — everything needed for a data center, everything we’re using in our phones and vehicles all have these heavy rare elements that make those products work infrastructure for the U.S. and for national security.”

Walker said Alcara chose to build in Vinton because the company recognizes the area has the talent to design, construct and operate the facility.

To ensure that industrial boom aligns with environmental defense, Hare noted that the CPRA actively invites incoming companies to the table to share their visions for the future.

“We can help them navigate how they prepare and plan out their sites so they don’t disrupt our restoration work or slow our programs down,” Hare explained. “Once we get a few months of those conversations under our belt, these companies realize that not only are we doing no harm, but we can actually accelerate a lot of what they need to succeed.”

Hare believes this intersection of industry and environment marks an unprecedented chapter in Louisiana’s history.

“It is an exciting time like no other in our state’s history,” Hare said. “What lies ahead is delivering on the core mission of the CPRA—providing long-term protection and sustainable restoration—while simultaneously fostering record-setting economic development and job growth to help hit that 100,000-resident milestone.”

Yet, marrying historic population growth with an industrial boom requires a physical foundation capable of withstanding the elements—a challenge that carries a staggering price tag.

Cameron Parish boasts 75 miles of coastline known for some of the best shelling in the world, according to Parish Administrator Katie Armentor.

“Our beaches are well-renowned for any type of recreational ecotourism. People come to swim, play and shell,” Armentor said. “The issue with our beaches is that they’re unstable.”

The Cameron Parish Police Jury is continually grappling with how to protect this extensive coastline—and how to fund the massive effort.

“Who can afford that investment? It would cost $1 billion today, $2 billion three years from now, and $5 billion 10 years from now. It’s critical that we invest now,” Armentor urged, noting that proactive spending will save the parish significantly more money in the long run.

Armentor emphasized that the region must take these vulnerabilities seriously, especially given the rapid industrial expansion happening locally.

“Now is the perfect opportunity to see coastal investment in Southwest Louisiana,” she said. “We have close to $100 billion of recognized LNG (liquefied natural gas) investment. Companies are coming to Cameron Parish because they see we have something to offer that nowhere else in the world can duplicate. We have the land, the port, the people, and the workforce. Now, we just have to make sure we have the coastal infrastructure to protect it.”

To combat these rising costs, Cameron Parish is attempting to take matters into its own hands. In 2025, the parish held a series of public meetings to map out its coastal master plan, which features a staggering 246 individual projects.

“The problem is we don’t have 246 funding sources,” Armentor said. “We know what we need to do, and we know what our issues are — we just don’t know how we’re going to afford it.”

To start bridging that gap, the police jury established a dedicated coastal trust fund in its fiscal budget last year. Though currently sitting at just $250,000, local officials plan to double that balance next year.

“That won’t get us very far yet, but it proves our jury isn’t waiting for someone else to save the day,” Armentor emphasized. “We aren’t waiting for the CPRA to come in and tell us how to fix our land and save our coastline. We know our priorities, and we’re going to start putting our own money into the budget to fix them.”

The parish hopes a shifting tax landscape will provide an influx of revenue to bolster the fund. As incentives from the Industrial Tax Exemption Program (ITEP) — a state initiative providing temporary property tax abatements to manufacturers — begin to expire and roll off the books, the expanding tax base should provide new financial opportunities.

However, Armentor cautioned that this incoming revenue isn’t a cure-all for discretionary spending.

“When ITEP rolls off, people assume it will instantly change how we do business in Cameron Parish, but it doesn’t,” Armentor explained. “We have a massive backlog of projects we could never afford. We are still recovering from Hurricanes Rita and Laura, which means our existing parish assets and infrastructure are outdated, aging, and desperately in need of repair.”

Faced with these staggering costs, regional leaders are finding creative ways to stretch every dollar by turning industrial byproducts into environmental assets.

Hare said the Port of Lake Charles is using its dredged material from the Calcasieu Ship Channel to replace material needed to create marshland.

“Are we doing better than we were doing 10 years ago, 20 years ago? Absolutely,” Hare said. “Can we do better? Absolutely.”

title: Rivian Lifts Guidance to 67K, Cybercabs Hit 544 [2026] - shattered.io
description:
Rivian lifted the floor of its 2026 delivery guidance to 67,000 vehicles this week, and the Rivian R2 is the reason.
Its headline claims: Rivian raised delivery guidance on R2 demand, Tesla expanded its robotaxi fleet, and Ford advanced low-cost EV plans.
Rivian R2 Becomes the Best-Selling Rivian The headline fact is simple.
Rivian Delivery Guidance: From 65,000 to 67,000 Floor Rivian now expects to deliver between 67,000 and 70,000 vehicles in 2026.
How much does the Rivian R2 cost?
text:
Rivian lifted the floor of its 2026 delivery guidance to 67,000 vehicles this week, and the Rivian R2 is the reason. The midsize SUV launched in June, and by the end of September it already outsold every other vehicle Rivian makes. A Stocktwits Zero To Sixty roundup, syndicated through TradingView and Asianet Newsable, pairs that news with two other EV storylines that landed in the same few days: Tesla’s Texas robotaxi fleet and Ford’s push toward a cheaper electric pickup.

The numbers deserve a close read, because they point in different directions. Rivian is climbing out of a long production plateau (our earlier Rivian Q3 earnings breakdown has the quarterly detail). Tesla is swapping Model Ys for purpose-built Cybercabs in its authorized fleet. Ford is still losing about $1.1 billion a quarter on EVs while it builds a platform meant to fix its cost structure. This analysis sorts the confirmed figures from the commentary and shows what each story means for buyers, investors and the hardware makers behind them.

A note on sourcing. Every figure below comes from named outlets, including Yahoo Finance, TechCrunch, 24/7 Wall St., Stocktwits, Electrive and Motley Fool earnings-call transcripts. Where outlets disagree, we use the more conservative number and say so. We found no on-the-record expert quotes we could verify for this piece, so the analysis rests on reported data and our own reading of it.

·

Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

Add now

What the Stocktwits Zero To Sixty Roundup Reported

The Stocktwits newsletter, which Asianet Newsable republished on Oct. 31, treats the three stories as a single weekly snapshot of EV sentiment. Its headline claims: Rivian raised delivery guidance on R2 demand, Tesla expanded its robotaxi fleet, and Ford advanced low-cost EV plans. Each claim traces back to separate reporting that we checked individually.

The roundup also tracks retail mood on the Stocktwits platform. By its count, sentiment on Rivian jumped from neutral to extremely bullish after the earnings report. Tesla sentiment stayed bearish. Ford stayed neutral. Those labels measure how retail traders talk online, which is a very different thing from fundamentals, but they show where attention went this week.

The roundup’s weekly stock moves read as follows: Rivian up about 3%, Tesla up about 7% and Ford up about 6%. Those are week-long figures. Single-day moves on Oct. 30, reported by 24/7 Wall St., looked different. Tesla slid 3% to $390.35, Lucid fell 2% to $3.14, and Ford eased 0.8% to $12.27. Rivian rose 5% in early trading to $12.06. Both sets of numbers can be true at once because they cover different windows.

Rivian R2 Becomes the Best-Selling Rivian

The headline fact is simple. In its first full quarter on sale, the R2 outsold the R1T, the R1S and the electric delivery van. TechCrunch reported that Rivian did not disclose exact R2 unit counts, so the claim rests on management’s word. Hard unit counts are missing, but the direction is clear. The company says the R2 will account for the majority of fourth-quarter deliveries.

Total Q3 deliveries reached 19,248 vehicles, a jump of roughly 45% over the same quarter a year earlier (outlets report 45% or 46% depending on rounding). Production came in at 19,751, according to reports of the earnings release. Revenue hit $2.155 billion, up 38% year over year, and beat the consensus that 24/7 Wall St. put at $2.02 billion.

Adjusted loss per share came to $0.48. Sources differ on the consensus it beat. Asianet cites a $0.56 loss estimate and 24/7 Wall St. cites $0.61, so we say only that Rivian beat the Street. TechCrunch put the net loss at $913 million, down from $1.2 billion a year earlier.

Why an SUV Beat the Trucks

Price likely explains much of it. The R1 family sits at premium price points, while the R2 targets a lower band, so it reaches a wider pool of shoppers. TechCrunch notes the gain came even after federal EV tax credits ended. A second shift at the Normal, Illinois plant lets Rivian build more of them, and the added capacity matters as much as demand does.

Rivian Delivery Guidance: From 65,000 to 67,000 Floor

Rivian now expects to deliver between 67,000 and 70,000 vehicles in 2026. The prior range was 65,000 to 70,000. The ceiling did not move, which is a cautious choice. Management raised only the bottom of the range, a signal that it feels sure about a floor but not ready to promise a higher peak. TechCrunch noted this is the second guidance increase this year.

The financial guidance moved too. Reports on the earnings call say Rivian now expects an adjusted EBITDA loss of $1.75 billion to $1.85 billion for 2026, a $100 million improvement at the midpoint. Management credited regulatory-credit revenue, a tariff receivable and higher expected deliveries. Capital spending guidance came down to $1.4 billion to $1.5 billion, per the Asianet roundup.

The prior EBITDA range in the table is implied from the reported $100 million midpoint improvement. We did not find the earlier range stated outright, so treat that cell as arithmetic and not as a quoted figure.

R2 Pricing: $44,990 to Just Under $60,000

Pricing is where the R2 story gets interesting. TechCrunch reports the starting price sits just under $60,000 today, with a Premium trim at $53,990 arriving later in 2026 and lower-cost versions as cheap as $44,990 in 2027. In the earnings call, as reported by 24/7 Wall St., management described a target band running from about $45,000 up to $57,000.

The two descriptions do not match exactly. The launch trims cost more than the long-term band, which suggests Rivian is selling the richer versions first while it ramps. That ordering helps margins now and widens the audience later. It also means the volume gains that drove the guidance raise came from buyers paying close to the top of the range.

If the cheaper trims arrive on schedule in 2027, the Rivian R2 would start overlapping the price bracket where Ford wants to compete with its own pickup. That timing matters for the competitive section below.

The Cost of Ramping: Losses, Capex and the Uber Milestone

Rapid growth carries a bill. According to 24/7 Wall St., R2 ramp costs ran about $120 million in the third quarter, inside an automotive segment gross loss of $80 million. In plain terms, Rivian lost money on each stage of the build-out even as unit sales climbed. Management says it expects to exit 2026 with a positive automotive gross margin run rate, a goal that depends on the R2 volume holding up.

The Asianet roundup adds an autonomy detail. Rivian’s chief executive said the company is on track to hit a year-end autonomy target that unlocks $250 million from the Uber investment. We could not confirm the technical definition of that target in the sources we reviewed, so we describe it only as a milestone tied to that payout.

Shares remain well below where they started the year. 24/7 Wall St. put Rivian stock down about 40% year to date even after the post-earnings pop to $12.06. A good quarter does not erase a bad year, and traders know it.

Tesla’s Robotaxi Fleet Flips to a Cybercab Majority

The Tesla story is a registry count. Texas Department of Motor Vehicles data, as covered by Yahoo Finance and Stocktwits, showed 1,051 vehicles authorized for Tesla’s robotaxi operations. Of those, 544 are Cybercabs and 507 are Model Ys. This is the first time the purpose-built two-seater outnumbers the converted crossover.

How Fast the Mix Changed

Earlier in October the registry showed roughly 319 Cybercabs against 420 Model Ys, per the same coverage. That works out to about 225 added Cybercabs and 87 added Model Ys in a matter of weeks. The Cybercab count rose roughly 70% while the Model Y count rose about 21%. Our own look at the Cybercab assembly line explains how a purpose-built vehicle can scale that quickly.

Authorized Is Not Operating

The count measures authorization, not vehicles on the road at any given hour. Reports say Tesla runs robotaxis in Austin, Houston and Dallas, plus parts of Florida, and that the Cybercab operates in Austin only for now. A registry entry shows permission, and nothing about utilization, ride volume or safety record. For context on how thin some earlier city claims turned out, see our check of Tesla’s Houston size claims.

The Asianet roundup adds a regulatory note. Italy signaled support for Tesla’s Full Self-Driving, and broader EU approval is targeted for early 2027. That is a target and not a decision. Until regulators sign off, European robotaxi plans stay theoretical.

Tesla Versus Waymo: The Fleet Count Is Not the Whole Race

A 1,051-vehicle authorization looks large until you compare it with mileage. We covered the gap in Musk’s robotaxi win claim against Waymo’s 7x mileage lead. Fleet size says how many vehicles a company may deploy. Miles driven say how much real-world proof it has gathered. Waymo leads on the second measure by a wide margin, which is why a registry jump moves sentiment more than it moves the competitive picture.

Still, the shift matters for cost, at least in theory. A purpose-built vehicle could be cheaper to run per mile than a converted Model Y. We lack confirmed per-vehicle economics, so we treat any savings figure as unproven. Our piece on the Cybercab $30,000 target and fleet-first sales plan lays out what Tesla has and has not committed to.

Stock reaction mirrored the ambiguity. The Stocktwits roundup shows Tesla up for the week, yet 24/7 Wall St. shows a 3% drop on Oct. 30. Retail sentiment stayed bearish throughout.

Ford’s Model e: A $1.1 Billion Loss and the Fathom Pickup

Ford’s EV unit lost about $1.06 billion before interest and taxes in the third quarter, according to 24/7 Wall St. Electrive and other outlets round the figure to $1.1 billion. The Asianet roundup says the loss improved roughly 25% from $1.41 billion a year earlier, on about $1.2 billion in revenue. Electrive reports that EV revenue and wholesales fell 31%, so the loss shrank because Ford is building fewer first-generation EVs, not because each one earns more.

Ford beat earnings expectations overall and raised its 2026 EBIT guidance, 24/7 Wall St. reports, so the EV loss sits inside a profitable company. Gas and hybrid trucks fund the electric bet. Reports of the earnings call put the full-year Model e loss near $4 billion and keep the breakeven target at 2029.

The low-cost plan centers on the Universal EV platform and a midsize electric pickup under the Fathom name. The Asianet roundup describes a sub-$30,000 truck under testing with a launch in late 2027. Earnings-call coverage mentions a roughly $30,000 pickup starting production next year and a wider lineup stretching into the high $30,000s. The details on trim, range and battery chemistry are not confirmed in the sources we reviewed. Our earlier coverage of Fathom’s 5,000-part unicasting explains the manufacturing idea behind the cost goal, and the Fathom home-power story covers the bidirectional charging angle.

Competitive Comparison: Three Strategies, Three Scorecards

Put side by side, the three companies are solving different problems. Rivian needs volume at a lower price. Tesla needs to prove an autonomy business. Ford needs to cut the cost of building an EV by a wide margin. Jefferies, in analysis reported by Yahoo Finance, argued the R2 could fill a product void between Tesla and Ford.

Lucid appears in the table only because 24/7 Wall St. included its stock move. We did not find confirmed operating details for it this week, so the other cells stay empty on purpose.

Market Reaction: Stocks Versus Retail Sentiment

Investors and retail traders did not agree on much. The table below sets the two measurements next to each other so the time frames stay clear.

Three readings stand out. First, Rivian is the only name where both measures turned positive together. Second, Tesla’s weekly gain sat alongside a sharp one-day drop, which tells you the week-long number hides some volatility. Third, bearish retail sentiment on Tesla did not stop the stock from rising over the week.

Sentiment indicators like this one lag price more often than they lead it. Treat the extremely bullish label on Rivian as a description of mood after the beat, and not as a forecast.

Historical Context: From Plateau to Ramp

TechCrunch described the R2 as the product that helped Rivian break a three-year production plateau, and it did so while the federal EV tax credit disappeared. Both facts matter. A plateau means the R1 family hit its demand ceiling at premium prices. The R2 raised that ceiling by moving down-market, and it did so without a subsidy to cushion the sticker price.

Ford’s story runs the other way. Management has rightsized production of its first-generation EVs, and the Model e unit now loses less because it sells less. Tesla’s path differs again, since it already had volume and now bets on a second business layered on top of it.

Pricing pressure shows up in the used market too. Our report on used EVs costing $579 more than gas cars shows how thin the affordability margin is for shoppers who cannot buy new.

Industry Impact: What It Means for EV Hardware

For hardware watchers, the week points to three trends. Rivian’s second shift at Normal shows that capacity, not just demand, now limits growth. Tesla’s Cybercab ramp tests whether a dedicated robotaxi can be built in volume. Ford’s Fathom plan bets that large unicastings and a simpler platform can bring battery-electric costs down to a mass-market price.

Each bet depends on parts suppliers, battery cells and chips. Our hardware coverage follows the compute and component side of that chain. We have not seen confirmed supplier orders tied to this week’s news, so we avoid guessing which vendors benefit.

Risks and Open Questions

Several things could undercut the optimism. Rivian’s R2 volume is undisclosed, so analysts cannot yet check the claim that it leads the lineup by a wide margin. The ramp cost of about $120 million in one quarter shows how quickly expansion eats margin. A fourth-quarter slowdown would put the new 67,000 floor under pressure.

For Tesla, the open question is utilization. For Ford, it is whether a late-2027 launch arrives in time. By then, Rivian’s cheaper R2 trims should be on sale, and rivals will have had a year to react. Jefferies, per Yahoo Finance, flagged that the new Ford platform may not reach meaningful production volume until late 2027.

Five Predictions for the Next Two Quarters

These are our forecasts and not reported facts.

Rivian lands inside its range. With the floor at 67,000 and R2 expected to dominate Q4, we expect full-year deliveries near the middle of 67,000 to 70,000, and a small chance of another floor raise.

The Cybercab share keeps climbing. The registry trend suggests Cybercabs will make up a clear majority of Tesla’s Texas authorizations by year end, though actual rides will lag the paperwork.

EU Full Self-Driving approval slips past early 2027. Regulatory targets rarely hold, so we put better odds on a later date than on the stated one.

Ford’s Model e loss shrinks again but stays above $0.8 billion a quarter. Fewer first-generation sales cut the loss, yet the platform spend continues.

R2 pricing becomes the headline battle in 2027. When Rivian’s $44,990 trim and Ford’s roughly $30,000 pickup near launch, buyers will compare them directly, even though they are different body styles.

The Takeaway

Rivian had the strongest verified week, with a record quarter, a raised delivery floor and a hit product. Tesla showed fleet growth that still needs proof of use. Ford showed a smaller loss that mostly reflects smaller volume. The Stocktwits roundup captures all three at headline level, and the details underneath reward a careful read.

FAQ

What is the new Rivian delivery guidance for 2026?

Rivian now expects 67,000 to 70,000 deliveries, up from a prior range of 65,000 to 70,000, according to TechCrunch and 24/7 Wall St.

How many vehicles did Rivian deliver in Q3 2026?

Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles, about 45% more than a year earlier, with revenue of $2.155 billion.

How much does the Rivian R2 cost?

TechCrunch reports a starting price just under $60,000, a Premium trim at $53,990 later in 2026, and lower-cost versions from $44,990 in 2027.

How big is Tesla’s Texas robotaxi fleet?

Texas DMV data shows 1,051 authorized vehicles, made up of 544 Cybercabs and 507 Model Ys. Authorization does not mean all are operating.

When does Ford’s low-cost EV pickup arrive?

The Stocktwits roundup points to a late 2027 launch for a sub-$30,000 midsize electric pickup, and earnings-call coverage describes production starting next year at roughly $30,000. The two timelines are not identical, so watch for Ford’s own confirmation.

How much is Ford losing on EVs?

The Model e unit lost about $1.06 billion to $1.1 billion in Q3, an improvement of roughly 25% from $1.41 billion a year earlier. Ford targets breakeven by 2029.

Did Rivian stock rise after the report?

24/7 Wall St. reported a 5% gain to $12.06 in early trading on Oct. 30, and the Stocktwits roundup shows about 3% for the week. The stock is still down roughly 40% this year.
