At the end of the day, the U.S. market needs reliable power at unprecedented scale and speed, and we believe Ansaldo Energia is well positioned to contribute.
Power Engineering: Looking beyond this first project in America, how is Ansaldo Energia evaluating the potential for a larger and longer-term presence in the U.S. market?
text:
Editor’s Note: This interview has been excerpted and edited for length and clarity. Watch the full conversation with Stefano Gianatti in the video above.

Power Engineering: What prompted Ansaldo Energia to re-enter the U.S. power generation market now, and how does the Pacifico Energy Project fit into that broader strategy?

Gianatti: First of all, the market opportunity is real, and it’s growing very fast. What we are seeing today is one of the strongest power demand growth cycles in decades, driven by AI factories, data centers, electrification and industrial reshoring. At the same time, customers are not simply looking for generation capacity; they need reliable and dispatchable power available when they need it. That’s why we believe this is the right moment for Ansaldo Energia to return to the U.S. market. The Pacifico Energy Project is a very important milestone because it marks our return to the U.S. new-build power generation market after more than 30 years. We will supply eight 64.3A gas turbines for a major AI factory initiative in Texas, with deliveries starting in 2027. This is a proven technology with more than 70 units installed worldwide and over 4 million equivalent operating hours. But honestly, we do not see Pacifico as a standalone opportunity. We see it as the first step in rebuilding a long-term presence in one of the most important power markets in the world. At the end of the day, the U.S. market needs reliable power at unprecedented scale and speed, and we believe Ansaldo Energia is well positioned to contribute.

Power Engineering: After decades away, I’m curious: what kind of interest have you seen from the U.S. market since announcing the Pacifico Energy project, particularly from data center developers, maybe utilities, IPPs, or other power producers?

Gianatti: What we are seeing is strong interest across the whole market. Of course, data centers are getting a lot of attention, but they are only part of the story. We are also having discussions with utilities, independent power producers, and developers that are facing growing demand and increasing pressure on grid reliability. What’s interesting is that the message to hear from all these customers is remarkably consistent. They are looking for reliable technology, operational flexibility and long-term fuel optionality. But if I had to highlight one priority, I would say speed, with no doubt, speed. Today, rapid deployment has become a key decision factor. Customers want certainty. They want projects that can be delivered on realistic schedules and that will perform reliably from day one. The discussion is increasingly shifting from adding megawatts to guaranteeing energy availability when and where it’s needed. What customers are telling us is very simple: they need fast and reliable power delivered on time.

Power Engineering: Gas turbine demand is extremely strong right now, but the industry is also dealing with supply chain constraints and long delivery timelines. How is Ansaldo thinking about that opportunity while making sure it can meet its commitments?

Gianatti: You are fully right. It’s a great opportunity, but it requires discipline. Demand for gas turbines is strong worldwide, and customers are paying as much attention to delivery dates as they are to technical performance. For us, growth has to remain balanced with execution capability. Our approach is very straightforward. Make realistic commitments and then deliver on them. We are continuing to expand our supplier base, strengthen strategic partnerships, and invest in additional manufacturing capacity. For certain critical components, we are also evaluating selective vertical integration to increase resilience, because the reality is that reliability today is not only about equipment; it is also about execution. Customers want predictable schedules, reliable delivery, and long-term support. The market rewards companies that consistently deliver, and that’s exactly where we are focused.

Power Engineering: As renewable penetration increases and grid conditions become more dynamic, how important is operational flexibility becoming for gas-fired generation?

Gianatti: I believe operational flexibility is becoming one of the most valuable characteristics of modern power systems. As renewable penetration increases, grid conditions naturally become more dynamic. As a result, operators need generation assets that can react quickly, operate efficiently under different conditions, and provide reliable, dispatchable power whenever required. In many cases, flexibility is becoming just as important as efficiency and power output. As an example, our GT36 H-class gas turbine, rated at 550 MW (more than 800 MW in combined cycle), is a good example. It combines around 63% combined-cycle efficiency with outstanding operational flexibility. It can ramp at up to 100 MW per minute, which is best in class, allowing operators to respond very quickly to changes in grid demand. Another good example is our F-class AE94.3A, rated at 340 MW (500 MW in combined cycle). This unit also offers excellent operational flexibility, with ramp rates above 50 MW per minute and a long track record of reliable operation. And there is another important aspect: modern grids need more than energy production. They need inertia, voltage support and stability services that rotating equipment naturally provides. In tomorrow’s power systems, flexibility will be every bit as important as traditional metrics such as efficiency and power output.

Power Engineering: Looking beyond this first project in America, how is Ansaldo Energia evaluating the potential for a larger and longer-term presence in the U.S. market?

Gianatti: The United States is clearly a strategic market for Ansaldo Energia, and the Pacifico project is a very important milestone, but we see it as the beginning of a broader journey rather than the final destination. We are actively evaluating opportunities across data centers and industrial applications, both grid-connected and behind the meter. Of course, any future expansion must be based on sustainable growth and strong customer relationships. But we also understand something very clearly: long-term success in North America requires localization. That means being closer to customers, strengthening local capabilities, building partnerships, and developing an increasingly local support structure. I do not want to go into specific initiatives today. But localization is certainly an important part of how we think about the future on this market. Our ambition is simple: we want to become a long-term technology and service partner in the United States, not simply an equipment supplier.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman August Pfluger (TX-11), Chairman of the United States Air Force Academy (USAFA) Board of Visitors, led the Board's fall meeting at the Academy in Colorado Springs this month. The meeting focused on the Academy's leadership priorities, infrastructure improvements, and cadet well-being.

Chairman Pfluger opened the meeting by reviewing the recommendations in the Board’s Semiannual Report. Members then heard from the Academy’s new Superintendent, Lieutenant General Paul Moga; Commandant, Brigadier General Brandon Tellez, and Provost, Brigadier General James Valpiani, about their priorities and discussed ways the Board can support their efforts. Under Secretary of the Air Force Matthew Lohmeier met with the Board during the Board’s Administrative Session. Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Manpower and Reserve Affairs Richard Anderson and Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Energy, Installations, and Environment Michael Borders also participated in the meeting.

A portion of the meeting was dedicated to discussing USAFA’s infrastructure. The Board heard from Assistant Secretary Borders on the urgency of funding infrastructure projects at the Academy. Department of the Air Force personnel also highlighted the importance of the USAFA Board of Visitors-led provisions in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

During their visit, the Board engaged with the Air Force Academy Association of Graduates Board of Directors, the Air Force Academy Foundation Board of Directors, and the Air Force Academy Athletic Corporation Board of Directors. The Board also identified a new focus area regarding cadet nutrition. Members plan to review cadet nutrition and Mitchell Hall funding more thoroughly.

Members of the Board experienced life at the Academy firsthand. They participated in an orientation experience at the airfield, attended classes, toured the dormitories, and had lunch with cadets in Mitchell Hall. They also visited the Academy’s new Visitor Center. These activities gave Members numerous opportunities to interact with cadets and USAFA staff.

"As Chairman of the Air Force Academy Board of Visitors, I was proud to lead a productive meeting in Colorado Springs. We focused on modernizing the Academy’s infrastructure so cadets have the facilities they deserve, and we’re committed to working with the Department of the Air Force leadership to make that happen. I also appreciated the chance to meet with cadets and staff, whose dedication and professionalism give me great confidence in the future of our Air Force. The Board is also taking a close look at cadet nutrition, because the men and women who will defend our nation should be properly fueled to perform at their best. The Academy shapes the leaders our nation will rely on, and it’s our duty to make sure it remains the best in the world," said USAFA Board of Visitors Chairman August Pfluger (TX-11).

text:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Costumed environmental activists joined Hawaiʻi lawmakers on Halloween Eve to warn of severe environmental consequences and push back against proposed federal legislation that would grant legal immunity to oil companies.

Protesters rallied against companion measures introduced in Congress: House Resolution 8330 and Senate Bill 4340, known as the “Stop Climate Shakedowns Act.” Sponsored by U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman, R-Wyo., the legislation is intended to “protect American energy from leftist legal crusades punishing lawful activity.”

If passed, the measures would shield fossil fuel producers by barring retroactive climate liability lawsuits, dismissing active court cases, and preempting state energy penalty laws.

“Legal immunity for big oil companies would provide an insurmountable challenge for those fighting to combat climate change,” said Ella Diaz of the Environmental Law Society.

Lawsuits target fossil fuel giants

Hawaiʻi and 10 other states have filed lawsuits against BP, Chevron, ExxonMobil, and other major energy producers. The complaints allege that fossil fuel companies understood for decades that their emissions contributed to global warming, yet misled the public while continuing aggressive promotion.

“It’s documented that they knew what they were doing,” said state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole, D-Kāne‘ohe, Kailua. “They took deliberate steps to mislead the public, caused confusion, and get people hooked on gasoline.”

Community leaders point to recent hurricane activity, storm surges, and localized flooding as evidence that climate impacts are arriving faster than communities can absorb them.

“So many coastal districts across the islands are facing huge costs for the coastal tidal rise that’s caused directly by global warming,” said state Rep. Kim Coco Iwamoto, D-Ala Moana, Kaka‘ako, Downtown.

Concerns over fast-tracking

With the general election approaching, U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda expressed concern that congressional leadership could try to fast-track the legislation quickly before new lawmakers take office.

“It’s just an insult to everyone who is fighting back against both the rising cost of gas, the obscene profits that oil companies are making,” Tokuda said.

text:
Over the past fifteen years, the global energy transition has witnessed an astonishing industrial transformation. Relentless manufacturing scale and technological learning have driven solar photovoltaic module costs down by over ninety percent, while wind turbine costs have fallen by two-thirds. Clean generation is now the cheapest bulk electricity source in history across most global markets. Yet despite this equipment deflation, total installed system costs are not falling at the same velocity.

Hardware now represents an ever-diminishing share of total project expenditure, while non-hardware frictions—including cumbersome permitting, archaic grid interconnection queues, and exorbitant financing charges—increasingly dictate deployment economics. According to authoritative research from the International Energy Agency and global benchmarks from the International Renewable Energy Agency, unlocking the next frontier of clean energy expansion requires pivoting policy attention from factory floor manufacturing to the soft institutional and financial barriers that inflate project delivery costs.

Figure 1: While core hardware costs have fallen precipitously over the past fifteen years

1. Hardware Deflation vs. Balance-of-System Inelasticity

The dramatic price collapse of solar modules and wind turbines exemplifies Wright’s Law of technological learning: with every cumulative doubling of global production capacity, unit manufacturing costs fall by roughly twenty to twenty-four percent. Consequently, solar photovoltaic modules now trade below ten cents per watt, representing less than a quarter of total utility-scale installation costs. However, balance-of-system expenditures—encompassing structural racking, inverters, high-voltage transformers, underground cabling, civil earthworks, and specialized construction labor—have resisted comparable deflationary trends. In contrast to semiconductor modules produced in highly automated, globalized fabrication facilities, civil works depend heavily on localized commodity inputs like structural steel, copper wiring, and domestic construction trades. Analytical assessments from BloombergNEF and engineering data from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory indicate that balance-of-system components now comprise over sixty percent of total capital outlays. Without standardized engineering designs, prefabricated civil foundations, and localized technical workforce training, stubborn balance-of-system inelasticity threatens to blunt the economic momentum of ongoing hardware learning.

Figure 2: Because renewable power generation requires zero ongoing fuel purchases, compressing capital financing costs from emerging market baselines to advanced economy levels cuts the levelized cost of solar generation by more than half.

2. The Financing Frontier and the Cost of Capital

Unlike conventional thermal plants, which distribute fuel costs across decades of operation, clean power facilities incur virtually their entire lifetime expenditure upfront during initial engineering, procurement, and construction. Consequently, the levelized cost of clean electricity is extraordinarily sensitive to the cost of capital. A solar facility financed at a weighted average cost of capital of four percent produces electricity at less than half the levelized cost of an identical facility financed at fourteen percent.

Comparative Policy Matrix: Cost Reduction Levers and Structural Impact Across Clean Energy Domains

Today, this financing divide severely penalizes developing nations. While developers in advanced economies secure project debt at nominal rates between three and five percent, clean energy sponsors across emerging economies confront hurdle rates between eleven and sixteen percent. Authoritative joint analyses by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and the Center for Global Development demonstrate that this sovereign spread reflects currency volatility, political risks, and financially distressed national utilities, suffocating clean deployment across the sunniest regions on earth.

Figure 3: Protracted interconnection queue backlogs and administrative delays inflate total project expenditures by fifteen to twenty-five percent through accumulated overhead and developer carry costs.

3. Permitting, Interconnection Queues, and Administrative Friction

Beyond financing hurdles, the most pervasive physical bottleneck throttling clean energy velocity is administrative and grid interconnection friction. Across major energy markets, the time required to navigate environmental reviews, secure local land zoning, and obtain grid interconnection approvals has expanded dramatically. In the United States and the European Union, clean energy generation assets frequently spend five to seven years idling in overloaded transmission queues before utilities finalize impact studies. These prolonged development cycles impose severe soft-cost penalties: developers must maintain expensive land options, absorb compounding legal overhead, and bear equipment inflation risks. Infrastructure research from the Asian Development Bank and project evaluations from the African Development Bank show that bureaucratic delay inflates final project costs by fifteen to twenty-five percent. Conversely, jurisdictions that adopt digitized, automated interconnection screening, standardized power purchase agreements, and master-planned solar parks compress project lead times from sixty months to under twelve months, radically diminishing overhead expenditure.

Figure 4: Unlocking over two thousand gigawatts of additional annual clean energy additions by 2040 requires pairing hardware deflation with comprehensive regulatory streamlining and multilateral financing de-risking.

4. Grid Integration, Transmission Expansion, and Storage Parity

As variable solar and wind generation penetration surpasses thirty percent of annual grid supply, total system integration costs begin to escalate unless complementary transmission and flexibility investments keep pace. In congested electricity grids lacking adequate transmission capacity, system operators are forced to curtail surplus renewable generation during midday solar peaks, directly eroding asset revenue and artificially raising the levelized cost per delivered megawatt-hour. Building long-distance, high-voltage direct-current transmission lines resolves this locational mismatch by transporting abundant, low-cost power from arid desert solar basins and windy coastal corridors directly to urban industrial demand centers. Concurrently, technical reports from the Rocky Mountain Institute and system integration studies by the World Bank Energy Sector Management Assistance Program confirm that pairing utility-scale battery storage with smart grid automation slashes balancing costs, minimizes transmission line congestion, and prevents costly curtailment, transforming variable renewable electricity into dependable, dispatchable clean baseload power.

text:
Utility-scale solar developers and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractors are turning to factory-built electrical balance of system (EBOS) solutions to mitigate mounting field labor costs and construction delays. Speaking at pv magazine USA Week 2026, Voltage Energy global director of engineering Jenny Levin detailed how factory-to-field assembly transforms high-risk field wiring into a standardized, plug-and-play installation model.

While solar photovoltaic modules represent the single largest equipment line item on a project site, overall installation labor accounts for up to 15% to 20% of total capital expenditure. Traditional DC field wiring requires running dedicated string lines back to combiner boxes, stripping insulation on site, and performing thousands of manual connector crimps in open field environments. On a modern utility site, these manual terminations multiply to tens or hundreds of thousands of individual connections, creating high exposure to connector mismatch, improper polarity, mechanical wire abrasion, and water intrusion.

To solve these compounding field risks, Voltage Energy utilizes custom factory-engineered harnesses and trunk bus architectures. By manufacturing cable runs, pre-set break-outs, and overmolded connections in a clean facility, every assembly undergoes factory quality control—including electrical continuity, contact resistance, insulation resistance, and Hi-Pot testing—before being spooled and shipped. The standardized kits roll directly out onto site cable management systems, reducing required field labor skill levels and accelerating overall commissioning schedules.

Pre-engineered EBOS systems also enable cost-optimized conductor selections. While traditional stringing relies entirely on copper conductors, factory-injected overmolded transitions allow projects to integrate high-strand aluminum trunk lines for long runs across array blocks while maintaining copper-to-copper plug interface connections in the field. Furthermore, as module and inverter manufacturers rollout 2,000 V system architectures, centralized trunk bus systems lower total system complexity by reducing combiner box counts and total cabling volume while increasing energy yield by 0.5% to 0.8%.

Q&A Highlights

Following the keynote presentation, I joined Jenny Levin to discuss domestic manufacturing ramp-up, supply chain flexibility, and high-voltage system readiness.

Ryan Kennedy: “You mentioned that Voltage has made a major push into U.S. manufacturing at your Timberlake, North Carolina facility. What can you tell us about the manufacturing plans in the U.S. and what was the motivation behind that decision?”

Jenny Levin: “International production is great for utilizing global talent and bringing costs down, but being able to manufacture in the U.S. is really about delivering the best product and service to customers. Having multiple production plants gives us tremendous flexibility. Certain customers are requiring U.S.-made products for domestic content, and other customers might need last-minute deliveries with short shipping times. Manufacturing locally allows us to be flexible and execute quickly.”

Ryan Kennedy: “Great. And is that factory currently in the ramp-up stage?”

Jenny Levin: “Yes, we have started production and we are currently in the ramp-up stage. As a mechanical engineer, I’m thrilled to see all the machines and to see jobs coming to North Carolina!”

Ryan Kennedy: “And how is Voltage preparing for the market’s eventual shift towards 2,000-volt system architectures?”

Jenny Levin: “We have already upgraded our product portfolio—including LINX Plus and our harness lines—to be fully rated for 2,000 volts. As sites begin shifting to 2,000V, we’re working closely with developers on optimized cable routing strategies to maximize the cost savings and efficiency gains that higher voltage unlocks.”

text:
The University of North Carolina Wilmington (UNCW) has overhauled its campus dining takeout model, becoming the first higher-ed institution in North Carolina to go fully plastic-free in residential dining. After a failed attempt at a reusable plastic container program—where 96% of containers were never returned—the university sought a more resilient and scalable solution.

The new system is built around stainless steel containers supplied by USEFULL, integrated with UNCW’s existing dining infrastructure. Unlike plastic containers, which degraded quickly and required constant replacements, the stainless steel version is built for repeated, long-term use. Since the switch, container losses have dropped to nearly zero, with return rates rising significantly—addressing both environmental goals and operational frustrations from the earlier program.

Students check out containers using their campus ID or mobile credentials through a Transact Campus integration. The process mirrors common student workflows, making the system easy to adopt. Participation is free, with penalties only for damaged, lost, or overdue containers—an accountability model that avoids up-front fees while encouraging responsible use.

Beyond just the materials upgrade, the containers deliver better performance: food stays hot or cold for up to five hours, and the containers are more durable under daily use. For students, it’s a better product. For the university, it's a more sustainable—and financially viable—system.

Data, Cost, and Health: Making the Business Case for Reuse

UNCW's plastic-free shift is a strategic operational change designed to reduce costs, cut waste, and support long-term sustainability metrics. The move away from plastic also supports growing interest in reducing exposure to microplastics, adding a public health dimension to the initiative.

USEFULL’s system includes detailed tracking of container use, enabling the university to measure waste diversion, water savings, and emissions reduction across individual and institutional levels. This data adds transparency and helps stakeholders—from administrators to students—see the real impact of the program.

title: Georgia and North Carolina stove deal takes aim at costly hurdle to ditching gas
description:
Avoiding an electrical upgrade could save roughly $3,000 overall compared with replacing a gas stove with another electric range that requires a higher-voltage outlet.
More background A conventional electric range typically requires a 240-volt outlet rather than a standard 120-volt connection.
Induction avoids both the indoor pollutants associated with gas cooking and the burning of planet-warming fossil fuels in the kitchen.
These stories follow households choosing between gas and induction and planning backup power for electric cooking.
• A UK homebuyer kept induction for the kids after weighing it against gas cooking.
text:
A standard three-prong outlet is enough to power a battery-backed induction range — and for households replacing a gas stove, that can mean avoiding the costly electrical work another electric model might require.

A group purchase campaign in parts of Georgia and North Carolina is offering $300 off one such appliance, making the switch more affordable for participating households.

Here's what to know

The initiative brings together New York City-based appliance maker Electra and Let's Go Electric, whose online platform connects participants with contractors and partners from government and other organizations, according to Canary Media.

Four local campaigns are participating: Electrify Decatur (outside Atlanta), Electrify Asheville-Buncombe (for western North Carolina), Electrify the Triad (in Winston-Salem and Greensboro), and Electrify the Triangle (for Raleigh, Durham, and Chapel Hill).

Electra's range costs $3,999 before the group-purchase discount.

Participating households may also be eligible for public rebates that reduce what they pay out of pocket.

The campaign lists Nov. 30 as the deadline for the $300 discount.

Avoiding an electrical upgrade could save roughly $3,000 overall compared with replacing a gas stove with another electric range that requires a higher-voltage outlet.

More background

A conventional electric range typically requires a 240-volt outlet rather than a standard 120-volt connection.

Making that change can cost thousands of dollars, complicating the switch even when the stove itself costs about the same as a new gas model.

Induction avoids both the indoor pollutants associated with gas cooking and the burning of planet-warming fossil fuels in the kitchen.

Households may spend less on energy each month because induction appliances use it more efficiently.

Support for induction is growing among chefs who find its cooking performance equals or exceeds that of gas.

What's being done?

Electra's workaround is a built-in, 5-kilowatt-hour battery.

The battery also allows households to cook as many as five meals when grid power is unavailable. It draws electricity from a standard outlet, then supplies power for demanding cooking tasks such as boiling water or searing cuts of meat.

text:
Toni Simonetti reports:

1st Selectman Kevin Christie’s administration will seek “upwards of $5 million” in federal tax credits for the geothermal energy system being installed at the new Long Lots Elementary School.

On Wednesday, the Board of Selectmen unanimously approved hiring a consulting firm to help obtain “the geothermal investment tax credit under the Inflation Reduction Act.” The credit would be requested through the town’s tax filings “to offset the cost of geothermal and ancillary energy related construction,” according to the request submitted by Westport finance director Gary Conrad. The request was presented at the meeting by LLS project manager Susan Chipouras.

The town is currently building a new elementary school at the site of the existing school. The total appropriation as approved in June 2025 is $110 million, plus interest costs. The new consulting contract with CliftonAllenLarson LLP would be paid under the original appropriation; no new funds were requested.

Construction is underway on the new Long Lots Elementary School. (Drone photo/Brandon Malin)

A state grant totaling about $12 million has been approved, and is included in the current state budget. The town says more state funding may also be on its way because the state legislature approved a space standards waiver, allowing for a greater proportion of the total cost to be reimbursed.

The total cost of the consulting contract was not known, and is dependent on the firm’s hours spent to research and develop the tax credit application. The multi-tiered agreement includes a $65,000 base fee, plus $10,000 in other fees for memo preparation and the like, and “ongoing project services” to be billed at variable professional hourly rates.

1st Selectman Kevin Christie questioned how the firm’s billed hours will be managed. Chipouras said she and the construction management firm would monitor the hours billed.

Chipouras said “all costs” related to the geothermal system would be included in the calculation, and that “30 percent of all these costs … could be substantial.” She declined to provide a more specific estimate.

The total amount of eligible costs was not provided to the Board of Selectmen and will be calculated by the consultants. Costs are eligible if they meet various wage, domestic content, function and timing criteria, among others.

In the publicly available cost documents for the Long Lots project, the HVAC systems total cost estimate is $12.74 million. A 30 percent tax credit would be $3.7 million if all those costs are eligible. In order to reach a $5 million or more credit, about $16.7 million in eligible costs, all at a 30 percent credit rate, would have to be submitted.

Third Selectman Don O’Day, who is also a member of the Long Lots Building Committee, stated that hiring the consultant at $75,000-plus “was an easy decision.”

“These substantial reimbursements … will go back into taxpayers’ pockets,” he said.

A response to a question regarding use of the tax credit funds is pending regarding whether proceeds received would go to the general fund or be used for an earmarked purpose.

text:
Green building materials manufacturer Fortera and tech giant Meta announced today a multi-year agreement under which Meta will purchase environmental credits from the production of cement with a carbon footprint 70% below than ordinary Portland cement (OPC).

According to Fortera, the deal will provide long-term revenue visibility to enable it to secure financing for new production facilities, with a strong corporate demand signal for low carbon cement.

Cement production is one of the more difficult industrial sectors to decarbonize, accounting for approximately 8% of global CO2 emissions.

Founded in 2019, California-based Fortera develops technology aimed at reducing emissions from cement production. The company’s proprietary ReCarb technology captures industrial CO2 emissions and converts them into feedstock for the production of its ReAct cement, which has a carbon footprint approximately 70% lower than OPC, according to Fortera. The technology can be integrated into existing cement and lime facilities, allowing manufacturers to retain their kilns and established distribution networks while producing cement at cost parity with OPC.

Ryan Gilliam, CEO of Fortera, said:

“Using waste CO2 as a primary feedstock turns cement decarbonization into a new economic engine for the United States. We’re bringing a new technology to enable communities with economies built around cement and lime production to remain strong as the industry decarbonizes.”

Under the new agreement, Meta will purchase environmental attribute certificates (EACs) associated with approximately 200,000 tons of Fortera low-carbon cement. Companies can purchase EACs associated with lower-carbon materials to address supply chain emissions and help finance the expansion of manufacturing capacity without necessarily purchasing the physical products.

Meta will also maintain the option to utilize the in its own construction projects and to expand the volume and duration of the partnership in future years.

Fortera said that the support the development of the its Fortera Cement Plant in Ste. Genevieve, Missouri. Meta added that the agreement connects its demand for low carbon cement with the development of domestic supply in markets where it is building, and demonstrates how long-term purchasing can help accelerate the integration of low carbon materials into the construction supply chain.

Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta, said:

“A multi-year commitment is what gets a cement plant financed. Our agreement helps Fortera move the Ste. Genevieve plant from plan to production, which means construction jobs and long-term manufacturing jobs in Missouri, and low-carbon cement available to builders well beyond Meta.”

text:
Dear Neighbor,

As the 2025-26 legislative session continues to draw to a close, the PA Capitol was a flurry of activity last week, as the House and Senate, along with the Governor and his team, worked to negotiate and finalize passage of key legislation. As you may know, each two-year session is standalone, and any unfinished business on November 30th (following the election on the first Tuesday) expires sine die and must be restarted from the beginning. That deadline is a key factor in bringing folks to the table to, in the words of the Governor, “Get Stuff Done.”

Unfortunately, again this year, the Republican-led Senate struggled to get the votes needed on a number of urgent and important issues, and we left Harrisburg with much unfinished business. While we were able to pass several important pieces of legislation — including bills to help attract and retain healthcare workers, help fire companies raise money, establish flood insurance protections for property owners, and require school districts to develop and establish bell-to-bell cell phone bans — hundreds of bills the House sent over to the Senate are very likely to expire. They include measures to rein in data center developers to protect PA communities and utility ratepayers, legalize and regulate so-called “skill games,” reform public school funding, and so much more.

Of course, I am particularly frustrated by the impending demise of some of my own bills, including one that was recently amended to provide tax credits and incentives for generating new clean energy, for creating advanced manufacturing jobs, and for incentivizing homeowners to undertake clean energy home improvement projects to save them money on their soaring utility bills.

Yet, while the prospect of so many great ideas and good pieces of legislation expiring sine die is disheartening in the short term, I am encouraged not only by the momentum and progress we’ve made thus far — which typically makes the next effort easier and often more successful — but by the prospect of a change in Senate leadership in the next session. My hope is that in the upcoming 2027-28 legislative session we can establish a more bipartisan, more proactive, and much more productive working relationship to get more Good Stuff Done for the people and communities of this great Commonwealth.

In addition to the focus on legislative deadlines, last week was also a time to celebrate. First was the decision by the PA Labor Relations Board confirming that Penn State Research Assistants are indeed considered workers and should be included in the Graduate Student union bargaining unit. I was proud to stand with them in the Capitol’s Main Rotunda to celebrate not only the PLRB decision, but Penn State’s announcement that they would not appeal the decision. I always stand on the side of workers and their right to organize and collectively bargain for better wages, benefits, and working conditions. Which is why I was also proud to stand with members of the United Auto Workers in the Rotunda to speak in support of commonsense legislation to support the working people and families of Pennsylvania.

I also had an opportunity to join my fellow “Representative-of-Hungarian-descent,” Rep. Valerie Gaydos, in welcoming delegations from the Hungarian American Coalition and from the Hungarian Embassy in Washington to celebrate passage of House Resolution 626 to recognize Oct. 23, 2026, as Hungarian Revolution Memorial Day in Pennsylvania. This year marks the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Uprising in 1956, as well as 37 since the fall of the Communist dictatorship there in 1989. And I remain hopeful that the elections earlier this year in Hungary, repudiating the recent slide into authoritarianism, also signal a new era of freedom, prosperity, and opportunity for the Hungarian people.

And finally, last week the House adopted my resolution recognizing Aug. 15, 2026, as “One Million Degrees Day” in the Commonwealth in honor of Penn State conferring its one millionth degree! This is a milestone that few institutions in the entire world can claim and demonstrates an unsurpassed record of longevity, achievement, and impact on our state, our nation, and our world.

description: Rivian shares surged Friday after its latest results boosted optimism that the long-struggling electric-vehicle maker is headed toward better times. The Irvine-based manufacturer announced Thursday that it posted $2.15 billion
text:
The 2027 Rivian R2 Launch Edition. (Henry Payne/The Detroit News/TNS)

Rivian shares surged Friday after its latest results boosted optimism that the long-struggling electric-vehicle maker is headed toward better times.

The Irvine-based manufacturer announced Thursday that it posted $2.15 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 38% from last year. Vehicle deliveries were up 46%, driven by the new R2, which launched in June.

The market applauded its results. Rivian shares, which had tumbled more than 40% this year, rose more than 6% Friday to close at $12.16.

Rivian hasn't been profitable since its founding in 2009 . It went public in 2021 and lost $3.6 billion last year.

Chief Executive RJ Scaringe said Rivian is targeting positive automotive gross profits by the end of 2026. It reported an automotive gross loss of $80 million for the third quarter this year, compared with a loss of $130 million in the third quarter last year.

The company said the lower loss was driven primarily by higher delivery volumes and an improved per-unit margin. The R2 was the company's best-selling vehicle by volume in the quarter.

Rivian produced 19,751 vehicles at its facility in Normal, Ill., and delivered 19,248 vehicles.

The company also raised the lower end of its full-year delivery guidance range to 67,000 units from 65,000.

"Raising the delivery guidance shows that R2 production is ramping up, and that's a good sign in the near term for Rivian," said Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein. "I'm optimistic that Rivian will continue to drive profitability through increased R2 volumes."

Rivian currently sells only the performance version of the R2, priced at $57,990, still expensive for many Americans but a step down from the company's typical prices of around $77,000.

The company said the R2 Premium will arrive in late 2026 for around $54,000, followed by an R2 Standard version in 2027 priced at $44,990.

The release of the lower-priced R2 will likely be another boost for the company, Goldstein said.

"This should open them up to a wider number of consumers," he said.

Rivian is also banking on its self-driving technology. Consumers can already buy the R2 with a universal hands-free driver assistance package.

"Regarding our technology roadmap, our autonomy platform is progressing rapidly," Scaringe said in a statement. "We are laying the foundations for a future that we believe will be fully electric , autonomous and AI-defined."

While the race to bring self-driving robotaxis to the mass market is in full swing, there's also great demand for similar technology in consumer vehicles.

Multiple vehicles from several automakers offer some degree of driver assistance, with Tesla firmly ahead of the pack with its autonomous software capabilities.

Rivian is beginning to catch up, said Chris Pierce, an analyst at Needham & Company.

"They're closing the gap with Tesla and widening the gap with legacy automakers like GM and Ford," Pierce said. "If they're going to have a car that has a road map to autonomy, and it retails for less than the average new car in the United States, that's a pretty positive formula."

text:
Eligible customers in Summit County, Park City, Oakley and Francis will be automatically enrolled unless they opt out

SUMMIT COUNTY, Utah — Rocky Mountain Power customers in Summit County, Park City, Oakley and Francis will begin receiving notices in November about a new clean-energy program that will automatically enroll eligible customers and add $4 per month to most residential bills beginning Jan. 1.

Customers who do not want to participate must opt out.

The Community Clean Energy Program applies to eligible Rocky Mountain Power customers in unincorporated Summit County, Park City, Oakley and Francis. Customers will remain Rocky Mountain Power customers.

Rocky Mountain Power says enrollment information will be sent by mail and email in November and December. The first notice will arrive by mail separately from customers’ monthly electric bills.

Most residential customers who remain enrolled will pay an additional $4 per month beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Households enrolled in Rocky Mountain Power’s Home Electric Lifeline Program will receive a credit offsetting the program charge.

Businesses will pay based on electricity use. Summit County lists the current rate at $0.00609 per kilowatt-hour, plus a 12-cent monthly low-income surcharge.

Customers can opt out online, by phone, or by mail. During the initial rollout, customers can leave the program without a termination fee through May 1, 2027. Beginning May 2, most residential customers who leave will be charged a one-time $30 fee. Low-income customers enrolled in Schedule 3 are exempt.

Residential customers with rooftop solar who participate in Rocky Mountain Power’s Schedule 135 net-metering program are not eligible.

The program is intended to add new renewable energy resources to Rocky Mountain Power’s system, including solar, wind, geothermal, and hydroelectric generation. Participating Utah communities have set a goal of eventually matching participating customers’ annual electricity use with renewable generation.

Summit County joined the program in April after the Utah Public Service Commission approved it in March. The program stems from legislation passed by Utah lawmakers in 2019 allowing participating communities to pursue a net-100% renewable electricity portfolio by 2030.

title: Scaling Markets for Distributed Energy Resources - RMI
description:
Early deals show the major potential for distributed capacity procurement, most notably Voltus’s recent gigawatt-scale Bring Your Own Capacity (BYOC) announcement with Google in PJM.
Large Loads are Starting to Fund Distributed Capacity Large load growth contributes to many of the grid’s current needs, but it also offers a significant pool of potential investment.
Recent transactions, most notably the Google-Voltus expansion in PJM, demonstrate that distributed capacity can be contracted at gigawatt scale and over long tenors.
What generalizable transaction structures best support bilateral distributed capacity procurement, and which elements can be effectively templatized?
Xcel Energy to Power New Google Data Center in Minnesota; Xcel Energy, February 24, 2026. https://newsroom.xcelenergy.com/news/xcel-energy-to-power-new-google-data-center-in-minnesota.
text:
Acknowledgements: The views presented in this piece are the author’s own. RMI thanks Ohm Analytics for providing supporting market data.

The US electricity grid is struggling to meet rising demand while staying reliable, and affordable for ratepayers.1,2,3 Flexible distributed energy resources (DERs), such as batteries, smart thermostats, and heat pumps, offer one potential solution. By shifting demand and supply power where and when the grid needs it most, DERs can add capacity quickly, increase grid utilization, and reduce rising electricity rates.4,5,6

Over the past several months, RMI’s Deal Lab team has engaged DER developers, virtual power plant (VPP) operators, financial institutions, data center operators, and policymakers to understand the current commercial landscape, including a range of bilateral discussions and a convening cohosted with Goldman Sachs Sustainable Finance Group in July 2026.7 These engagements highlight an emerging consensus on the value of flexible DERs in meeting current grid demands, with two major opportunities to expand their scale and impact.

First, the market must develop replicable transaction structures that let new big electricity users — especially data centers — invest directly in new distributed capacity (aggregated DERs that can reliably deliver power or reduce demand when the grid is stretched). Early deals show the major potential for distributed capacity procurement, most notably Voltus’s recent gigawatt-scale Bring Your Own Capacity (BYOC) announcement with Google in PJM.

Despite these promising signs, the market still has a long path to full maturity. Transactions to date have relied on a single hyperscaler anchor, Google, and none has yet publicly shown how the grid benefits of DERs turn into direct benefits for specific data center projects. To keep scaling, the market will need replicable deal structures that work across jurisdictions, a wider pool of counterparties, and access to project-specific energy procurement budgets.

The second opportunity is for financiers and developers to find effective ways to build flexibility-based value into financing structures. Developers cannot reliably borrow against revenue from grid services to finance DERs, and so cannot deploy assets where they would help the grid most. Transactions with creditworthy hyperscalers offer one near-term solution and potential for market learning. Over the medium and long term, however, DER deployment will depend on developing tailored financial products that capture flexibility-based value across the full DER lifecycle.

This article explores both opportunities and the potential for coordination across power system stakeholders to catalyze a more efficient and effective market for power flexibility.

Large Loads are Starting to Fund Distributed Capacity

Large load growth contributes to many of the grid’s current needs, but it also offers a significant pool of potential investment. Large loads face significant delays to interconnection due to lack of grid headroom and concerns about impacts on electricity rates.8,9 Flexible DERs can help mitigate both challenges by quickly creating capacity to alleviate peak- and location-specific grid congestion and by placing downward pressure on electricity rates.

Recent work by the Brattle Group on behalf of Everyday Electric shows that achievable expansions in residential VPP participation have major rate benefits for both participating and non-participating households,10 while detailed grid modeling by Piq Energy on Base Power assets indicates the potential for distributed capacity to relieve major transmission constraints in ERCOT.11 These benefits can enable win-win transactions, with large loads sponsoring new distributed capacity deployment to alleviate grid impacts from their interconnection.

Early deals show promise, with limits

The market is undergoing a period of rapid experimentation in transaction structures to realize this value. Three recent deals show early “bring your own distributed capacity” transactions: Google’s procurement of aggregated resources from Voltus in PJM, Xcel’s “Capacity*Connect” procurement of distributed storage with Sparkfund in Minnesota, and the SHARE VPP partnership in PG&E’s service territory in Northern California. Of these, the Google-Voltus transaction is by far the largest, with both parties having recently announced an expansion to more than a gigawatt of aggregated resources in PJM.12,13

While these transactions are a promising signal, exhibit 1 illustrates some of the remaining limitations for scaling and replication. Google is the only hyperscaler participant across all three transactions, and each uses a different commercial template: a privately funded pilot, a contribution to a utility program, and a bilateral capacity contract. None yet publicly demonstrates a mechanism translating the system-level benefits of DER capacity into project-specific benefits for a sponsor, such as accelerated interconnection or protection from curtailment.14

Public comments by Voltus CEO Dana Guernsey highlighting the value of long-duration contracts in demonstrating durable capacity to regulators are suggestive of potential site-specific accreditation or benefits, but these details are not yet publicly disclosed. 15 Without such mechanisms, future transactions may struggle to access the project-level energy procurement budgets that offer the most direct route to continued scale.

Source: RMI analysis, drawing on Pacific Gas and Electric Company for SHARE VPP16; Xcel Energy17 and Minnesota PUC Docket No. E-002/M-25-37818 for Capacity*Connect; and Voltus,19 and Energy-Storage News20 for Voltus BYOC, with the October 2026 expansion as cited in note 11. On disclosed returns, see note 13. Scale figures are not directly comparable: a pilot target, a program authorization, and contracted capacity, respectively.

Value transfer mechanisms connect grid benefits to buyers

Flexible DERs can create grid services that are a good match for large-load-created demands, but individual transactions are primarily determined by value transfer mechanisms: contractual or regulatory devices that convert system-level DER value into a benefit assignable to the specific entity paying for it. These mechanisms vary significantly by jurisdiction and transaction structure and will determine the ultimate value delivered to the sponsoring large load (see non-exhaustive examples in exhibit 2). While distributed resources create value, the transfer mechanism is what will define specific products that large loads may be willing to pay for.

Exhibit 2: Example value transfer mechanisms linking distributed capacity to large load requirements

Source: RMI analysis, from “States Are Opening the Door to Data Center Investment in Virtual Power Plants,” RMI, September 2026. Mechanisms differ significantly by jurisdiction; examples are non-exhaustive.

With limited public reporting and a rapidly evolving deal landscape, it is not possible to catalogue with certainty which transfer mechanisms have been successfully deployed, but for the market to mature, it will need clear product categories with differentiated pricing based on that value transfer. Of the transactions to date, the Google-Voltus PJM agreement has most clearly signaled the potential for clear transfer mechanisms, and any further public disclosure would be a major development for the market.

Four example product structures that could make deals replicable

Bilateral hedge (cost reduction): In regions with forward capacity markets in which large loads are exposed to capacity prices, purely bilateral contract-for-differences structures can provide hyperscalers with cost hedging against future price changes, but these transactions in isolation do not impact interconnection speed or service reliability.

Trilateral interconnection (speed to power): In trilateral structures with a load-serving entity (LSE), an LSE may offer accelerated interconnection in return for delivered accredited capacity or other grid services, but this relies on individual contract terms, for which there is not yet a public demonstration project.

ISO compliance purchase (firm service): In markets with Bring Your Own New Capacity (BYONC) mandates for which aggregated DERs are eligible, hyperscalers may pay DER developers for regulatory compliance, with the direct value depending on the regulatory incentive or cost. PJM’s interim resource adequacy service (IRAS) proposal contained such a mechanism, with aggregated DERs qualifying to protect large loads from priority curtailment, allowing hyperscalers to effectively purchase service reliability as a product from DER aggregators. IRAS was rejected on primarily jurisdictional grounds, but similar structures may emerge from ongoing regulatory proceedings around the US.21,22,23

State compliance purchase (firm service/speed to power): In states with large load tariffs or other regulatory requirements, DERs may qualify for conditions on interconnection, curtailment protection, or other regulatorily imposed requirements. RMI recently catalogued advancements in state-level regulations that establish clear value transfer mechanisms.24 One notable example is New Jersey’s Data Center Fair Share law, enacted in July 2026, which directs the creation of a flexibility trading mechanism by which large loads could pay other actors to provide flexibility in lieu of direct data center curtailment.25 As with the defunct IRAS proposal, this would effectively allow DER aggregators to sell service reliability as a product to large loads.

Due to the speed and scale of digital infrastructure development, the distributed capacity procurement discussion has focused on alleviating data center grid impacts through hyperscaler-sponsored deployment. Beyond data centers, however, these mechanisms offer an opportunity to establish effective market-based approaches for valuing the grid services created by flexible DERs, and with modification, could help facilitate future sources of load growth such as advanced manufacturing, industrial electrification, and electric mobility.

Financing Needs to Catch Up to Grid Value

As flexibility-based value becomes increasingly important to the US electricity market, whether through defined utility programs, direct wholesale market participation, or large-load-sponsored transactions, it is exposing limitations in current financing approaches for DERs.

DERs have traditionally been financed against their value to the host site (households and commercial or industrial facilities), whether as direct owners or through third-party ownership (TPO) structures. In this model, deployment is financed based on household credit or contracted cashflows from a lease or PPA structure. This model has successfully scaled in residential solar and increasingly for attached storage, with more than $16 billion in solar-based asset-backed security (ABS) issuances rated by Kroll Bond Rating Agency (KBRA) through mid-2025.26

Grid services, however, make up an increasing portion of the value proposition for distributed energy resources. Defined-payout utility VPP programs offer one transparent benchmark for grid services value, and in some jurisdictions, payments could now cover a significant portion of total system cost for battery-based systems (exhibit 3).27,28

As operational advances allow for better quantification of local distribution-system value and grid demands continue to rise, these values are likely to increase.

Exhibit 3: Annualized battery costs and VPP payment magnitudes, $/kW-yr

Currently, these revenue streams are effectively excluded from up-front and takeout financing. This exclusion reflects significant challenges around grid services revenues, from merchant-like revenue from market-based programs to binary risks around program duration and cancelation,29 which lead to compounding steep discounts by actors along the value chain. In contrast to the billions raised in DER-based ABS issuances to date, no grid services revenues have been directly credited in rated ABS cashflows. However, as grid services revenues continue to grow as a portion of system value, VPP programs become better integrated into utility planning, and data availability improves, this exclusion will become an increasing source of capital inefficiency for the market. Conversely, developers and financiers who can capitalize grid services revenues will have business model flexibility to rapidly respond to demand signals from large loads, accelerate deployment, and strengthen return profiles.

This exclusion hampers the availability of capital for DER deployment, especially behind-the-meter battery systems in locations where grid value is especially high, but household incomes or credit do not support traditional lease-based deployment and financing. Early programs converting long-term grid services value into discounted customer leases, such as Tesla’s Powerwall discounts for Energy Storage Solutions participants in Connecticut,30 show the potential for this model, but will need to move beyond developer equity to scale.

Most immediately, demand for capital may be met through bilateral procurements with creditworthy hyperscaler offtakers. Google and Voltus’s recently announced agreement opened the door for 10+ year contracted revenues that can replace merchant-like cashflows from grid services, allowing effective up-front financing for behind-the-meter C&I battery installations.31 In the medium and long term, however, the sector will benefit from incorporating grid services revenues from transactions beyond hyperscaler-anchored procurement.

This integration opportunity will extend to a broad category of financial instruments across the DER deployment and monetization lifecycle (exhibit 4). These instruments are not fundamentally new: warehouse facilities for asset deployment, price floors for firming merchant revenue, and securitization for capital recycling are well-established instruments across multiple sectors.

Exhibit 4: Financial products across the DER lifecycle

Source: RMI analysis.

Each, however, will require tailoring to incorporate the value of flexibility-based revenues, whether including grid services revenues in ABS cashflows or valuing credited distributed capacity in support of M&A activity. Development of these fit-for-purpose instruments represents a significant opportunity for financial institutions to develop new customers and product lines, and the emergence of better-tailored financial products will in turn reduce how much flexibility-based value goes unrealized.

Conclusion: Scaling Depends on Replicable Deals and Financing Models

Flexible DERs have the potential to fill a large and valuable role in the US power sector, both in managing the near-term impacts of data center development and in developing cost-effective models for sustained load growth in the coming decades.

While technological and regulatory developments will each play a major role in facilitating this growth, the emergence of effective, replicable transaction and financing models will be critical to realizing the full potential of flexible DERs.

Recent transactions, most notably the Google-Voltus expansion in PJM, demonstrate that distributed capacity can be contracted at gigawatt scale and over long tenors. What remains to be proven is whether transactions can scale to more than one buyer, through replicable structures, and with clear and well-priced value transfer mechanisms.

These opportunities are interlinked, with hyperscaler-anchored contracts offering a near-term route to making flexibility revenue financeable and creating an opportunity for market experimentation. In the medium term, however, financing for flexibility-based revenues should expand beyond reliance on hyperscalers as a credit backstop and create new opportunities for deploying flexible DERs where the grid benefits are greatest.

RMI’s Deal Lab is actively working to support the development and dissemination of these models. In our upcoming small-group technical workshops and public research, we will explore the key open questions the market needs to answer to mature, including:

What value transfer mechanisms between aggregated DERs and large loads can markets currently facilitate, and how will large loads value them?

What generalizable transaction structures best support bilateral distributed capacity procurement, and which elements can be effectively templatized?

What are the enabling conditions, including regulatory policy, market structure, and utility partnerships, required for each transaction structure, and what are the most efficient ways to adapt transactions to function across jurisdictions?

What financial instruments, including revenue firming, capacity pre-pays, and alternative credit structures, can most efficiently begin to capitalize flexibility-based value for DERs?

As standardized products develop, what role can market-making balance sheets and secondary market trading play in providing liquidity, price discovery, and risk transfer, and how can they help scale the market and improve bankability?

If you are a DER or large load developer, utility, financier, policymaker, or other power system stakeholder interested in participating in Deal Lab, please reach out.

title: Climate Lawsuits Reach the Supreme Court—with States Closely Watching
description:
The case began in 2018 when Boulder County and the City of Boulder sued ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy under Colorado law.
The theories differ, but the practical objective is similar: obtain compensation from energy companies for alleged climate-related impacts in a global emissions context.
However, in March 2026, Maryland’s highest court upheld the dismissal of climate claims brought by Baltimore, Annapolis, and Anne Arundel County.
The Supreme Court heard arguments in Suncor on Oct. 5, and its decision could help define the boundaries of state-law climate liability nationwide.
Whatever the Court decides, state legislatures will have greater reason to examine where environmental enforcement ends and open-ended climate liability begins.
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court began its new term with a case that could shape the future of climate litigation nationwide. In Suncor Energy (U.S.A.) Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County, the justices will determine whether federal law prevents state courts from requiring energy companies to pay for local harms allegedly tied to global greenhouse-gas emissions.

The case began in 2018 when Boulder County and the City of Boulder sued ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy under Colorado law. The local governments allege that the companies contributed to climate change, misled the public about their products’ risks, and should help pay for costs associated with wildfires, flooding, damaged infrastructure, and other local impacts. The surviving claims include public nuisance, private nuisance, trespass, unjust enrichment, and civil conspiracy.

The companies argue that issues involving emissions across state and national borders belong under federal, rather than individual state, authority. The primary question before the High Court is whether federal law precludes such state-law claims seeking relief for alleged global climate impacts. Beyond the immediate legal questions, Suncor represents a growing nationwide trend of state and local governments using traditional tort claims to pursue damages for the alleged consequences of global emissions.

In September 2026, Reuters reported that ExxonMobil and Suncor had identified nearly 60 state and local governments that brought comparable lawsuits seeking billions of dollars. The theories differ, but the practical objective is similar: obtain compensation from energy companies for alleged climate-related impacts in a global emissions context.

While the litigation is widespread, it is not moving uniformly. Honolulu pursued climate-related claims against oil companies, yielding a victory at the Hawaii Supreme Court on the federal preemption question. Similarly, Chicago took home a major federal appellate victory in its climate suit, where the Seventh Circuit rejected the defendant’s attempt at federal removal. However, in March 2026, Maryland’s highest court upheld the dismissal of climate claims brought by Baltimore, Annapolis, and Anne Arundel County. In April, a California court paused coordinated climate cases while awaiting the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Suncor. Further, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken legal action against several states and municipalities—including Hawaii, Michigan, New York, and Vermont—seeking to block these very climate suits.

At their core, these suits seek to extract billions from energy producers for alleged harms too remote to support traditional tort claims. The nature of these suits highlights an important federalism concern: while states retain significant authority over energy and environmental policy within their borders, allowing a single state court to impose liability based on worldwide emissions could produce regulatory and economic consequences extending far beyond that state’s jurisdiction. Those consequences could affect far more than the individual companies named in these lawsuits. A patchwork of potentially billions of dollars in state and local liability could create greater uncertainty for domestic energy production and investment, with implications for infrastructure development, energy supply and, ultimately, the prices paid by families and businesses. A single multibillion-dollar verdict could influence energy markets and business decisions nationally and globally—all initiated by one individual city. Perhaps most concerning, however, is that these far-reaching consequences—jurisdictional overreach, regulatory repercussions, and financial penalties extending across the global energy industry—are not merely haphazard consequences of the notorious municipal climate lawsuit; they are its intended objective.

Litigation with such ambition thrives in the absence of democratic policymaking. Major policy decisions carrying consequences for energy affordability and reliability are better addressed transparently by elected lawmakers through clearly defined statutes and regulations rather than developed piecemeal through litigation.

The ALEC model Energy Security and Independence Act would bar claims seeking relief for the alleged effects of climate change against businesses lawfully engaged in fossil fuel production. Taking a broader approach, the ALEC model Energy Producers and Consumers Protection Act protects covered lawful energy, agricultural, and industrial activities against specified climate-related liability for covered conduct, and includes an exception requiring proof of a specific federal environmental-law violation and direct, identifiable harm. Both models aim to keep major energy-policy decisions with elected lawmakers and to curb frivolous litigation targeting an industry indispensable to the fundamental operation of American society.

The diversity among the states in how standard tort liability is applied, combined with the complexity of the federal-state entwinement, underscores the magnitude of the impending Suncor outcome. The Supreme Court heard arguments in Suncor on Oct. 5, and its decision could help define the boundaries of state-law climate liability nationwide. Whatever the Court decides, state legislatures will have greater reason to examine where environmental enforcement ends and open-ended climate liability begins. As lawsuits and legislative proposals continue to develop, states can be expected to debate and define clearer rules for lawful energy activity, civil liability, and the proper role of the judiciary in energy production.

name: Clean Energy
title: BAAJA Sets a New Standard for Data Center Accountability | Third Way
description:
It will unlock new electricity in the US and set standards for data center accountability.
But because of their unique strain on the energy system, BAAJA would impose new, stronger ratepayer-protection rules on data centers.
BAAJA would require data centers to pay for the upgrades they need, protect other customers from bearing the costs of a canceled project, and create options to reduce data center electricity use during peak hours.
BAAJA sets a national baseline on data center requirements.
While most data centers are built with private funding on private land, the Trump administration is trying to permit 17 data center campuses on federal land.
text:
In a few weeks, the Senate will decide whether to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), and its success in that chamber will have a huge impact on its chances in the House. If passed, the bill would allow us to build the energy infrastructure America needs without placing an undue burden on everyday ratepayers.

It will unlock new electricity in the US and set standards for data center accountability. It will make energy affordable and create jobs. It will lead to new clean energy infrastructure and help the US fight climate change. And yes, it will protect ratepayers and hold data centers accountable.

The bill’s opponents, however, mistakenly claim that BAAJA is a giveaway to data centers. To be clear, it isn’t. Data centers are one of many industries facing long project timelines, political whiplash, and redundant reviews. But because of their unique strain on the energy system, BAAJA would impose new, stronger ratepayer-protection rules on data centers.

That’s the balance lawmakers are trying to strike: meeting growing electricity demand without driving up costs for American families or undermining grid reliability. The answer cannot be to simply stop building.

As policymakers continue to review BAAJA, we wanted to highlight some of the most relevant issues around data center growth, ratepayer protections, and state control of energy infrastructure.

Data centers will be required to pay their fair share.

Overall, BAAJA has the strongest provisions we’ve seen from Congress to make data centers pay their fair share, and it’s likely the best opportunity under the Trump administration to get meaningful protections for ratepayers. BAAJA would require data centers to pay for the upgrades they need, protect other customers from bearing the costs of a canceled project, and create options to reduce data center electricity use during peak hours.

BAAJA sets a national baseline on data center requirements. None of the provisions take away a state’s ability to set its own rules. States could still require data centers to bring in their own power, set limits on how much electricity they can use, and determine when they can use it. BAAJA doesn’t require states to implement stricter standards or take any of these steps, but it sets an important floor necessary to protect residential ratepayers across the country.

BAAJA will help clean energy and batteries displace projected natural gas growth.

Permitting reform is designed to provide predictable timelines, better-defined windows for judicial review, and clearer procedures that will have a huge impact on electricity infrastructure - something crucial for energy users and households across the country. As electricity demand skyrockets and data centers place unique strain on the grid, natural gas and behind-the-meter generation have become go-to power solutions.

Passing BAAJA makes more clean generation available instead. 1,300 GW of new generation is waiting to join the grid, 75% of it solar and wind, alongside huge amounts of new energy storage. BAAJA will make it easier to expand and modernize the US grid and shorten interconnection queues, enabling data centers and other large electricity users to access power more easily.

BAAJA does offer some support for behind-the-meter resources, including natural gas, and streamlines permitting for certain natural gas pipelines. But those provisions are intended to give grid operators more flexibility, options, and access to fuel. They do not alter the Clean Air Act or alter quality standards for data center projects. They also apply to all kinds of qualifying generation, from batteries to gas generators. Ultimately, the transmission provisions in BAAJA make it easier to access clean energy while ensuring a diverse energy mix when needed.

BAAJA does not open federal land to data centers.

While most data centers are built with private funding on private land, the Trump administration is trying to permit 17 data center campuses on federal land. The proposals are on shaky legal ground, and BAAJA would not change that. BAAJA’s certainty provisions and revamped judicial review provisions for statutes like NEPA, NHPA, and the Clean Water Act are meant to prevent lawful permits from getting unfairly canceled. Legal protections against unlawful permits, however, remain strong. Violating the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), for example, would still lead courts to issue injunctions and stop projects from proceeding.

BAAJA will fix the broken status quo.

BAAJA won’t solve every challenge that comes with data center growth, but it gives us something we don’t have today: a way to build the energy infrastructure we need while holding the companies driving half of our growing electricity demand accountable.

The status quo on permitting is not working. Through BAAJA, policymakers have a historic opportunity to fix it.

BENTONVILLE, Ark., Oct. 30, 2026 — Walmart today announced a strategic investment in Base Power, a Texas-based energy company, along with an agreement that will make Base’s home energy offerings available to Walmart customers and Sam’s Club members – expanding access to affordable energy solutions that can benefit both households and the grid. “Customers and members count on Walmart and Sam’s Club to help them make the most of their budgets,” said Shayne Wahlmeier, SVP of Walmart Energy. “Base Power gives them a practical way to help lower energy costs, have backup power during outages and support a more reliable grid. We’re proud to make these solutions more accessible through Walmart and Sam’s Club.”

Starting in Texas

Texas is Base Power's largest and most established market, where Base serves more than 35,000 members. More than 20,000 of those households have a Base battery at home, and the remaining members have their electricity from Base. Walmart is launching these offerings in Texas first and expects to expand to additional locations and markets over time.

Product availability, savings potential, installation requirements and pricing vary by location, utility service area and customer circumstances.

Customers and members can meet with Base representatives at participating Walmart and Sam's Club locations to learn about available services, ask questions and enroll.

text:
In-brief analysis

The share of solar generation with co-located battery storage is increasing

Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators.

Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028.

When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment.

We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies.

Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average.

title: Elon Musk vs. Tesla? His Midterm Money Could Work Against His Own Cars
description:
While EV federal tax credits would benefit electric vehicle companies like Tesla Inc., CEO Elon Musk is helping the Republican Party this election.
The proposed Cheap Energy Act would bring back the tax credits that were part of the Inflation Reduction Act enacted in 2022.
Going Against Tesla Tesla has been a leader in EVs in the United States and benefited from the tax credit for years.
While a Democratic majority in congress could benefit the EV sector and Tesla, Musk is putting his money directly to support the opposite happening.
A true Tesla investor and fan likely would rather have the tax credit back to sell as many Tesla vehicles as possible.
text:

Electric vehicles could see increased demand going forward in the United States thanks to higher gas prices and newer lower-cost models coming soon. EVs could also get back in the spotlight if Democrats win next week's midterm elections to win back control of Congress and pass legislation to bring back federal tax credits.

While EV federal tax credits would benefit electric vehicle companies like Tesla Inc., CEO Elon Musk is helping the Republican Party this election.

EV Tax Credit Comeback

Don't call it a comeback, but new legislation from Reps. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) and Sean Casten (D-Ill.) seeks to bring back federal EV tax credits of $7,500 for new vehicles, a credit that expired last year.
