The legislation has the backing of at least 160 House Democrats and could gain further support if the Democratic Party wins back the majority, according to Politico.

The proposed Cheap Energy Act would bring back the tax credits that were part of the Inflation Reduction Act enacted in 2022. Along with the tax credit, the bill has proposals to modernize the electricity grid to help make sure consumers don't have to pay for data center upgrades, according to InsideEVs.

Not all Democrats are on board with the legislation. Some see supporting the bill as a liability ahead of the election, while others think that the credits appeal to the wrong people: wealthy coastal elites. One way around this would be to put income level caps on the credits and apply it to working and middle-class families, according to the report.

Passing legislation would also require the signature of President Donald Trump or face the need to override a veto that would require two-thirds majority from the House and Senate, more than a potential majority the Democratic Party would have in each chamber.

A record 1.3 million new EVs were sold in 2024 in the United States, the last full year the tax credit was available to new buyers. EV companies would likely welcome back the tax credits that could bring their vehicle prices more in line with traditional automotives and also help companies achieve profitability.

Ford Motor, General Motors and others have launched EVs and not been able to make them profitable, a situation made worse after the tax credit disappeared.

Going Against Tesla

Tesla has been a leader in EVs in the United States and benefited from the tax credit for years. Nowadays, the tax credit could help Tesla less than its competitors. Tesla already makes profitable vehicles and has some of the lowest starting costs for EVs compared with traditional automotives.

Musk even supported the ending of the federal EV tax credit previously, saying it would help Tesla by having it gone more than it helps the company by having it.

This could help ease the mind of Tesla shareholders.

While a Democratic majority in congress could benefit the EV sector and Tesla, Musk is putting his money directly to support the opposite happening.

Musk has donated $366 million to the Republican Party and GOP candidates for the midterms, according to media reports..

In 2024, Musk donated around $250 million to Trump and the Republican Party. He is now one of the largest donors in the 2024 and 2026 elections.

A Trump win helped boost Musk's presence in politics, got him a position in the Department of Government Efficiency and has helped him navigate potential regulation across several industries. Musk was also able to get a NASA director who loves his SpaceX company.

A Republicans win in the midterms would likely end any talk of bringing the EV tax credit back, as there is not as much support among that party.

A true Tesla investor and fan likely would rather have the tax credit back to sell as many Tesla vehicles as possible.

Musk would rather take the hit on vehicle sales to make sure he keeps his personal political power.

description:
While Congress cannot force an end to the war, Democratic control of either or both chambers will likely intensify efforts to control the purse strings.
The scale of a Democratic victory could influence whether Republicans defect to challenge the administration's waiver authority through defense legislation.
Growing concerns over electricity affordability could reshape the administration's data center acceleration initiative, despite likely bipartisan backing for AI and data center infrastructure expansion.
View detailed data Democratic congressional control could complicate broader efforts to expand conventional energy production and roll back environmental regulations.
A sizable Democratic victory could strengthen their leverage, potentially complicating passage in the lame-duck session.
text:
The U.S. military escalation against Iran appears increasingly likely despite growing pre-election pressure, with both Washington and Tehran maintaining entrenched negotiating positions. The conflict has proven impervious to pre-election off-ramps, expanding in scope with Houthi entry into the war. Regional talks in Tehran and Vice President Vance's reported outreach to Iran's hardline Supreme National Security Council secretary suggest the administration is calibrating rather than reversing course.

The critical strategic question is whether U.S. military action will constitute a final strike before withdrawal, or will be a more extensive operation designed to finish the job and orchestrate regime change. Some regional actors warn that a brief escalation followed by hasty exit would essentially amount to an Iranian victory despite reconstruction costs. Others caution that a sweeping military campaign dramatically increases the risk of Iranian retaliatory strikes on critical civilian infrastructure, including desalination facilities, alongside expanded proxy attacks on U.S. allies throughout the region.

While Congress cannot force an end to the war, Democratic control of either or both chambers will likely intensify efforts to control the purse strings. Even if the administration maintains veto authority over broad policy reversals, Democratic gains could embolden Republicans to challenge the administration's authority on Iran war funding through year-end defense legislation. With the size of Tuesday's Democratic victory determining the degree of Republican defections likely, the midterm results will substantially influence congressional leverage over military spending and escalation decisions heading into 2027.

A Democratic House victory would trigger a wave of hearings and investigations on energy deals involving administration insiders and military actions affecting major global producers. Venezuela will face intense scrutiny, with lawmakers seeking to determine whether oil companies had advance knowledge of the January military operation against Nicolás Maduro. Inquiries could expand to examine whether companies received privileged information or benefited from the operation, and challenge the Pentagon's authority to take a 35 percent stake in North American Blue Energy Partners.

"Even if the [Democratic] party only captures the House of Representatives, we anticipate a wave of hearings and investigations on energy deals involving administration insiders, as well as military actions/foreign policy decisions involving key global producers."

Helima Croft, Head of Global Commodity Strategy and MENA Research, RBC Capital Markets

Russia sanctions waivers and the recent diesel deal will draw bipartisan criticism, particularly from GOP Russia critics including Senators Susan Collins, Mitch McConnell, and Lisa Murkowski. Democratic-led committees will review the administration's suspension of sanctions measures mandated by the Graham Act, which authorizes 100 percent secondary tariffs on imports from Russia oil purchasers and imposes further restrictions on Russian banks and energy investment.

The scale of a Democratic victory could influence whether Republicans defect to challenge the administration's waiver authority through defense legislation. Beyond Venezuela and Russia, congressional reviews will likely examine government equity stakes in critical mineral firms and CFTC investigations into large energy trades around Iran war developments.

Growing concerns over electricity affordability could reshape the administration's data center acceleration initiative, despite likely bipartisan backing for AI and data center infrastructure expansion. The House's bipartisan passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act signals growing support for requiring data centers to shoulder their own costs. Democratic control would pursue stricter oversight, with House Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin already investigating major hyperscalers over nondisclosure agreements with local governments regarding data center projects.

View detailed data

Democratic congressional control could complicate broader efforts to expand conventional energy production and roll back environmental regulations. New majorities could investigate federal leasing decisions, environmental deregulation, and DOE funding allocations. Clean energy developers could benefit from heightened oversight of restrictions on offshore wind and solar approvals, though presidential veto authority and existing executive powers would limit Democrats' ability to reverse policies or reinstate repealed incentives.

Bipartisan permitting reform offers the clearest avenue for legislative cooperation, yet skepticism remains that this historical nonstarter could succeed post-election. The recently introduced American Affordability and Jobs Act seeks to accelerate energy infrastructure development across conventional and renewable technologies, though Democrats increasingly demand assurances against discriminatory treatment of clean energy projects. A sizable Democratic victory could strengthen their leverage, potentially complicating passage in the lame-duck session.

Ultimately, Democratic gains could constrain the administration's energy agenda through congressional oversight and legislative leverage, even as the administration pursues priorities through executive and regulatory authority.

text:
ANN ARBOR, Mich. (WXYZ) — A new affordable housing development in downtown Ann Arbor is embracing geothermal energy as drilling gets underway for a system that will heat and cool the building using energy stored underground.

The geothermal system is being installed as part of a future 20-story affordable apartment building planned for the corner of South Fifth Avenue and East William Street. City officials say the project aligns with Ann Arbor's broader sustainability goals and could help reduce utility costs for residents over time.

WATCH 7 News Detroit reporter Tiarra Braddock's story in the media player below:

Drilling underway for geothermal-powered apartment tower in Ann Arbor

How the geothermal system works

According to Joe Lange, senior energy analyst with the City of Ann Arbor's Office of Sustainability and Innovations, geothermal technology uses resources beneath the Earth's surface to regulate a building's temperature.

"Geothermal is essentially you're using the resources that are in the ground, geo, to help heat and cool the building, thermal," Lange said.

Unlike traditional systems that rely on natural gas, the future apartment building will operate using electricity and geothermal energy.

"Because geothermal isn't using fossil gas, it uses electricity to kind of move things around," Lange said. "That is something that can be renewably powered through things like solar and wind energy in the long term."

Potential health and environmental benefits

Lange said geothermal systems can offer benefits beyond reducing fossil fuel use.

"If you're not using gas, you don't have gas inside the building," he said. "That can create a healthier environment. You don't have to worry about potential gas leaks or some of the subtle off-gassing that occurs when you have gas appliances in a building."

City officials hope to expand the use of geothermal technology in future developments throughout Ann Arbor.

"We are hoping to have more types of buildings and other houses on these kinds of systems where we can," Lange said.

Community reaction is mixed

Residents who live and work in the area had differing views on the project.

Theresa Zavisa, a longtime Ann Arbor resident and business owner, said she supports the city's continued growth and the addition of housing downtown.

"It's important to look beyond how tall the buildings are or what the buildings look like," Zavisa said. "I think it's important to look at the people that are in them also."

Others are less enthusiastic about the ongoing development.

"I miss Ann Arbor, it's not here anymore," resident Dave Hutchinson said.

Construction timeline

Residents and visitors near South Fifth Avenue and East William Street may continue to see drilling activity as work on the geothermal system moves forward.

Construction on the apartment development is expected to be completed in 2028.

text:
There’s still time for organizations to apply! The City’s Request for Proposals (RFP) for construction training and clean energy career pathways is open through November 16.

At the beginning of this month, the City of Seattle announced it will invest more than $3.1 million in programs that recruit, train, and place workers from communities impacted by economic, racial, and environmental inequities into well-paying construction and clean energy careers.

The investments, provided through a joint initiative by the City’s Department of Finance and Administrative Services (FAS) and our office, have the potential to prepare upwards of 200 workers annually for construction apprenticeships and clean energy careers through pre-apprenticeship training, job readiness programs, and comprehensive wraparound supports.

Organizations interested in applying can submit a proposal through the City’s portal by November 16 at 11:55 PM.

Well-paying climate careers, investing in clean energy job training programs, and creating job opportunities that support local businesses will be priorities of Seattle’s upcoming Climate Action Plan. Our office is leading the development of the Climate Action Plan, which will serve as the City’s five-year plan to reduce pollution, prepare for the impacts of climate change, and build a healthier city for everyone to thrive.

“Meeting our climate goals will take skilled hands,” said Lylianna Allala, Director of the Office of Sustainability and Environment. “With this $3.1 million investment, we are training the electricians, building operators, and clean energy technicians who will power Seattle’s transition away from fossil fuels. This funding opens careers to the people and neighborhoods that have carried the heaviest burden of pollution, so everyone benefits from the clean energy economy.”

We’re partnering with community to help young people learn more about job opportunities and easy-to-access career pathways and job training programs. On Oct. 28, we hosted Powering Your Future, a free workshop at the Duwamish River Community Hub in South Park that introduced young people ages 13 to 26 to clean energy careers and training opportunities.

The workshop brought together organizations and community, including Sphere Solar Energy, Electric Era Technologies, and Emerald Cities Collaborative, previous recipients of the fund, and Villa Comunitaria, the Port of Seattle, Duwamish Valley Sustainability Association, and Seattle City Light, to help connect young people with information and opportunities.

Read the rest of the announcement by FAS below or on their blog!

Expanding access through Priority Hire

The funding will be awarded to local organizations through a competitive Request for Proposals (RFP) that’s open now through Nov. 16. Selected organizations must prioritize the placement of workers historically underserved in construction careers, a designation the City of Seattle calls Priority Hire.

The City, led by FAS, administers a Priority Hire program that’s designed to connect individuals residing in economically distressed ZIP codes, women, and/or Black, Indigenous and other people of color (BIPOC), with career opportunities on City-funded construction projects. The program also establishes apprenticeship utilization requirements and participation goals for women and people of color.

Since its creation in 2013, the Priority Hire program has generated more than $139 million in wages for Priority Hire workers—an amount the City estimates is more than double what would have been earned without the program. Through Priority Hire, workers have access to pathways into 20 building trades, including ironwork, carpentry, cement masonry, and plumbing.

“Seattle’s Priority Hire program has shown what’s possible when we intentionally connect workers who have historically faced barriers to skilled, family-wage jobs in the trades,” said Kiersten Grove, director of the Department of Finance and Administrative Services. “This investment builds on that success by providing the training and wraparound support workers need to enter these careers, advance, and build greater economic security for themselves, their families, and ultimately Seattle’s communities.”

Investing in Seattle’s clean energy workforce

The investment also advances Seattle’s efforts to build an inclusive clean energy workforce as the City works to reduce climate pollution from its two largest sources: transportation and buildings. Our climate workforce strategy calls for expanding equitable pathways into the green economy and ensuring that BIPOC workers and women have access to living-wage careers as the City works to transition away from fossil fuels. FAS, which also oversees the City’s 4,000-vehicle fleet, has also set ambitious goals to achieve a net-zero greenhouse gas fleet emission by 2050.

The RFP will expand access to emerging and high-demand career pathways, including heat pump installation, electrical upgrades, solar installation, building controls, weatherization and building performance auditing.

Programs selected through the RFP will be required to provide supports designed to help workers not only enter the workforce but advance and remain in their careers. These may include mentorship, mental health support, certification and upskilling opportunities, career navigation, and assistance obtaining licenses, work gear, and transportation.

text:
DOVER, Del. — Governor Matt Meyer today announced that Aternium’s proposed $380 million hydrogen and heavy water production facility in Dover has been accepted into the JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator, advancing the administration’s efforts to attract private investment, create good-paying jobs and position Delaware as a leader in next-generation energy and advanced manufacturing.

The Delaware-based clean hydrogen startup plans to develop the facility at Garrison Oak Business and Technology Park in Dover, creating approximately 50 permanent technical, engineering, operations and manufacturing jobs with salaries in the low six figures, along with hundreds of construction jobs. The project would produce high-purity hydrogen for Mid-Atlantic customers and heavy water, also known as deuterium oxide, for industries including pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, defense and advanced technology.

“When a company chooses Delaware, our job is to make sure government helps them succeed instead of standing in their way,” said Governor Matt Meyer. “Aternium is bringing the kind of cutting-edge manufacturing, private investment and good-paying jobs that will help grow our economy. Through JobsFirst, we’re bringing state agencies together to cut unnecessary red tape and get the projects Delawareans need over the finish line.”

“America needs a reliable domestic supply of heavy water, and Aternium is bringing that production back to the U.S. – starting in Delaware,” said Andrew Cottone, Founder and CEO of Aternium. “With Governor Meyer’s leadership and support from the JobsFirst Accelerator, we’re turning that vision into reality. Our Dover facility will strengthen national supply chains, power Mid-Atlantic industry with high purity hydrogen and create the high-paying careers that will help build Delaware’s future.”

Aternium’s proposed facility represents a significant opportunity to establish domestic production of heavy water, a specialized material used in advanced manufacturing, scientific research and emerging technologies. The United States currently relies on imported heavy water, and the Dover facility could help strengthen domestic supply chains while supporting Delaware’s growing advanced manufacturing sector.

The announcement builds on the state’s previous support for Aternium. In September 2025, the Delaware Division of Small Business awarded the company $1 million through the State Small Business Credit Initiative’s Delaware Accelerator and Seed Capital Program to support the expansion of its clean hydrogen production capabilities.

This proposed $380 million facility is expected to begin construction in late November 2027, with an estimated 18-month construction period. The project is currently in the planning phase, and local, state and third-party approvals have not yet begun.

Established through Executive Order 18, the JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator coordinates permitting across state agencies by providing accepted projects with a single point of contact, streamlining interagency reviews and increasing transparency and accountability throughout the permitting process. The program targets completion of complex state permitting reviews within 120 business days while maintaining Delaware’s environmental, public safety and regulatory standards.

The Accelerator is designed to help projects that deliver meaningful public benefits move through the permitting process more efficiently, including developments that expand housing, strengthen energy infrastructure, create jobs and attract private investment.

Aternium joins previously accepted JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator projects advancing housing, energy, broadband and critical infrastructure development across Delaware.

Delawareans can learn more about the JobsFirst Permitting Accelerator and track participating projects here.

title: The EV Revolution is Real. It's Just Not Happening Everywhere. - ARC
description:
What does EV penetration look like in the U.S.?
Georgia, at 4.5% EV penetration, is fairly close to the median: ranked 21 out of 51 (including the District of Columbia).
Fuel costs likely play a role as well: the correlation between gasoline price[4] and state-level EV penetration is moderately strong, at .67.
With 6.0% of households reporting at least one EV, Atlanta is close to the median.
That also makes EV ownership a bit more common in metro Atlanta than in the rest of the state.
text:
With the national average price for regular gasoline topping $4 per gallon,[1] many households may be looking to alternatives such as electric vehicles (EVs). What does EV penetration look like in the U.S.? How does Metro Atlanta compare to other top metros?

To answer these questions, we use data from the 2025 American Community Survey 1-year release,[2] which included a new question on EVs.[3]

Figure 1 presents a map showing the percentage of households with at least one EV by state. Categories are based on the Jenks “natural breaks” method, which helps highlight meaningful differences and identify outliers.

Figure 1: Percent of Households with an EV by State

Data Source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2025 1-Year Estimates, Table B25147

As this map shows, California is a clear outlier, with more than one in eight households (13.8%) possessing at least one EV. EV penetration is highest in the west, particularly Washington state (8.9%), Hawaii (8.5%), and Nevada (8.2%), as well as in parts of the northeast such as Vermont (7.7%). It is lowest in the mountain west such as North Dakota (1.3%) and Wyoming (1.6%) as well as in parts of the deep south such as Louisiana (1.6%) and Mississippi (1.8%). Georgia, at 4.5% EV penetration, is fairly close to the median: ranked 21 out of 51 (including the District of Columbia).

California’s stricter emissions standards almost certainly contribute to its high rate of adoption. Fuel costs likely play a role as well: the correlation between gasoline price[4] and state-level EV penetration is moderately strong, at .67.

How does metro Atlanta compare to its peers? Figure 2 shows the percentage of households with at least one EV for the top 20 metros by population. The reference line denotes the nationwide EV adoption rate of 5.5%.

Figure 2: Percent of Households among the 20 Most Populous Metros with an EV

California’s four top-20 metros, along with Seattle, occupy the top five slots. Oil rich Dallas and Houston, as well as the Motor City, occupy the bottom three spots. With 6.0% of households reporting at least one EV, Atlanta is close to the median. That also makes EV ownership a bit more common in metro Atlanta than in the rest of the state.

How does EV ownership vary within our region? We’ll take that up in an upcoming post.

Notes

[1] According to the American Automobile Association’s (AAA) Fuel Prices (external link) website, the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline was $4.2258 as of October 29, 2026.

[2] Because the question has only been asked for a single year, these data only exist for larger geographic units (population of 65,000 or more) for which 1-year estimates are available. That allows us to examine states, metro areas, and counties. It will be another four years before we can dig down to the Census tract level, but don’t fret– we’ll be ready when the data are available.

[3] The precise question wording is “Do you or any member of this household own or lease an electric vehicle? Include both all-electric and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.” Note that the question, as worded, allows us to know presence or absence of an EV in a household but not how many of that household’s vehicles are EVs. Also note that plug-in hybrids, which can run some distance on a charge before switching to gasoline as a hybrid vehicle, are included in the definition of EV in this question.

[4] Measured as the average price of one gallon of regular fuel on October 29, 2026 according to the AAA.

text:
Hershey, PA – The Shapiro Administration is investing $971,006 through the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection’s (DEP) RISE PA program to help Jubilee Dairy LLC install an anaerobic digester and combined heat and power system that will turn agricultural waste into renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Today, DEP Secretary Jessica Shirley and Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture Secretary Russell Redding visited Jubilee Dairy, a 10th-generation dairy farm and cheese producer operated by the Nissley family, to highlight the investment and the role innovative technology can play in helping Pennsylvania farms reduce emissions and make productive use of agricultural waste.

The planned system will process manure, food waste, and other organic material to produce biogas. The biogas will fuel a combined heat and power system that generates electricity and heat for the farm. The process will also produce digestate, a byproduct that can be used as fertilizer or animal bedding.

The project is expected to reduce Jubilee Dairy’s greenhouse gas emissions by 38 percent. Over time, the system is expected to generate enough electricity to meet 100 percent of the farm’s electricity needs, with additional heat available for use.

“The RISE PA program is excited to work with award recipients like the Nissley family, who are thinking innovatively about how they can save money on energy costs, reduce air pollution, and continue to grow their dairy farm and cheese business for their children and future generations,” said Secretary Shirley. “Since the launch of this program, I’ve visited printing presses, steel mills, pharmaceutical companies, manufacturers, and more who all are looking at how they can increase energy efficiency, use renewable energy, and help reduce or eliminate pollution, while also continuing to grow their business and position Pennsylvania as an energy and industrial leader.”

RISE PA is a $396 million statewide industrial decarbonization grant program(opens in a new tab) funded through the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Climate Pollution Reduction Grants. RISE PA offers grants for small-, medium-, and large-scale projects at agricultural and industrial facilities that reduce emissions through investments in energy efficiency, renewable energy, electrification, and other pollution-reduction technologies, such as anaerobic digesters.

“The Nissley family is a great example of the forward thinking and resourcefulness that have sustained Pennsylvania agriculture for generations,” said Secretary Redding. “They are looking at what they have on their farm – from manure to food waste – and finding innovative ways to turn those resources into energy, reduce costs, and create new opportunities for their family’s 10th generation and beyond. Through investments like these, we are helping farm families build on their legacy while preparing Pennsylvania agriculture for the future.”

In April, the Shapiro Administration announced $267 million in first-round RISE PA Medium- and Large-Award Track grants, which includes Jubilee Dairy, LLC as a MAT recipient. The program is one of the largest federal grants received in Pennsylvania and highlights the Shapiro Administration’s continued commitment to supporting Pennsylvania businesses while also working to ensure clean air, water and land for all in the Commonwealth.

“For a 10th generation farming family, grant programs like RISE PA provide funding for projects that otherwise would not be possible,” said Kendra Nissley of Jubilee Dairy. “We appreciate both DEP and Agriculture for their support of our anaerobic digester project, and our farm. This project will help us continue the growth of our farm in a sustainable manner.”

Pennsylvania Protects Air, Land, and Water Under Governor Shapiro’s Leadership

DEP’s mission is to protect Pennsylvania’s air, land, and water resources and to provide for the health and safety of its residents and visitors. Under Governor Shapiro’s leadership, the agency has:

Plugged over 500 wells, more than the past two administrations combined.

Announced the first round of the RISE PA grants providing $267 million in Medium- and Large-Award Track grants, part of one of the largest federal grants received in Pennsylvania.

Eliminated historic backlog of more than 2,400 permits that were overdue and on-the-clock as of November 1, 2023.

Launched the Streamlining Permits for Economic Expansion and Development (SPEED) program to speed up and streamline permitting process.

Had access to Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) funding to protect the health and safety of Pennsylvanians through plugging wells and reclaiming abandoned mine land through a lawsuit filed by Governor Shapiro(opens in a new tab) against the federal government.

Pennsylvania’s Agriculture Sector is the Backbone of the Commonwealth

With more than 48,800 farms contributing over $153.2 billion a year to the economy and supporting nearly 600,000 jobs in Pennsylvania, agriculture is foundational to the Commonwealth’s heritage and future. Governor Shapiro has prioritized strengthening both agriculture and food security — helping farmers, families, and communities thrive – and last week unveiled Pennsylvania’s first-ever, 10-year Strategic Plan for Agriculture. The ten-year plan outlines the necessary steps to address four critical industry needs including access to capital, efficiency and profitability, modernization and innovation, and public engagement. Through this plan, the Shapiro Administration is working to support farmers and ag producers and build a stronger, more competitive, and more connected agriculture industry.

The 2026-2027 bipartisan budget(opens in a new tab) Governor Shapiro signed earlier this year continues this work by:

Maintaining $10 million for the Agricultural Innovation Grant Program(opens in a new tab) to continue driving innovation in Pennsylvania agriculture.

Continuing $13.8 million to fully fund the Pennsylvania Farm Bill(opens in a new tab) to support business planning, infrastructure, and workforce development.

Increasing the cap for capital development projects, which includes agricultural projects, in the Pennsylvania Industrial Development Authority (opens in a new tab) (PIDA) program from $200,000 to potentially up to $2 million.

Directing funding to the Agricultural Business Development Center(opens in a new tab) and the Centers of Plant(opens in a new tab), Beef(opens in a new tab), Poultry & Livestock(opens in a new tab), and Dairy Excellence(opens in a new tab) to support farmers and producers with resources and services that enhance the long-term vitality of Pennsylvania farms.

Sustaining funding for the nation’s leading farmland preservation program(opens in a new tab), protecting 6,781 farms and 671,082 acres in 58 counties from future development.

The Shapiro Administration highlighted $165 million in investments to strengthen Pennsylvania’s animal diagnostic laboratory network, including expansions at Penn State’s Animal Diagnostic Laboratory ($65 million),(opens in a new tab) a new PennVet laboratory ($94 million),(opens in a new tab) and the Keystone Animal Diagnostic Center at Penn State Beaver ($6 million(opens in a new tab)).

With these investments the Shapiro Administration is planning to maintain this momentum for future farm families and the Pennsylvania ag industry.

Find Pennsylvania’s Strategic Plan for Agriculture here(opens in a new tab) and learn more about Governor Shapiro’s support for Pennsylvania farmers and nation-leading agriculture industry here(opens in a new tab).

text:
It’s spooky season, and for Charlotte’s climate activists, there’s nothing spookier than hyperscale data centers.

“Data centers are definitely the hot topic right now; they are just in the news a lot, and it's what a lot of people are talking about,” said Faith Silva, coordinator for nonprofit Charlotte-Mecklenburg Climate Leaders.

The Charlotte-Mecklenburg Climate Leaders are a volunteer group working to raise climate awareness in the city. They’re taking aim at one of environmentalists’ biggest boogeymen: data centers. They hosted a data center-themed trivia night Tuesday evening at Patagonia Charlotte in South End.

It’s timely, since the Charlotte City Council voted Monday to extend its data center moratorium by 11 months. The event drew a small group — about 20 players. Some teamed up; some went it alone, like Nundy Silva. He named his team of one after a Renaissance fair act, “Hey Nunnie Nunnie!”

There were questions about water use, utility rates and local politics. When the evening wrapped up, the winners walked away with some new outdoor wear. Everyone else got the best consolation prize: knowledge.

“I didn't realize the moratorium was as long as it was, so that was good,” Nundy Silva said. “That was kind of good to find out. That made me hopeful.”

Luckily for these trivia players — and the Charlotte City Council — they have almost a whole year to learn about data centers before the moratorium expires on Oct. 18, 2027.

name: Congress
title: A Democratic Wave In the Midterms Could Change How Companies Talk About Climate
description:
Democratic control of congressional committees would give Democrats new subpoena power and new dedicated staff to conduct investigations.
And members will debate funding levels for clean energy programs that survived cuts under Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill last year.
What is the role of clean energy in the power system?
How might clean energy affect competitiveness?
A bank might underscore how it’s financing clean energy technologies.
text:
For the last year, I’ve been asking corporate executives how they might expect anticipated Democratic victories in the midterm elections to shape the future of the U.S. climate and energy agenda. I was surprised how often they gave the same answer: investigations.

Democratic control of congressional committees would give Democrats new subpoena power and new dedicated staff to conduct investigations. Companies may be compelled to turn over documents, and CEOs could be called to testify before Congress about how they have approached a range of issues.

Climate may not be a top priority on its own for Democratic politicians in 2026, but it will come up in Washington for two key reasons. The first is rising fuel and power costs. Democrats in Congress will want to probe how companies have responded to current energy market conditions triggered in part by rapid growth in demand for AI and the war in Iran, and whether their actions have raised costs. You can expect those questions to take a pro-clean energy bent. And then there is the corruption discussion, which has emerged as a key theme in Democratic midterm campaigning. Democrats will want to probe any company or industry that is perceived to be close with the administration, including the oil and gas industry.

In September, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat from New York, and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, released a report that gives a hint at the expected line of argument. It highlights donations from oil and gas executives and links them to the Trump Administration’s regulatory rollback. And, to conclude, it suggests that those decisions have contributed to higher prices for consumers.

For understandable reasons, analyses of how the election might shape the future of energy and climate tend to focus on policy outcomes. And there are many areas to follow closely. The results will shape efforts to pass a permitting reform bill in the time between the election and when new members of Congress take office in January. And members will debate funding levels for clean energy programs that survived cuts under Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill last year. We will also see the seeds of bigger discussions about how the U.S. might rethink its approach to climate change if Democrats regain the White House, too.

But the bigger story may indeed be the zeitgeist shift that a big Democratic wave would portend. Investigations and congressional testimony will force companies to answer questions in the public sphere that they have largely been able to elide recently. What is the role of clean energy in the power system? How might clean energy affect competitiveness? And how are you approaching risks related to climate change?

In this new environment, incentives change. A utility CEO might emphasize the role of renewables in bringing down costs. A bank might underscore how it’s financing clean energy technologies. And an oil-and-gas CEO might focus on how they’re cutting methane emissions. In general, executives decline to speak on the record about how they are preparing, but in background conversations the story is clear. Companies are lawyering up. Public relations firms are crafting modulated messages to address concerns. And CEOs are reaching out to Democratic members of Congress to plead their case.

text:
Blink Charging is changing its name to Blink Energy, reflecting its expansion into energy management and battery energy storage.

Energy management and battery energy storage are becoming vital parts of the EV charging ecosystem. These technologies help charging site operators avoid utility demand charges and get around limits on available electrical capacity.

Blink operates more than 48,000 networked EV chargers worldwide—a good foundation for offering energy management software and battery storage solutions to both existing customers and new prospects.

EnergyConnect, Blink’s energy management platform, works alongside Blink chargers to balance charging loads in real time, manage peak demand and help sites add chargers within their existing electrical capacity. The platform is currently deployed at 52 Blink-owned DC fast charging sites, including 26 sites using load management to control charging demand. Early utility billing data indicates that energy management is lowering peak demand. At one site, billed peak demand declined 23% within the first month of implementation.

Blink plans to expand EnergyConnect’s availability to its customer base in the US and Europe, and has identified several locations where it plans to deploy battery energy storage.

“EV charging remains at the core of our business, and our charging footprint gives us a strong foundation to address the energy challenges our customers face,” said President and CEO Mike Battaglia. “Customers want to add charging capacity while keeping electricity costs under control. Blink Energy reflects our strategy to bring charging, energy management and battery storage together to meet those needs—and build a broader recurring revenue business in the process.”

name: EPA
title: Wetlands 'created Florida.' A new proposal could threaten their existence.
authors: Clinton Engelberger | Suncoast Searchlight, Clinton Engelberger, Suncoast Searchlight
description:
As much as 86% of wetlands in Florida could lose federal protections under the proposed changes, Tyrna said.
What losing federal protections for wetlands could look like Developing over unprotected wetlands isn’t just about disrupting ecosystems.
In a storm-prone state like Florida, Lewis said it’s another example of wetlands acting as vital infrastructure for communities.
In coastal areas of Florida, wetlands provide nearly $2 million worth of protection from major storms for every square mile, a 2020 Sun and Carson report found.
“Wetlands are what created Florida,” Tyrna said.
text:
As much as 86% of wetlands in Florida could lose federal protections under the proposed changes, Tyrna said.

At issue is a proposal by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to narrow the definition of “waters of the United States,” which determines which wetlands and waterways are covered by the federal Clean Water Act. It follows a 2023 U.S. Supreme Court decision that limited federal protection for wetlands. The agencies are now working to translate the court’s ruling into new policies.

The EPA said the rule is intended to provide a clearer definition of federally protected waters and establish a framework for federal and state authorities to work together. In a statement to Suncoast Searchlight, the agency called a “clear and durable definition” of protected waters a “top priority for the Trump EPA,” and said local authorities are best positioned to understand their water resources.

The EPA and Army Corps have also acknowledged potential environmental trade-offs. In an analysis accompanying the earlier proposal, they said that when affected waters are damaged or developed without measures to avoid, minimize or compensate for the impacts, the result could be “forgone benefits over time, including habitat support, recreation, and aesthetic benefits.”

The agencies have not finalized the rule. A public comment period for the September supplemental proposal closed Oct. 9.

Tyrna said there’s no projected implementation for the proposal and that legal challenges could draw out the process for at least a year.

Loosening federal guardrails doesn’t mean these wetlands immediately become fair game to real estate developers. State and local laws would still apply –– including Florida laws around mangrove trimming and vegetative removal –– and projects can face other local permitting requirements.

But environmental advocates warn that wetlands excluded from federal jurisdiction could have fewer safeguards going forward.

Suncoast staples like Peace River, Wellen Park and Myakka State Park would be impacted by the proposal. Sarasota is especially at risk since most wetlands in the region are isolated, Tyrna said.

“It’s just going to put all of the things that we hold dear about Florida at risk,” Tyrna said.

What losing federal protections for wetlands could look like

Developing over unprotected wetlands isn’t just about disrupting ecosystems.

David Lewis, an associate professor at the University of South Florida specializing in ecology, said wetlands help filter drinking water by removing pollutants from surface waters.

“I’m troubled by how little science often enters into public discourse about policies that would be good for the vast majority of people,” Lewis said. “Regardless of how you feel about environmental advocacy issues in the abstract, everybody needs an adequate supply of clean water.”

Lewis said losing protections for isolated wetlands could hurt water quality because wetlands are often connected underground. They help filter and regulate water that eventually flows into rivers and streams.

“They’re only isolated in the sense that you draw a circle around them on a map and see that they’re not adjacent to a river,” Lewis said. “Isolated is actually a very misleading descriptor because they are connected through groundwater.”

Wetlands also protect against tropical storm and hurricane damage. In a storm-prone state like Florida, Lewis said it’s another example of wetlands acting as vital infrastructure for communities.

In coastal areas of Florida, wetlands provide nearly $2 million worth of protection from major storms for every square mile, a 2020 Sun and Carson report found.

Headwaters, or the small stream where rivers begin, in Manatee County alone save more than $130 million in potential damages from future tropical storms or hurricanes, a 2024 Suncoast Waterkeeper newsletter estimates.

“If you don’t have wetlands, rivers will be raging flash floods after rains, and then tiny dry trickles in between,” Lewis said. “But with wetlands in the landscape around rivers, they’ll absorb a lot of storm water as it’s raining, and then release that slowly during dry periods, which dampens the peaks and troughs in water flow rate in a river.”

Humans aren’t the only ones that rely on wetland resiliency to function.

Some species, including salamanders, wood ducks and muskrats, depend on wetlands to survive.

Developing over these wetlands would put animals and plants that rely on them to complete their life cycle at risk.

Additionally, without these ecosystems thriving, Lewis said Florida’s reputation as a tourist destination could be in jeopardy.

“People come to Florida and spend money here because of the tourism opportunity, and it’s not all to go to theme parks,” he said. “We are a jewel of subtropical biome that you can’t find anywhere else in North America, really north of the border with Mexico.”

Sarasota’s own wetland protections might not be enough

On top of federal and state protections, Sarasota County has local ordinances in place that protect local wetlands.

No development over wetlands or other sensitive natural environments can be carried out without obtaining a permit from the county. The public also has the right to file a complaint against any entity that obtains a permit.

The county ordinance also refers to wetlands as a collective whole, and does not differentiate isolated versus connected ones, like the EPA’s proposal.

Still, Tyrna said she worries that local regulations may not be enough if federal protections are loosened.

“The plan gives too much leeway to mitigation and devalues degraded wetlands,” Tyrna said.

She pointed out that without federal protections, it’s much easier for local governments to alter their own rules.

She noted the recently-approved expansion in Wellen Park to make way for Village One, a community of new homes. The 54-acre project encompasses 28 acres of wetlands, but just two wetlands –– or less than half of what’s there –– are protected, she said.

Tyrna said zero wetlands would have been protected under the new federal regulations.

Developing over land crucial to regulating water quality and cycles would create numerous ecological issues, especially at a time when Sarasota is facing extreme water shortage conditions.

Suncoast Waterkeeper has put out calls to action for people to write letters to the EPA and Army Corps of Engineers urging them not to extend the rule and has submitted comments pushing back to both agencies.

“Wetlands are what created Florida,” Tyrna said. “If you love anything in nature that Florida has to offer, that was brought to you by a wetland. If you like drinking water, swimming water, eating fish, wetlands provide the services that allow you to enjoy that.”

text:
The Trump administration is providing support for nearly half of all coal plants connected to the electric grid, according to a new analysis from environmental advocacy nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund.

That federal support comes in the form of taxpayer-funded payments, exemptions from pollution regulations and mandates for certain plants to continue running past their retirement dates — all actions the Trump administration has taken over the last two years to buoy an industry that has been in decline for more than a decade.

As of this summer, 90 of the country’s 184 grid-connected coal plants have received some kind of federal assistance, the Environmental Defense Fund found. Under the Biden administration, federal support for the industry mostly consisted of tax credits for carbon capture and money to help communities transitioning away from coal.

Since early 2025, the Trump administration has reversed course. Seventy coal plants have been granted Clean Air Act exemptions that allow them to get around the 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards. Hundreds of millions in public dollars — some of which was originally appropriated for carbon-capture programs — are going to 24 plants, including two projects to build new coal-fired units in Alaska and West Virginia. And six plants have been ordered to continue operating past their retirement dates, which the Environmental Defense Fund says has “already added hundreds of millions of dollars to families’ electric bills.”

Trending

The group’s analysis shows just how quickly the Trump administration has moved to support coal — a push that comes as that industry scrambles to stem its downturn. Despite the federal support, coal continues to become a smaller part of the U.S. electric grid.

The administration’s actions are in line with what the coal industry has asked for. Michelle Bloodworth, president and CEO of America’s Power, a trade association representing coal plants, wrote to Energy Secretary Chris Wright in March 2025 suggesting many of the actions the Trump administration eventually announced. She floated using emergency orders to keep coal units operating for longer, asked for economic support for coal-fired generators and said repealing Environmental Protection Agency regulations could help keep plants online.

Bloodworth also suggested using the Defense Production Act to “preserve the coal supply chain.” Roughly a year later, President Donald Trump issued an executive order to that effect.

Wright has framed the administration’s support for coal as a necessary step to keep the grid reliable.

“Forcing reliable, dispatchable coal generation off the grid would compromise energy reliability and needlessly raises energy costs for Americans,” Wright said in a statement in September after issuing emergency orders to keep two coal plants in Indiana online.

Burning coal has gotten more expensive. The Environmental Defense Fund’s analysis found it was 28% more expensive to generate power using coal in 2024 than it was in 2021.

“They are propping up the coal industry precisely because it is not economically competitive,” said Seth Feaster, an energy data analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

Even utilities are skittish about continuing to use coal, he said, as the plants, many of which were built in the 1950s, become increasingly obsolete.

Gas plants are more efficient, take less people to run and can turn on and off faster to balance the needs of the power grid — a key aspect of reliability, especially as renewable energy becomes a bigger part of the mix. Many gas plants can get up and running within an hour, while most coal plants take half a day to boot up.

Renewables, too, are getting cheaper. The Environmental Defense Fund’s analysis found that almost every coal plant in the U.S. was more expensive to run in 2021 than to replace with wind or solar.

Coal plant owners themselves have balked at the idea of keeping old, expiring facilities online. Electric utilities that own a coal-fired unit in Colorado asked the Energy Department to reconsider a mandate to keep the facility open after a mechanical failure.

The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals last month shot down the Trump administration’s effort to force a Michigan coal plant to stay online past retirement, but the administration has continued reissuing orders for other plants.

Several of the coal plants that are being kept online by orders from the Energy Department aren’t actually generating power. But keeping those plants online is still costing power customers money, Feaster said.

“That bill hasn’t come in yet, but it’s going to be very expensive,” he said. Even more so if plants are forced to do major repairs to remain open.

Despite its wide reach, the Trump administration’s efforts to prop up coal plants may not have lasting impact. As 2028 draws closer and the marketplace moves further from coal, Feaster said he anticipates more utilities will request retirement dates for their plants.

“The moment that it looks like those kinds of policies are gone, you will see a whole bunch of coal plants retire officially because they’re not economically competitive,” he said.

text:
As the U.S. expands nuclear power to provide reliable, carbon-free electricity, it still faces a major challenge: managing the radioactive waste left behind by spent reactor fuel.

​To help tackle that problem, U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly on Thursday announced a $5.4 million award to the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station (TEES) to develop reactor fuel technology that could turn long-lived nuclear waste into a new energy source.

​”America’s energy future depends on bold innovation and strong partnerships between the federal government, national laboratories, universities and industry,” Danly said. “This project demonstrates how we can address long-term nuclear waste challenges while advancing technologies that strengthen our nation’s energy security,” he added.

Nuclear waste into fuel

​U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) grant supports the project led by Lin Shao, a professor in the Department of Nuclear Engineering at Texas A&M University. According to the University, Shao is examining the possibility of turning nuclear waste into a fuel using a thorium molten salt reactor under this project.

​Besides investigating methods to address the long-term burden of radioactive nuclear waste, the project would also focus on developing advanced reactor technologies that can provide the reliable energy for future generations, said Shao. Researchers will integrate fuel preparation, experimental testing, computational modeling, and reactor design throughout the project.

More from Energy

See All

​Texas researchers will collaborate with scientists from Savannah River National Laboratory and industry partner Natura Resources under this project.

Waste disposal alternatives

​Meanwhile, other labs across America are looking at alternative nuclear fuel recycling technologies to slash the radioactive waste storage from thousands of years to just hundreds.

​Scientists at the Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) have started building technologies that could recycle used fuel for use in advanced reactors. Researchers are turning to pyroprocessing, a technique that uses high temperatures to physically or chemically change solid materials, to convert used fuel into material that can be reused in advanced nuclear reactors.

​In addition to funding research to recycle nuclear waste into fuel, DOE is also funding studies to find methods to permanently dispose of the radioactive waste left after used nuclear fuel is recycled.

According to a study published by the Department over a month ago, researchers found that deep boreholes could provide a safe and relatively low-cost way to permanently discard the radioactive nuclear waste.

Deep Isolation, a California-based company founded a decade ago, is working toward real-world deployment of underground disposal of spent nuclear fuel and hazardous nuclear waste. In January 2026, the company launched a full-scale, at-depth commercialization pilot in Cameron, Texas, to demonstrate its deep-borehole disposal system.

​Underground disposal of nuclear waste is also being pursued by other countries, including Finland, Sweden, and France. However, the technology used by these countries are different from the American deep-borehole technology. The former approach builds geological repositories by blasting and digging massive underground tunnels, shafts, and caverns.

​Located in Eurajoki, Finland, the facility is the world’s first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel. Built at a depth of more than 400 meters (1,312 feet) deep into 1.9-billion-year-old crystalline bedrock, it will encapsulate and permanently dispose of nuclear waste for over 100,000 years, placed inside disposal canisters designed to keep radioactive spent fuel completely isolated.

text:
Before breaking for October recess, Congress held a total of 14 environmental, energy, and climate-related hearings. The House of Representatives held 12 of these hearings across six different standing committees, while the Senate held two across two standing committees. Hearings covered issues ranging from domestic produce and natural gas bans to securing critical resources and supply chains.

Wildlife and conservation—highly bipartisan topics on the Hill—were the focus of four hearings, three under the House Committee on Natural Resources and one in the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. One House hearing, Recognizing American Historical Sites and Promoting Proper Land Management, discussed bills on the threat of mountain pine beetle infestations (H.R.9999) and the protection of wild horse populations (S.1377). The Examining Water Rights and Habitat Management Policies hearing saw wildlife bills on manatee protections (H.R.9590), invasive mussel species (H.R.3717), and reassessing protections for alligators (H.R.10117). Another Senate hearing on pending legislation focused on the conservation of aquatic ecosystems (S.5402), giant sequoias (S.4103/H.R.2709), and hot springs (S.5101).

Nuclear energy, another area of bipartisan agreement, was the second-most discussed topic in September, with two hearings on nuclear waste and one on nuclear reactors. One Senate Environment and Public Works Committee hearing examined U.S. nuclear waste management policy and proposals to update disposal technology. The House Energy and Commerce Committee examined nuclear spent fuel policy and the potential of proposed nuclear lifestyle innovation campuses to reduce waste. In a separate hearing, the Energy Subcommittee under the House Committee on Energy and Commerce discussed the nuclear energy renaissance, highlighting the importance of nuclear reactors and Department of Energy programs that support these technologies. Subcommittee Chair Randy Weber noted that these reactors could support growing U.S. energy demand, including energy demand from data centers.

As the United States begins to experience the impacts of the 2026-2027 Super El Niño, disaster preparation has continued to garner interest on the Hill. Accordingly, the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology held a hearing, Innovation in Disaster Prevention: Advancing Technology for Prediction and Response, to assess the use of AI, autonomous systems, and advanced sensing to detect natural disasters.

To keep up with these hearings, get EESI’s weekly Environmental and Energy Congressional Round-Up by subscribing to our biweekly newsletter, Climate Change Solutions.
