Detroit taxpayers will likely bear the burden of millions of dollars in fixes related to testing and replacement of contaminated backfill at hundreds of demolition sites across the city.

Detroit’s top attorney said Friday that the contractor responsible for the “dirty dirt” is unlikely to have the resources to cover the costs and, absent state or federal grants, the bill for remediation will most likely fall on Detroiters.

“Unfortunately, what we have is a cost burden to the citizens that they should not have to bear, directly related to what we believe to be at least significant contractual violations if not criminal behavior that has resulted in all of these costs,” Corporation Counsel Conrad Mallett told BridgeDetroit following a special session of the Detroit City Council.

The city has grappled with a $20 million-plus price tag to address 655 questionable sites stemming from the work of the now-defunct contracting firm Gayanga Co., which is now the subject of city, state and federal investigations, as well as a site in Milford that provided the contaminated backfill dirt.

Mallett’s Friday statements come after the Law Department previously signaled that Detroit would pursue a cost recovery action against Gayanga for total damages, which Tim Palazzolo, director of the city’s Demolition & Construction Department, told BridgeDetroit Friday is “pushing the $20 million mark.”

Detroit-based Gayanga Co. and its owner, Brian McKinney, have been accused by the city of using contaminated dirt to backfill demolition sites. The company and McKinney have been the focus of federal, state and city investigations.

Mallett said Friday that investigations being conducted by the state’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) and the Detroit FBI office are ongoing. The city’s Office of the Inspector General suspended Gayanga and McKinney last fall from doing work in Detroit based on the contaminated dirt findings. Gayanga had been awarded tens of millions in city demolition contracts since 2018.

McKinney announced in May that Gayanga was shutting down and filing a defamation lawsuit against the city, noting the court action, “arises from false and materially misleading public statements.” On Friday, Mallett said that McKinney had not yet been served with legal action from the city.

Detroit City Council President James Tate, who convened the Friday meeting, asked Mallett whether Detroit could recover testing and remediation costs from Gayanga.

“I don’t have good news,” Mallett told council members. “I think that the Gayanga organization, if not bankrupt, soon will be. Therefore, our ability to collect for what we think is, in fact, bad acts will be difficult.”

Additionally, the city’s environmental insurance company “is resisting, forcefully, responsibility for this particular program.”

Steps can be taken by the city for future contract language, Mallett said. At this time, Detroit will continue to focus on the insurance company for recovery. Iron Horse, the Milford site that supplied much of the contaminated fill dirt, Mallett noted, did not have a contract with Detroit when the material was provided. Rather, it was an approved site for dirt based on a consultant.

Mallet said Friday that he wanted to assure the council that, thus far, the contamination concerns appear to be isolated.

“There has been no evidence that we have discovered ourselves that would suggest that this was a systemic problem that extended beyond Gayanga,” he said.

Detroit officials said Friday that the city expects costs of around $12 million to remediate the remaining demolition sites with contaminated dirt.

Palazzolo said that the majority of the sites identified – 533 overall – are owned by the Detroit Land Bank Authority. Of the publicly-owned sites tested, 500 have not met safety standards.

As of Friday, 380 haven’t yet been excavated – and 195 sites present an “elevated risk,” Palazzolo said.

“The nature of contamination (for the 195 parcels) is such that it could evaporate and rise up through the soil and potentially get into adjacent structures and cause unsafe air over time to those areas,” Palazzolo said Friday. “Those are properties with the biggest concern. Those are the properties we need to remediate first.”

Palazzolo pegged that fix at around $6.7 million. The estimated replacement cost per property is $34,554, he said. The city has divided the remaining work into three priority tiers. The first two are slated for completion by 2029 based upon the time it will take for contracting, approvals and seasonal limitations, Palazzolo told BridgeDetroit.

A dedicated cost center was established within the Construction & Demolition Department’s budget for the remediation work via blight funding. Palazzolo said Friday that $8.4 million remains from the original $15 million set aside in late 2025 to address the site testing and remediation.

“One of the things I want to make clear is that this fund of money is not used for any other purpose,” said Palazzolo, adding within the department’s current fiscal budget there’s separate dollars for emergency demolition and stabilization work.

Council Member Angela Whitfield-Calloway argued Friday to Detroit’s Chief Public Health Officer Ali Abazeed that the city should declare a public health emergency over the contamination.

“This is, to the public health director, a public health emergency. It may not be in your opinion, but it really is and should be declared as so,” said Whitfield-Calloway, noting that the temporary orange fencing around the sites “is not containing the dirt.”

“It’s still seeping out into the air. There are air particles that, if there’s a wind, the dirt is flying everywhere. It’s traveling everywhere. I don’t know how far it’s getting on people’s properties, cars. Kids are walking through it, adults are walking through. It’s landing on the sidewalk. It’s not contained.”

Abazeed, who joined the department this spring, said he can’t speak to how things were handled before he arrived. But under Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield, health officials are closely scrutinizing the potential health impacts, he said.

The department, he said, is taking the issue “seriously and urgently,” but stressed to council members that “contamination does not always equal exposure.”

Council Member Denzel McCampbell said he wants assurances that the city won’t encounter similar issues in the future with soil supply sites and contractors.

Mallett acknowledged Friday that there were past “hiccups” in the city’s contracting process, and some contractors did not have adequate documentation in place before contracts were authorized. But those “have been corrected” and they “won’t happen again,” he said. The city, he said, is also exploring whether it can secure its own fill dirt in the future.

Although the great majority of sites being reviewed for contamination are publicly owned, the city is also contending with 120 privately owned parcels.

The city reached out to those property owners earlier this year, seeking permission to test those sites. Fifty of those owners have approved the request, seven others have denied the city’s request, and Detroit did not get responses from 63 others. If the city doesn’t hear from those remaining property owners by spring, the city will pursue an administrative warrant.

“What I want to assure the public is, if there are public health implications in which we are consulting with the health department about, we will move more quickly than the springtime that I talked about,” Mallett added after the meeting.

As another measure toward process improvements, Palazzolo reiterated Friday, is that the demolition department now sources its backfill materials from just seven public pits with native gravel and soil from longstanding operations – down from 14 source sites previously. Two of the sites are located in Milford, and the others are in Pinckney, Washington Township, Petersburg, Milan and Maybee. The sites are inspected monthly by the demolition department and its environmental consultants. The soil is also sampled and analyzed before it leaves the source sites.

Earlier this year, the council approved a $3.5 million contract increase with Mannik and Smith Group, environmental consultants conducting due diligence related to the dirt issues. Originally, a $1 million contract was approved with Mannik and Smith for general environmental consulting services. The $3.5 million amendment was to cover costs associated with backfill testing.

For more information about locations and progress on testing and excavation, visit this webpage on the testing, removal and replacement process and an FAQ. Questions can be directed to demo-info@detroitmi.gov or (313) 224-4737.

BridgeDetroit reporter Jasmine Snow contributed to this report.

text:
Renewable energy will account for nearly three-fourths of new generation built under Xcel Energy’s five-year, $70 billion capital plan that the company unveiled Thursday during its third-quarter earnings call.

The new plan — up 17% from its previous $60 billion spending plan — calls for building 9.2 GW of renewable generation, 2.3 GW of energy storage and 3.3 GW of natural gas generation. Xcel expects the renewable portion of the buildout would cost about $21.7 billion. The plan also includes 2,400 miles of new transmission and $4 billion for wildfire mitigation.

“These investments are critical to serve growing electric demand, to keep customer bills low, to deliver clean energy, and to ensure system safety and reliability,” Chairman, President and CEO Bob Frenzel said, later adding that Xcel “continue[s] to lead a clean energy transition” and believes its commitment to clean energy will attract additional data centers to its service territory.

About $7 billion of the capital plan will go to data center projects already under contract at Xcel. Xcel could spend an additional $10 billion for projects not included in its spending plan, according to Frenzel. That spending would cover the more than 15 GW that is included in pending utility requests for proposals, high-voltage transmission projects and infrastructure needed to serve the 4 GW of new data centers the company expects to contract before the end of next year, he said.

“As we think about future data center growth, our contracting principles are based on our longstanding commitment to ensure that the needs of our customers and our communities are met,” Frenzel said. “We believe in responsible development. We believe that existing customers should not subsidize new large loads.”

To finance the updated capital plan, Xcel will take on $26 billion in debt and issue $8 billion in equity, about 40% of which is already contracted, CFO Brian Van Abel said. The company also agreed earlier this month to sell gas and electric assets in Michigan — including 9,000 electric customers and 6,000 gas customers — valued at $150 million to Upper Peninsula Power Co. and SEMCO ENERGY Gas Co. Van Abel said the sale should close by the end of 2027 and that the price was confidential.

Xcel’s net income jumped 83% to $960 million in the third quarter, up from $524 million a year ago, the company said. Favorable weather, increasing electric sales and this year’s “heavy rate case calendar” all helped Xcel increase its third-quarter earnings, Van Abel said.

A July order by the Minnesota Public Utilities Commission approved a 2.9% annual rate increase expected to generate $211 million over two years. Xcel filed a rate stability plan in Minnesota on Oct. 9 that would freeze rates at this level in 2027 and 2028, as an alternative to the rate case it is due to file in 2027. In Colorado, a September decision by the CPUC approved a 1.7% annual rate that will bring in $184 million. The company expects a final decision on a rate case in New Mexico by the end of this year.

name: EPA
title: EPA Proposes Broader Rollback of Methane Waste Safeguards
description:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing another round of changes to its 2024 rule establishing requirements to reduce methane emissions from oil and gas operations.
When operators waste gas produced from publicly owned resources, federal, state and tribal governments can lose potential royalty revenue.
Eliminating the Super Emitter Program EPA proposes eliminating the Super Emitter Program, which addresses methane releases of at least 100 kilograms, or about 220 pounds, per hour.
Other emissions requirements could still apply to a release, but this specific mechanism for requiring an investigation would disappear.
Allowing more reliance on flaring EPA proposes changing the regulatory approach to associated gas, the natural gas produced alongside oil—sometimes unintentionally.
text:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing another round of changes to its 2024 rule establishing requirements to reduce methane emissions from oil and gas operations. After delaying implementation and loosening some requirements, the agency now proposes eliminating its Super Emitter Program for investigating large methane releases, reducing safeguards at certain wells, and allowing more gas to be burned rather than captured.

EPA presents these changes as a way to lower costs for operators. But they would weaken safeguards intended to prevent natural gas from being wasted through leaks, deliberate releases, and flaring. EPA’s own analysis projects more pollution under either of its two proposed approaches. Compared with a baseline that incorporates the 2024 rule, the agency estimates an additional 60 million short tons of methane emissions between 2027 and 2050 under its approach for low-producing wells. Its alternative approach for conventional wells would add an estimated 88 million short tons over the same period.

For taxpayers, the concern extends beyond emissions. Natural gas is a valuable resource. When operators waste gas produced from publicly owned resources, federal, state and tribal governments can lose potential royalty revenue. Weaker monitoring and response requirements also raise questions about how much waste will be detected and addressed.

Moving beyond delays to weaker requirements

EPA’s 2024 rule required oil and gas operators to find and repair leaks, restricted routine flaring, and established a process for investigating unusually large methane releases. It set standards for new and modified facilities and directed states to develop plans for existing facilities.

The agency has already delayed implementation of several requirements. In April 2026, it also extended the time operators could temporarily flare gas during certain interruptions and loosened monitoring requirements for flares and other combustion devices.

This proposal would make broader changes to the safeguards themselves. It would eliminate the Super Emitter Program, reduce monitoring and equipment requirements for certain well sites, and allow greater reliance on burning gas instead of capturing it for sale.

Eliminating the Super Emitter Program

EPA proposes eliminating the Super Emitter Program, which addresses methane releases of at least 100 kilograms, or about 220 pounds, per hour. The program created a process for approved outside organizations to report large releases detected through technologies such as satellites and aircraft. EPA reviews those reports before notifying the relevant operator. That notification triggers requirements for the operator to investigate and report its findings.

The proposal would remove that process, including the approval of outside monitoring organizations and technologies and the requirement for operators to respond to program notifications. Other emissions requirements could still apply to a release, but this specific mechanism for requiring an investigation would disappear.

In its latest proposal, EPA questions whether the evidence supporting the program adequately establishes how often these events occur, how long they last and what causes them. It also argues that other emissions requirements make the program less useful. The agency cites difficulties identifying responsible operators, limited participation by outside organizations and concerns about its legal authority. TCS is skeptical but will more thoroughly assess these claims as we prepare comments on the proposed rule.

Reducing requirements for low-producing or conventional wells

EPA is proposing a loophole that would allow operators of certain wells to operate under reduced requirements – the only question is who will qualify. EPA is considering two alternatives:

Marginal Wells: The first is based on production. “Marginal” wells produce no more than 15 barrels of oil equivalent per day, averaged over the previous year. Oil equivalent is a way to express oil and natural gas production in a common unit. To qualify as a marginal well site, all wells at the location would have to be marginal, and their combined production could not exceed that same daily threshold.

Conventional Wells: Broadly, this means a site where all wells draw from deposits that do not require intensive techniques, such as multistage fracking, to produce oil or gas. The conventional-well alternative could apply to sites producing more than the marginal-well threshold.

Under either approach, operators at qualifying sites would still have to inspect every three months using sound, sight, and smell to identify leaks or malfunctioning equipment. For leaks found through those inspections, operators generally would have to attempt a repair within 15 days and complete it within another 15 days, although exceptions could allow delays. The proposal would also allow certain equipment that uses and releases natural gas to remain in service.

Allowing more reliance on flaring

EPA proposes changing the regulatory approach to associated gas, the natural gas produced alongside oil—sometimes unintentionally. Under current rules, EPA rules favor capturing associated gas and delivering it to a sales pipeline, bringing more domestic energy to our homes and businesses. Now, EPA is proposing to favor burning it in a flare or another device that reduces emissions by at least 95 percent. This would make flaring a broader option for meeting the standards.

EPA argues that operators cannot always control access to pipelines and other infrastructure needed to bring gas to market. It says the 2024 rule assumed that infrastructure would become available in time, and that those assumptions have not been borne out. Connecting wells to pipelines can require agreements with other companies, permits and substantial investment.

What EPA counts as savings

EPA estimates that the proposed changes would save operators approximately $2.5 billion a year in compliance costs under the marginal-well approach and approximately $2.3 billion under the conventional-well alternative. These annualized estimates cover 2027 through 2050, are expressed in 2024 dollars, and account for changes in the value of gas recovered. EPA also projects changes in energy production and prices.

EPA projects more methane and other air pollution under either approach. Those estimates do not cover all the proposed changes, including elimination of the Super Emitter Program.

EPA is counting the savings for operators, but taxpayers deserve a full accounting of what more wasted gas and less oversight would cost them.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy announced that Alliant Energy could get a $5.1 billion loan to invest in new natural gas plants, gas pipelines or battery storage systems across Iowa and Wisconsin.

“The investments will add more than 2.6 gigawatts of new or upgraded power generation capacity and deliver up to $1.2 billion in electricity cost savings for American families and businesses across both states,” Alliant spokesperson Taylor Adams wrote in an email.

Alliant estimates most of those savings — roughly $800 million — would be for Iowans.

Adams said the loan could help projects like the Bobcat Energy Center, a new 720-megawatt natural gas plant in Marshalltown, and the Lansing Battery Energy Storage System, a lithium-ion battery storage system at the decommissioned Lansing Generating Station site. Additional projects could be included, too.

“Examples include new natural gas generation, Advanced Gas Path projects, gas pipelines and battery energy storage systems,” Adams wrote.

Meanwhile, Linn County is trying to stop plans for an Alliant natural gas plant near Cedar Rapids.

The federal loan announcement came the same day Linn County supervisors sent a request to the Iowa Utilities Commission to deny a generating certificate for Alliant’s proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center.

Linn County supervisors had previously unanimously denied the rezoning request that would have allowed for the 720-megawatt natural gas plant. Supervisors said they're concerned for ratepayers, worried about air quality and convinced the plant doesn’t fit the county’s comprehensive plan.

“With prevailing winds carrying emissions towards Cedar Rapids, we must consider the potential consequences for public health,” said Supervisors Chair Kirsten Running-Marquardt. “This is not a fair balance between economic development and the well-being of our community, especially when Alliant already has some of the highest utility rates in the area, and our county faces some serious concerns about asthma and cancer rates.”

Supervisor Sami Scheetz voted against the rezoning, but said he had trouble making a decision.

“This could become a state project controlled by the Iowa Utilities Commission, and not Linn County,” he said. “The county could lose the ability to enforce its own natural gas ordinance, the strictest ordinance in Iowa.”

Alliant Energy said the plant is critical to meet growing energy demand. Linn County said Alliant didn’t meet the threshold to prove that. But if the state utilities commission agrees with Alliant, it could override the county’s decision.

The Iowa Utilities Commission is set to hear the proposal on Dec. 7.

text:
The clean energy transition has created an environment where companies recognize the benefits of collaborating instead of pursuing projects individually. Partnerships allow various companies and departments to share the responsibility and the finances that are involved in the energy project, especially if the entities are able to complement each other effectively. Ultimately, this increased sense of togetherness has been essential to the ability of companies to take massive strides toward reaching their clean energy targets. On that note, X-energy, Amazon and AEP push ahead with plans for a 960 MW nuclear project in Indiana, putting nearly a gigawatt of advanced reactor capacity on the table.

Assessing the overall importance of X-energy in advancing the nuclear sector

X-energy is a leading designer of advanced small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) and fuel technology developed to establish a new standard in clean, safe, reliable energy. The company’s intrinsically safe Xe-100 high-temperature gas-cooled reactor and TRISO-X particle fuel expand applications for nuclear technology, with commercial projects across grid, industrial, and AI.

The energy company has played an integral role in advancing the U.S. nuclear sector over the years, and industry experts believe that it will not be slowing in the coming years despite the tremendous amount of success that it has achieved. Nuclear energy continues to be a pivotal part of the U.S. energy and security sector.

Together, X-energy’s technology drives enhanced safety, lower cost, faster construction timelines, and scalable deployment when compared with other SMRs and conventional nuclear.

X-energy, Amazon and AEP push ahead with plans for a 960 MW nuclear project in Indiana

A press release from X-energy revealed that the company has entered into a Joint Development Agreement to advance feasibility work for a proposed 960 MW Xe-100 small modular reactor project in Indiana. This is a massive announcement that shows the amount of revenue that companies stand to generate from the energy industry.

In the joint agreement, Amazon.com, Inc. is expected to provide certain project development funding for the effort, marking the second commercial deployment under X-energy and Amazon’s partnership that is aimed at bringing more than 5 GW of new nuclear capacity to the U.S. grid by 2039.

X-energy and AEP are expected to evaluate the development of a 12-unit Xe-100 plant near the former site of the retired Breed Generating Station in Sullivan County, Indiana. The proposed project would redevelop the AEP-owned brownfield site for advanced nuclear power, adding clean baseload capacity to help meet growing demand for safe, reliable energy across Indiana and the region.

What does the project signify for X-energy as it seeks to finish the year strongly?

Building on Amazon’s investment in, and ongoing collaboration with X-energy, the project is intended to be a second grid-scale partnership to support grid reliability with new clean generating capacity, joining Energy Northwest’s Cascade Advanced Energy Facility in Washington State.

While a huge focus for the U.S. has been on diversifying the energy portfolio of every state, there are still places that are seen as the hub for the generation of certain energy sources. For instance, Indiana has made advanced nuclear energy a central part of its energy strategy as part of the state’s all-of-the-above approach to affordable, reliable power.

The anticipated transformation of the nuclear sector expected in 2027

X-energy’s Xe-100 is an 80 MWe high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, using helium as a coolant, and powered by Tri-structural, Isotropic (TRISO) fuel, described by the U.S. Department of Energy as the most robust nuclear energy fuel on earth because of its ability to handle extreme temperatures without melting.

Collaborations on their own are not enough to guarantee the completion of a project because companies must still be able to complement each other effectively instead of just relying on the past success that they have enjoyed.
